2
CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES
OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
IV. HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES
Utilization of Plan Allocation for North-Eastern States
Recommendation/Observation
1.1 The Committee is not aware of any follow-up action taken so far on the measures
suggested in the mid-term appraisal of the 11th Plan. The Committee, therefore, recommends to
the Department that all possible efforts and follow-up action should be taken to take care of the
above suggestions. (Para 2.23)
Action Taken
1. Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Development of AYUSH Hospitals and Dispensaries
provides financial assistance in ratio of 90:10 Shares for NE States and other hilly States (Himachal
Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Jammu and Kashmir). As regards the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for
Development of AYUSH Institution and National Mission on Medicinal Plants are 100% funded by
Central Government for all States.
2. The guidelines for the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Development of AYUSH Hospitals
and Dispensaries stipulate that the Empowered Programme Committee (EPC) and Mission Steering
Group (MSG) chaired by the Secretary, Health and FW and HFM respectively, set up under NRHM
will consider and approve changes, as deemed necessary, in this scheme. The enhancement of Unit
cost of construction in NE States would be taken up with EPC/MSG.
3. The existing guidelines for CSS for upgradation of AYUSH Institutions provide for one time
assistance on 50:50 matching share basis upto Rs. 10 crore for opening of new AYUSH Institutions/
Universities in the States not having such Institutions. Under the scheme an amount of Rs. 8 crore
was released as 1st installment to Tripura Sundari Ayurveda Medical College at Udaipur, Tripura
South during 2010-11. With regard to the special assistance on 100% basis, for setting up of at
least one AYUSH college along with teaching hospital in each of NE State would be taken up with
EPC after approval of 12th Five Year Plan.
4. The matter regarding reservation of seats in MD (Homoeo) for NE States students and
increase number of seats at BAMS level would be taken up with the concerned State Government/
Colleges.
Recommendation/Observation
1.2 The Committee notes that the Eleventh Plan has concluded; however, the 12th Plan outlay
of the Department is yet to be approved. The Committee feels that the delay in approval of the
12th Plan outlay is sure to impinge on the process of EFC/CCEA approvals which entails further
delay in finalization and implementation of the Schemes/Programmes of the Department for the 12th
2

3
Plan. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Government to hasten the approval of 12th
Plan outlay and related proposals so that the Department is not hamstrung by lack of necessary
approvals and the consequent delay in finalization and implementation of various schemes/
programmes in the 12th Plan period. The Committee desires to be apprised of the reasons for delay
in approval of the 12th Plan outlay of the Department. (Para 2.25)
Action Taken
12th Plan Outlay is yet to be approved by the National Development Council However, to
minimize delay in implementation of schemes the Department as a prelude to the 12th Plan is in
the process of appraisal of schemes by appointing evaluating agency. Moreover, the Department has
made comprehensive proposal for 12th Five Year Plan and geared up to implement it meticulously
after the approval is granted.
IV. HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES
CGHS Expansion in Dispensaries
Recommendation/Observation
1.3 The Committee is constrained to note the policy paralysis in regard to opening of AYUSH
dispensaries under the CGHS. On the one hand the DGHS had sent proposal for opening 13 new
AYUSH CGHS units and on the other, the Department of Health and Family Welfare was not
allowing any expansion of infrastructure of the CGHS in the name of introduction of a Health
Insurance Scheme for the Central Government Employees and Pensioners. While taking a serious
view in the matter, the Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation made in its 49th Report
presented to Parliament on the 4th March, 2011 which is reproduced below:
“It is very strange that though the Mid-term assessment of Eleventh Plan had emphasized
to provide AYUSH facilities in 10 CGHS dispensaries by 2011-12, the Ministry of Health and
Family Welfare has decided to halt any further expansion of infrastructure in CGHS on the
ground that a Health Insurance Scheme is being contemplated for Central Government
Employees. At a time when the avowed objective of the Government is to bridge the gaps
in health infrastructure and human resources, the Committee is at a loss to understand as
to why such a retrograde decision has been taken, especially in view of the dismal picture
of health infrastructure in the country. The Committee is of the view that even if the CGHS
is restructured, Health infrastructure created under it would not go waste, but contributes
to outreach of health care services in one way or the other. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Ministry should shed its indecisiveness in the matter and take concrete
action towards extending AYUSH facilities in CGHS dispensaries as per the Mid-term
Appraisal of the Eleventh Plan.” (Para 4.8)
Action Taken
CGHS scheme is implemented by the Department of Health and Family Welfare and all
policy decision regarding expansion and budgetary support are taken by them. They have informed
that the current administrative set up of CGHS is basically allopathic system oriented and to expand
AYUSH in CGHS, it would require creation of a proper administrative set up to deal the matters
related to AYUSH in a more effective manner. The Department of Health and Family Welfare/CGHS
has taken up the matter afresh and a more comprehensive proposal with detailed financial
implications and other logistic requirements is being worked out to expand AYUSH units in other
CGHS locations.

4
The Department of AYUSH is regularly funding some AYUSH CGHS Dispensaries from its
own budget provision. In the 11th Five Year Plan, funds to the extent of Rs. 2.85 crore
(provisional) has been released for supporting one Ayurvedic dispensary in Trivendrum, one
Homoeopathic dispensary each in Trivendrum and Guwahati, one Unani dispensary in Delhi, one
Siddha dispensary in Chennai and one yoga centre in Delhi.
National Medicinal Plants Board (NMPB)
Recommendation/Observation
1.4 From the information furnished by the Department, the Committee notes that presently, only
seven States, namely, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra and
Tamil Nadu have full-fledged State Medicinal Plants Boards for proper implementation and
monitoring of the Schemes and Programmes of NMPB and twenty seven SMPBs are registered as
societies. The Committee would like to be apprised of the specific steps taken by the Department
to encourage the other States to set up full-fledged SMPBs. (Para 7.24)
Action Taken
Presently, only Seven States, namely, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Karnataka,
Kerala, Maharashtra and Rajasthan have full-fledged State Medicinal Plants Boards (SMPB) for
proper implementation and monitoring of the Schemes and Programmes of NMPB and twenty nine
SMPBs are registered as societies. The remaining States have been requested to set up full-fledged
SMPBs.
VIII. QUALITY CONTROL OF ASU&H DRUGS
Recommendation/Observation
1.5 The Committee observes that the quality and standardization of ASU&H products and
stringent implementation of the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act are very vital for the
credibility of ASU&H drugs. However, the drug testing requirements of ASU&H drugs cannot be
met without setting up adequate number of quality control laboratories and strengthening of the
enforcement mechanisms of the States. The Committee also observes that the existing Drug Quality
Control Scheme suffers from certain inherent inadequacies due to which the off-take under the
Scheme in the Eleventh Plan has been very poor. The Eleventh Plan started in 2007 and has
completed in March, 2012. The Department should have sorted out the constraints with needful
modifications much before. The Committee expects that the Department would, at least from this
year onwards, act with greater promptness and iron out the hindrances in the implementation of
the Scheme with a sense of urgency. (Para 8.5)
Action Taken
During the 11th Five Year Plan, thrust was given to accelerate the work of standardization
and quality control of drugs. In this direction, Pharmacopoeia Commission of Indian Medicine
(PCIM) has been set up to provide overarching umbrella organization to the Ayurveda, Siddha and
Unani Pharmacopoeia Committees for augmenting the pace of developing standards of drugs. Apart
from the strengthening of Pharmacopoeial Laboratory of Indian Medicine (PLIM) and Homoeopathy
Pharmacopoeia Laboratory, which are the central appellate laboratories for pharmacopoeial work
and testing of ASU&Homoeopathic drug respectively, the Department has supported 29 State Drug
Testing Laboratories to enhance their infrastructural and functional capacity. State Licensing
Authorities have been supported to improve the enforcement mechanism and testing of drug

5
samples. In order to increase the base of drug testing facilities in the country, a regulatory
provision was made in the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules for recognition of private laboratories. With
this provision as many as 47 laboratories have been approved for testing of ASU&H drugs and the
number is likely to increase with recognition of more and more laboratories as the demand and
regulatory needs for testing of drugs have raised a lot with amendment of legal provisions.
Through the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Quality Control of ASU&H drugs, the
Department has assisted 29 State Drug Testing Laboratories, 46 State Pharmacies, 30 State Drug
Licensing Authorities for improving enforcement mechanism, 29 Drug Licensing Authorities for
testing of drug samples and 63 GMP compliant private manufacturing units for improving the
inhouse infrastructure of quality testing of drugs. It is envisaged to revise the scheme suitably in
the 12th Five Year Plan by broad-based consultative process with stakeholders for larger benefit
of the potential takers in accordance with the emerging needs of quality production and testing of
ASU&H medicines. Department has taken cognizance of the constraints that hindered the effective
implantation of the scheme in 11th Plan and would strive to iron out the hindrances in the
implementation of the scheme with a sense of urgency.
XIII. INFORMATION, EDUCATION AND COMMUNICATION (IEC)
Recommendation/Observation
1.6 The Committee observes that the enforcement of provisions of Drugs and Magic Remedies
(Objectionable Advertisement) DMR (OA) Act leaves much to be desired. The Committee is
therefore of the view that the effectiveness of the said Act needs to be looked into closely. The
Committee also observes that the Department should not feel satisfied by merely issuing directions
to the State Governments and instead acquaint itself with the progress made towards
implementation of the directions so issued. The Committee also notes that regulation of content of
ads aired over the electronic and published in the print media falls within the exclusive domain of
Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and the Department of AYUSH and the concerned State
Governments should also approach that Ministry for containing such misleading ads. The
Committee would, therefore, advise the Department to bring instances of misleading advertisements
concerning AYUSH over TV and Radio and in print media to the notice of Ministry of Information
and Broadcasting for necessary remedial action. (Para 13.5)
Action Taken
The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisement) Act 1954 is implementable by
the State Governments and the Department of AYUSH has been directing State Licensing Authorities
to take action against the defaulters. The efforts for checking the impact of misleading
advertisements about AYUSH drugs have been reinforced with IEC and public awareness activities
through AROGYA Health Melas, National Campaigns, short films, video-clips, advertisements on TV ,
newspapers, and other print media about the safety and efficacy of medicines. The Department of
AYUSH will follow the advice of the Parliamentary Standing Committee to take up the matter of
objectionable advertisements with Ministry of Information and Broadcasting for imposing
appropriate remedial measures.
Recommendation/Observation
1.7 The Committee was given to understand that a considerable number of AYUSH practitioners
are making tall claims of very effective cure and treatment of various ailments, viral/bacterial/fungal
infections, AIDS, cancer, Hepatitis etc. The Committee recommends that instead of ignoring such
claims, the Department should make all out efforts to verify these claims and find out whether

6
there is any substance therein. In case any of these claims are found to be true, the Department
should initiate further research thereon and assist such claimants in developing their line of
treatment in public interest. (Para 13.6)
Action Taken
The claims and such references received in the Department of AYUSH about the efficacy
of AYUSH remedies are referred to Research Councils for verification and appropriate scientific
studies. Further, extramural research activities and revitalization and validation of local health
traditions and midwifery practices are being supported.

7
7
CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES
NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT REPLIES
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation
2.1 The Committee observes that long pending UCs and unspent balances are not something
new. The Committee can also well-understand the limitations of the Department in getting the
liquidation of pending UCs and unspent balances expedited by the State Governments. However, the
Department could have anticipated these problems and accordingly made realistic projection for
requirement of funds. Thus it is obvious that there are shortcomings in the budgetary planning of
the Department and that the shortfall in utilization of the budgeted funds could have been avoided
and the unspent amount utilized more gainfully somewhere else had the Department assessed
requirement of funds properly for the purpose of making Budgetary Estimates as realistic as
possible. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Department to ensure that the entire
requirement of funds is assessed realistically so that the quantum of unutilized funds is minimized
in future. The Committee also appreciates the efforts made by the Department as it could convince
the Planning Commission for allocating Rs. 990 crores i.e. 10% more than BE 2011-12 and 52.31%
more than RE 2011-12 in spite of the fact that only Rs. 610 crores could be spent during the
previous year. (Para 2.7)
Action Taken
The Department undertakes budgetary planning meticulously. The issue of pending UCs got
aggravated due to change of stand by Ministry of Finance and States not coming forward to
provide requisite UCs along with supporting documents. To ensure that the entire requirement of
fund is assessed realistically so that the quantum of un-utilized funds is minimized in future, the
Department has been reviewing comprehensively and adopting appropriate strategy w.r.t. the
expenditure profile of each major schemes/programmes at regular intervals and apply the result of
such analysis at the time of budget estimates and revised estimate.
Recommendation/Observation
2.2 The Committee is happy to note that the Department has put in place a system of closer
monitoring of utilization of the budgeted funds. The Committee would like to be apprised of the
efficacy of this scheme in ensuring better financial performance. (Para 2.9)
Action Taken
As the system of closer monitoring has been put in place recently, the Committee will be
apprised of its efficacy after some time.

8
Recommendation/Observation
2.3 The Committee is aware of the fact that health needs of a vast and diverse country like
India cannot be met by a single healthcare system of medicine and AYUSH healthcare systems have
a very vital role in expanding the outreach of health care to the people because of their inherent

VIII. QUALITY CONTROL OF ASU&H DRUGS
Recommendation/Observation
2.19 Since the Committee does not have detailed information concerning Central Drug Controller
for ASU drugs, it would not give any value judgement. However, the Committee would like the
Department to furnish a detailed Status Note in the matter so as to enable it to examine the entire
spectrum of issues involved and make an observation accordingly. (Para 8.7)
Action Taken
The Ayurveda Siddha Unani (ASU) Drugs Consultative Committee (ASUDCC), which
consists of State ASU Drug Licensing Authorities and chaired by Drug Controller General (India),
in its meeting held on 17th June, 2010, had recommended that a separate Central Drug Controller
for ASU Drugs may be created. Similar recommendation was made by the Mashelkar Committee
for strengthening the drug control infrastructure for AYUSH at the central and State levels by
appointing separate Drug Controllers / Drug Inspectors for speedy enforcement of the provisions
of Drugs & Cosmetics Act. The ASUDCC also specifically recommended the strengthening of drug
testing facilities in the State Laboratories. The Government accepted the Mashelkar Committee
report and thereafter in 2005 Department of Health mo ved a Bill in Rajya Sabha for amendments
in Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 to inter alia  set up Central Drug Authority inclusive of dedicated
regulatory structure for AYUSH drugs. The Bill however was referred to the Parliamentary Standing
Committee, who in turn after listening to various stakeholders and Government Departments,
recommended for broad-based strengthening of the regulatory mechanism with comprehensive
infrastructure and structures. The Ministry accordingly could not materialize the proposal of setting
up Central Drug Authority, but the Drug Controller General (India) for allopathic drugs was
strengthened by sanctioning 175 posts and renamed as ‘Central Drug Standards Control
Organisation’ (CDSCO). However no posts were sanctioned for the regulation of drugs of Indian
Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy. Similarly, the State Drug Testing Laboratories funded by
Department of AYUSH under the quality control scheme failed to deliver the desired outputs for
want of adequate scientific manpower. Based on these grounds, the Department of AYUSH moved

19
a proposal to create the Central Drug Control infrastructure for Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and
Homoeopathy (ASU&H) drugs along with strengthening of drug regulation system and the state
testing laboratories by equipping them with necessary technical manpower. In October 2010, the
Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) chaired by Secretary (Expenditure) cleared the proposal for
setting up the infrastructure for Central ASU&H Drug Controller and scientific manpower for State
Drug Testing Laboratories. Thereafter, the matter has been taken up with the Department of
Expenditure for creation of regular posts as well as for hiring of manpower on contractual or
outsourcing basis for five years in State Drug Testing laboratories. Allocation of Rs. 160 crore for
this purpose has been sought in the Twelfth Five-Year Plan and the proposal is included in the
annual plan 2012-13.
The need for a separate Drug Controller for ASU&H drugs is required at the Central level
is justified on the following grounds:–
(i) The convention of having only one Drugs Controller in developed western countries
and US may not be apt in India because of medical pluralism and diverse nature of
medicinal products of AYUSH systems. In western world, the traditional medical
systems like Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani are not recognized and their products are
treated in the same way as allopathic products for the purpose of quality control and
regulation. Contrary to this our country has well developed and officially recognized
medical systems including Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homeopathy with wide range
of manufacturers and medicines. The needs, demands and services of these systems
are regulated through different laws and rules and hence are governed by a separate
department in the Ministry i.e. Department of AYUSH. The Central Drug Standards
Control Organization (CDSCO) does not have any expertise in ASU&H drugs and thus
they have to rely on the inputs and advice of the Department of AYUSH in related
matters.
(ii) Unlike western developed countries, owing to specific needs and requirements we
have separate councils (Indian Medical Council, Central Council for Indian Medicine
and Central Council of Homoeopathy), separate Acts (Indian Medical Council
Act, 1956, Indian Medicine, Central Council Act, 1970 and Homoeopathy Central
Council act, 1973) to regulate medical education and practice of allopathic system,
Indian Medicine (Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani) and Homoeopathy respectively. The
Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 contains separate chapter for ASU drugs and related
schedules and rules.
(iii) A YUSH is distinct from allopathic system in its philosophy, principles, concepts and
applications. Accordingly, the quality control and regulation of AYUSH systems is on
different plane. Specific regulatory requirements of ASU&H drugs necessitate setting
up a separate Central Drugs Controller in accordance with the recommendations of
the Mashelkar Committee and ASUDCC to provide for establishment of central
regulatory structure to deal with specific drug issues and enforce regulatory
provisions. The recommendations aim at strengthening the drug control infrastructure
for AYUSH at the Central and State levels by appointing separate Drug Controllers and
Inspectors for speedy enforcement of the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act and
strengthening of the Drug Testing facilities in State Laboratories.
(iv) Consequent upon the acceptance of the Mashelkar committee’s report by the
Government of India, the office of the Drug Controller General (India) has been
strengthened with the sanction of 175 posts for modern medicine experts. On similar
ground, sanctioning of posts and creation of a dedicated regulatory structure for
ASU&H drugs at the central level is, therefore, justified.

20
(v) There are 8644 drug manufacturing units of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and
Homoeopathy in the country and it is estimated that not more than 100 manufacturing
firms would have an annual turnover of Rs.5.00 crores and above. This brings out
a strong indication of requirement of a separate infrastructure with technical expertise
to handle the regulatory matters of different kinds.
(vi) In order to enhance acceptability of ASU & H Drugs, there is need to develop
formulations based on globally accepted practices like Good Agricultural and
Collection Practices (GACP), Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP), Good Clinical
Practices (GCP) and Good Laboratory Practices (GLP). Apart from good industry
practices, manufacturers need to have established accreditation mechanism for
various processes of manufacturing. Regulatory norms laid out by US Food and Drug
Administration (USFDA), European Medicines Evaluation Agency (EMEA), Australian
Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) and other such regulatory bodies, where
ASU & H Drugs may attempt registration for market authorization to expand their
international trade, need to be complied. These needs at present are not being taken
care of by the Central Drugs Controller Office due to non-availability of requisite
expertise and due to huge workload of matters related to allopathic drug.

2.22 The Committee places on record its appreciation for the achievements made by the four

as far as the standardization of classical AYUSH formulations, AYUSH therapies and validation of
classical AYUSH drugs are concerned. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department

quality and holistic research in AYUSH and facilitate scientific validation of AYUSH remedies. The

studies and get the health outcomes accruing from the research projects of the four Councils
evaluated by an independent agency. (Para 12.3)

The steps taken/proposed to be taken by each of the Councils on the concerns raised by
the Committee are outlined as follows:–

22
Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences:
1. Standardization of Classical AYUSH formulations:
The Government of India set up ‘Pharmacopoeial Commission of Indian Medicine (PCIM),
an autonomous organization of Government of India in 2010 to strengthen the quality standards of
Classical Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani formulations by evolving referral Pharmacopoeia
• Standards.
• All Pharmacopoeial committees viz. Ayurveda Pharmacopoeia Committee, Siddha
Pharmacopoeia Committee and Unani Pharmacopoeia Committee work under this
umbrella.
• The prime objective of the Commission is to coordinate and harmonize the laying down
of Pharmacopoeial standards for classical Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani Single drugs and
Compound formulations and subsequent publication in the form of ASU Pharmacopoeias.
2. Validation of AYUSH Therapies and Classical AYUSH Drugs:
• The Council has formulated a comprehensive Plan of Action for Scientific Validations of
Classical Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeial formulations under Twelfth Five Year Plan.
• This component of Twelfth Five Year Plan comprises Pre-clinical (Safety and Toxicity)
(about 33 formulations) and Clinical validation (about 37 formulations) of Classical
Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeial formulations.
• This is being implemented in a phased manner by setting the targets in the Annual Action
Plan of each financial year.
• Furthermore, the Council has formulated an Intra Mural Research Policy which focuses
on ‘System validation of Ayurveda Therapies’ and validation of Classical Ayurveda
formulations.
Central Council for Research in Yoga and Naturopathy:
12.1 The Central Council for Research in Yoga and Naturopathy (CCRYN) is involved in
conducting research studies to establish the efficacy of Yoga and Naturopathy systems in various
disease conditions by providing financial assistance to established/renowned Yoga and Naturopathy
institutions as well as Medical institutions. The Council has completed 37 research studies in past.
41 research papers have been published in National/ International Journals so far. The research
findings of some of the completed studies have been published as research monographs for
dissemination of the outcome of the studies among the Physicians and Researchers. 12 research
monographs have been published by the Council so far.
Central Council for Research in Homoeopathy:
In the process of laying down standards of Homoeopathic Medicines, up till now nine (09)
volumes of Homoeopathic Pharmacopiea of India (HPI) has been published which includes data of
956 drugs. As per action plan submitted to the Department of AYUSH for completing the
standardization of Homoeopathy medicines in the Twelfth five year plan, HPC of the Department
of AYUSH has proposed for completion of standardization of 256 drugs thereby completing the
target of 1200 drugs (commonly used in Homoeopathy). Preparation of Monographs on
homoeopathy drugs after drug standardization has been initiated in the year 2012-13 with a target
of 45 drugs (35 drugs by HPC and 10 drugs by CCRH).

23
Apart from intramural research studies on RCT design, Gold standard of Clinical Research,
Council has undertaken high end research in collaboration with the Institutes of excellence such as
IIT, Delhi, JIPMER, Kolkata Puducherry, University of Madras, School of Tropical Medicine,
Kolkata, Bose Institute, Kolkata, DIPAS, Delhi etc. to scientifically validate and to promote quality
and holistic research in Homoeopathy.
All the clinical trials are being registered under Clinical Trial registry of India since 2009. Till
now 17 clinical research trials have been registered and 09 trials are under process of registration.
Central Council for Research in Siddha:
Validation of AYUSH Therapies and Classical AYUSH Drugs:
• The Council has formulated a comprehensive Plan of Action for Scientific Validation of
siddha formulations under Twelfth Five Year Plan.
• This component of Twelfth Five Year Plan comprises Pre-clinical (Safety and Toxicity)
(about 15 formulations) and Clinical validation (about 15 formulations) of siddha formulation.
• This is being implemented in phased manner by setting the targets in the Annual Action
Plan of 2012-13.
Central Council for Research in Unani Medicine:
• The Council is also engaged in the development of the pharmacopoeial standards of
Unani single and compound drugs. This work is being done at seven drug
standardization Units of the Council. The Council has so far developed pharmacopoeial
standards of 298 single drugs and 100 compound formulations. This work has been
incorporated in Unani Pharmacopoeial of India in different volumes. The work carried
out by the Council is being utilized by the Unani drug industries in order to manufacture
quality drugs.
• The Council has scientifically established efficacy of Unani therapeutics in different
diseases. During Eleventh Plan studies on 43 formulations undertaken. It has also
validated regimental therapies in different disease conditions at the Council’s centres.
• Scientific validation of classical Unani drugs has also been undertaken by the Council.
Studies on 25 classical drugs in 10 disease conditions has been complete.
AYUSH Research Portal (www.ayushportal.ap.nic.in.)
The Department of AYUSH, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India
emphasizes on dissemination of the merits of AYUSH systems across the globe. A web based
‘AYUSH Research Portal has been launched on 18th April 2012. The Central Council for Research
in Ayurvedic Sciences is the coordinating body and the National Institute of Indian medical heritage
(NIIMH) Hyderabad is maintaining the web portal in collaboration with National Informatics Centre,
Hyderabad.
AYUSH Research Portal is meant for dissemination of Research outcomes in AYUSH systems
and allied sciences making them accessible. The key objectives of the Research Portal comprise:
• Showcase the research findings in an organized fashion
• Preempt duplication of work
• Encourage interdisciplinary research
• Generate evidence for wider acceptance of AYUSH system worldwide
• Enhancing translational potential of core strengths and merits.

24
• The major categories of AYUSH System including research on related sciences viz. Clinical
Research, Pre-clinical Research, Drug Research and Fundamental Research are
covered in this portal
• The information embodied is categorized as per individual
• AYUSH medical system against standard set of Medical conditions, based on WHO disease
classification ICD-10, and navigation is provided according to ICPC’s (International
Classification of primary Care) in select disease categories.
• The Portal provides the relevant indigenous name of the medical conditions pertaining to
each medical system, which further adds to clarity. The users can browse from a
dashboard which provides access to all the categories with visually clear buttons meant for
the purpose. On selection of the displayed results, the user will get information in the form
of abstract and wherever possible, full text of the article.
• An important value addition of the portal is categorization of Clinical Research work into
Grade A, B, C based on “General Guidelines for methodologies on Research and Evaluation
or Traditional medicine” published by World Health Organization (WHO). The grading allows
the researchers and also policy makers to access the current R&D status of AYUSH and
plan further to fill in the gaps.
• The application has been developed by Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic sciences
(CCRAS), and the content is being provided by all AYUSH Research councils, drug
standardization laboratories, and National Institutes. AYUSH Research Portal is accessible
through www.ayushportal.ap.nic.in. Specific usernames and passwords have been provided
to research Councils, National institutes and Pharmacopoeial Laboratories functioning under
department of AYUSH.
• The portal content development is a three tier experience through rigorous consultative
process by Central Co-ordination Committee, Editorial Committee and Search.
• and Peer Review Committee to ensure its high quality content.
• So far information on about 11394 published research papers, conference proceedings,
postgraduate and PhD works etc. has been incorporated in the portal.

corrective measures. Afterwards, a Review Meeting has been held in the Department on 31st July,
2012 in which progress in construction, purchase of equipment, furnishing of the hospital, creation
of posts and fund utilization were reviewed.
Further Recommendation
3.29 The Committee observes that the reply of the Department is silent as regards the
actual progress made till date and by when the Institute would be fully operational. The
Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation for early operationalization of the
Institute.

constrained to observe that at a time when there is increasingly greater emphasis on optimal
utilization of scarce resources, such inefficiencies in execution of the Project can no longer be
overlooked. The Committee, therefore, feels that there is a case for spelling out monitorable goals
in respect of operationalising the project and putting in place a mechanism for holding people. The

work of the building construction could be completed so far. The Committee is constrained to

of heavy machinery necessitating repair, distant location, road blocked by agitators etc. are the
main reasons for the delay. However, the Department is monitoring progress of the institute
vigorously. A Project Management Committee constituted to monitor the progress quarterly. This

It advised Director of the institute to prepare plan for total 40 acres of land which has been
allotted for construction of the institute. Further, the PMC directed to furnish a quarterly status
report indicating quarterly targets and achievements and reasons of variations, if any, and
proposed corrective measures. Progress on progress of construction, purchase of equipment,
furnishing of the hospital, creation of posts and fund utilization have been further reviewed on
31st July, 2012.
Recommendation/Observation

of the word until the requisite faculty and staff is appointed. The Committee, therefore,
recommends to the Department to move quickly towards sanctioning and recruiting the requisite
faculty and staff. The Committee is not satisfied with the efforts made by the department for
operationalisation of the North Eastern Institution of Folk Medicine. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department should make all out efforts for making the institutes operational.

operationalisation of the North Eastern Institution of Folk Medicine. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Department should make all out efforts for making the

VI. Assistance to Accredited AYUSH Centres of Excellence in Non-Government/Private
Sector Engaged in AYUSH Education/Drug Development and Research/Clinical Research/Folk
Medicine etc.
Recommendation/Observation
3.35 The Committee is constrained to observe that this is yet another case of inefficiency in
budgetary planning and calls for urgent corrective measures. The Committee would have been
happy if the Department of AYUSH, instead of gloating over the under-utilization of budgeted funds
in 2011-12, analyzed the reasons behind non-receipts of eligible proposals and taken corrective
action accordingly. The Committee would, therefore, like the Department to analyse the reasons for
non-receipt of suitable proposals under this head and take remedial measures accordingly and also
ensure expenditure monitoring and financial discipline so that the budgeted amount for 2012-13
does not meet the same fate. (Para 6.3)
Action Taken
3.36 The reasons behind non-receipt of eligible proposals in 2011-12 were analyzed and important
reasons are as follows:
1. There are very less reputed and credible organizations working in the AYUSH sector,
which may be upgraded to the level of excellence.
2. Most of such organizations have received grant under the Centres of Excellence scheme
during the initial years of the 11th plan period.
3. To receive grant under the Centres of Excellence scheme, the organizations have to
possess a minimum specified level from which, it will be upgraded to a higher specified
level. In AYUSH sector there are very few non-profit NGOs which are eligible to be
upgraded to the level of excellence.
Further, the scheme would be evaluated by third party. The expenditure under the scheme
shall be reviewed and corrective measures taken.
Further Recommendation
3.37 The Committee notes the reasons for under utilization. However, the Committee notes
that the Department has not clearly spelt out as to how it contemplates to tackle the problems.
The Department needs to take remedial measurers. The Committee reiterates its
recommendation that efficient expenditure monitoring and financial discipline may be ensured.

35
VII. Research and Development including medicinal plants
Development of AYUSH hospitals and dispensaries and mainstreaming of AYUSH
Recommendations/Observations
3.38 The Committee notes that by the end of the Eleventh Plan only 10% AYUSH hospitals could
be upgraded. Upgradation work of AYUSH dispensaries is negligible. Work of supply of AYUSH
drugs has been completed. The Committee observes that more than 90% of the upgradation work
is yet to be completed. Since upgradation of AYUSH hospitals and dispensaries is main work under
the Centrally Sponsored Scheme, the Committee strongly recommends to the Department to make
all out efforts and take all possible measures to achieve the target of upgradation of all AYUSH
hospitals and dispensaries in the first two to three years of the Twelfth Plan period. The State
Government authorities should be pursued vigorously to achieve the target. In order to achieve the
target, the Department should approach the Ministry of Finance for allocation of more funds at RE
2012-13 stage as also for more funds for the next financial years so that the desired targets are
achieved at the earliest. (Para 7.3)
Action Taken
3.39 Since, the State Governments are the implementing authorities with regard to up-gradation
of the AYUSH dispensaries; they will be pursued vigorously to achieve the targets. In this regard
Department has identified the nodal officers among the officials of the Department for each State,
so that they will make one to one contact to the state Government and coordinate in implementing
the programmes by the states and timely submission of the UCs. In due appreciation of the
recommendations of the committee the Department shall make all out efforts to upgrade AYUSH
hospitals and dispensaries in first two to three years of the Twelfth Five Year Plan.
Further Recommendation
3.40 The Committee once again emphasizes that upgradation of AYUSH hospitals and
dispensaries should be achieved in a dedicated time-frame and the Department needs to
chalk out an action plan in this direction. Simultaneously, the Department should pursue
with the Ministry of Finance for more funds for the scheme for ensuring completion of the
upgradation work in a targeted time-frame. The Committee would also like to be apprised
of the outcome as a result of appointing the nodal officer for each State.
Recommendation/Observation
3.41 The Committee further desires to be kept apprised of the outcome of the proposals made
by the Department to the Department of Health and Family Welfare to include them in the NRHM
Cabinet note. (Para 7.11)
Action Taken
3.42 The Department of Health has not included the AYUSH proposal of AYUSH Flexipool under
NRHM cabinet note. However, they have suggested that Department of AYUSH may move separate
cabinet note for AYUSH Flexipool. Now, Department of AYUSH is bringing a proposal for
consideration of Cabinet on AYUSH Flexipool.
Further Recommendation
3.43 The Committee suggests that the Department should prepare a comprehensive and
realistic proposal for AYUSH Flexipool for consideration of cabinet and apprise the
committee of its outcome.

CHAPTER-IV
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH
FINAL REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT ARE STILL AWAITED
X. Development of Institutions
Recommendation/Observation
4.1 The Committee notes that the Mid-term Appraisal of the Scheme—Development of AYUSH
Institutions had pointed out certain implementation constraints and suggested corrective measures.
However, the Planning Commission and Department of Expenditure did not support the proposals
of the Department for amendments to the existing scheme. The Committee notes there has been
massive under-performance of this Scheme, apparently due to constraints in its implementation and
structure. The Committee is at a loss to understand as to how the Scheme would be able to fulfill
its objective of bridging the critical gaps observed on compliance of the minimum standards and
norms of CCIM and CCH if the constraints are not taken care of. The Committee, therefore,
recommends to the Department to approach the Planning Commission and Department of
Expenditure again for the purpose of obtaining their support for carrying out the amendments to
the existing Scheme. (Para 10.5)
Action Taken
An independent appraisal and evaluation of Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Development of
AYUSH institutions is proposed to be taken up. In addition to this, a concurrent evaluation by a
Departmental Committee of three officials is also being done. Considering the evaluation reports and
after its scrutiny within the Department, the proposal for amendment to the scheme for
implementation during Twelfth Plan would be taken up. The Department would seriously pursue the
recommendations of the committee.

2
CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES
OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
I. INTRODUCTION
CARE, SUPPORT AND TREATMENT
Recommendation/Observation
1.1 In Bihar, where HIV and visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) interact and co-infection is a
problem, the Committee recommends as a first step-in areas that are endemic for Kala-azar –
Department of AIDS control should consider actively screening people living with HIV for this life-
threatening disease. Co-infected patients should then be given antiretrovirals as soon as possible
after starting anti-kala-azar therapy. (Para 1.8)
Action Taken
Visceral Leishmaniasis (kala – azar) is one of the disease which is endemic in the State of
Bihar. Kala-azar among HIV positive patients requires regular screening as it is regarded as one of
the Opportunistic Infections(OI) in endemic areas. Thus, at the time of pre-ART registration and
thereafter, all PLHIV are screened for such OIs and then referred to the diagnostic facilities
available under National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme for confirmatory diagnosis of
kala-azar. All PLHIV with co-infection of kala-azar are regarded as “WHO Clinical Stage – IV” as
per the existing case definition and are provided ART as soon as possible after starting anti kala-
azar therapy irrespective of CD4 count.
IV SETTING UP OF NEW BLOOD COMPONENT SEPARATION UNITS
Recommendation/Observation
1.2 The Committee appreciates that the targets set by the Department under NACP-III for
setting up of BCSUs have been achieved more or less. The Committee would, however, like to be
updated regularly of the targets set and success achieved by these units. (Para 4.2)
Action Taken
In the beginning of NACP III there was a target of setting up new BCSUs in 80 tertiary
care hospitals in addition to continuing support for 82 BCSUs which already existed.
As of date (June 2012), all of the proposed 80 centers are licensed.
The targets have been achieved with efforts of close follow up by the programme for
obtaining site allocation by the state, equipment installation, allocation of funds as per pattern of
assistance, follow up with the office of DCG(I) for central license at all stages.
2

3
NACP 2007-08 2008-09 2009-10 2010-11 201 1-12 2012-13 T otal
III
Target T* A* T A T A T A T A T A
80 0 0 40 19 40 28 12 26 7 4 3 3 80
(*T denotes Target and A denotes achievement)
Recommendation/Observation
1.3 The Committee notes that not only quantity but also quality matters. Blood transfusion is
life-saving treatment in many situations. But transfusions can also be a quick and easy route for
the transmission of infectious agents such as HIV , HBV , HCV , and malaria. NACO has been
entrusted the task of setting up and expanding blood banks across the country. Several studies
reviewing the current scenario in transfusion medicine (TM) in India indicate an urgent need for
restructuring the blood transfusion services with extreme variations in management and quality.
These studies note that compliance with quality assurance and GMP is not ensured. A large number
of blood banks are unlicensed. The Committee feels that since quality of blood banks is regulated
under the Drugs and Cosmetic Rules, under schedule ‘F’, Department of AIDS Control and the
DCGI should jointly come up with a plan to urgently address the issue of quality of blood banks
in the private and public sector. (Para 4.3)
Action Taken
NACO is focusing on quality management systems in Blood Banks in the country. Quality
management modules were prepared at NACO with the assistance of a group of experts in
Transfusion Medicine and Quality. These quality management modules are to be used in Blood
banks at the state level. So far 12 workshops covering 28 states for Quality Management have been
completed by NACO.
Efforts are also being made to monitor the blood banks and core committees have been
constituted in all states comprising Blood Bank experts and representative of the Drug Controller
at the state level, to monitor all blood banks.
Department of AIDS Control and the DCGI will also make a joint plan to execute the above
in a smooth manner.
Blood Transfusion service in the respective state is implemented by State level
functionaries. DCG (I) at the centre and its counterparts in the state are responsible for the
regulation and licensing of Blood Banks. Department of AIDS Control (DAC) is making all efforts
by working with the states and providing funds for augmenting voluntary blood donation and
ensuring provision of safe and quality blood in the country by reducing HIV transmission through
blood to < 0.5%.
V. SETTING UP OF NEW DISTRICT LEVEL BLOOD BANKS
Recommendation/Observation
1.4 The Committee also recommends to the Department to take special cognizance of the
underserved districts of Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand. The Committee further
recommends that the Department should keep assessing the requirements of Blood Banks based on
the actual needs in various States due to migration and other factors. (Para 5.4)

4
Action Taken
NACO is taking special cognizance of the underserved areas including districts of
Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand. NACO regularly assesses these states as per their
requirement for blood as per the population.
In Uttarakhand, support for a district level blood bank by NACO has been approved during
2012-13for the newly created district of Ranikhet. 21 newly created Blood Component separation
units of Uttar Pradesh are being given financial support of annual recurring grant in the financial
year 2012-13. In Jharkhand, NACO is taking initiatives for licensing of the three blood banks at
Saraikela, Chatra and Koderma.
VI. INTEGRATED COUNSELING AND TESTING CENTERS (ICTCS)
Recommendation/Observation
1.5 The Committee is at a loss to understand the rationale on the basis of which the
Department, in the first place fixes the target and fails to achieve the same year after year. A plain
reading of the target set vis-à-vis the achievement shows that the Department is not following its
own yardstick of fixing of target each year on the basis of achievement of the previous year,
which shows poor foresight of planning by the Department. The Committee, therefore, enjoins
upon the Department to seriously set realistic and achievable targets. Once targets are fixed, all
efforts should be made to achieve them. (Para 6.4)
Action Taken
As per the targets set under NACP III, the Department, through year wise scale up, had
to reach an end-line annual target of 22 million per year by the end of NACP III i.e. 2011-12. This
is inclusive of the target of counselling and testing of 75 lakh pregnant women.
To achieve this, the Department scaled up HIV counselling and testing facilities from 4567
in 2007-08 to 10,515 in 2011-12. Programme coverage has increased from 7.8 million in 2007-08
to 19.4 million in the year 2011-12.
During the year 2011-12 (April 2011 to March 2012) the Department has achieved the target
of counselling and testing 19.4 million attendees including 85.6 lakh pregnant women. Thus overall
achievement is 88% and the achievement of coverage of pregnant women is 113% as against the
target set for the last year of NACP III.
Recommendation/Observation
1.6 Testing of pregnant women raises several ethical questions. The Committee feels these
ethical issues have to be addressed at the time of rolling out routine testing of pregnant women
under NRHM. Testing with counseling is key. Support services for domestic violence and
discrimination within the family and community are also crucial. Treatment needs of women who
test positive should also be the top priority. Absence of these components will have an adverse
impact on the uptake of ante-natal services if they are identified with routine HIV testing of
pregnant women. The Committee feels that a detailed study on the testing of women who, are
pregnant – their treatment and the discrimination they face, – must be immediately undertaken and
should be used to shape a more sensitive and humane testing programme for pregnant women.
(Para 6.5)
Action Taken
Under the routine counseling and testing services for pregnant women provided under

5
NACP, all pregnant women are offered counseling and testing for HIV . These Pregnant women have
the right to “opt-out” under the existing strategy . Counseling is provided to all pregnant women
before and after HIV test. Any HIV positive pregnant women detected by the ICTCs is offered
PPTCT services and linked to Care Support and Treatment services.
The recommendations of the Committee for conducting a detailed study on testing of
women who are pregnant – their treatment and discrimination they face, will be taken up by the
Department.
VIII. ANTIRETROVIRAL TREATMENT (ART) CENTERS
Recommendation/Observation
1.7 The Committee notes that stockouts of ART medicines were reported throughout 2011 in
many states including UP, Bihar, Maharashtra, Manipur etc. The Committee fails to understand as
to how performance of RITES has been called satisfactory in such circumstances. The Committee
recommends that the Department take a more serious note of such lapses and have closer
monitoring mechanism in place since such gaps in supply only add to drug resistance apart from
the obvious inconvenience. (Para 8.3)
1.8 The Committee has noted that throughout 2011, there have been regular incidents of HIV
drug (first, Second and pediatric doses) in different States, which has been reported by different
PLHIV networks. The Committee feels that this is a serious issue since stock outs mean drug
interruptions which can lead to increased public health risks of HIV drug resistance. The
Committee recommends that an investigation and report be undertaken to list the numbers of
stock outs and to document the reasons for the stock outs. NACO should also outline to this
Committee what measures have been planned to prevent and to deal with incidents of stock outs.
The role of the PLHIV Networks should be to continue this good work of monitoring HIV
treatment at ART Centres and reporting problems like stock outs of NACO. PLHIV networks
should be further encouraged to continue reporting such incidents. Stock outs are related to
inefficiencies such as poor planning, incorrect projections of local requirements, poor distribution
and supply at treatment facilities, expiry of medicines as the stock that was received earlier is
not distributed first. The Committee recommends that NACO immediately reform the
pharmaceutical supply management system for HIV medicines as it is an important element in
treatment programmes. (Para 8.4)
Action Taken
As per the information captured in the Computerised Management Information System
(CMIS) under the programme, during 2011, 32 sites had shown stock-out of ARV drugs, most of
them only for few days. On detailed analysis, it was found that the stock out of ARV drugs for
more than a week was found only in 4 ART centres in two States of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. The
corrective measures were initiated immediately by relocation from other ART centres with surplus
stocks.
Subsequently, in order to prevent such situation of stock-out of ARV drugs in future, NACO
has decentralised the allocation of ARV drugs through SACS instead of directly sending to ART
centres, so that State level monitoring of stocks is ensured.
Now each State AIDS Control Society has a designated official at the level of Joint Director
to ensure distribution and supply chain management of various ARV drugs in their respective States.
Further, NACO now has a dedicated Logistic Coordinator at the central level, which looks after
stock position and supply management of various ARV drugs in each State/UT.

6
A drug estimation committee has been constituted consisting of eminent medical specialists,
having expertise in the field for proper forecasting of ARV drugs, to ensure adequate quantity of
ARV drugs are indented for procurement.
In the State Grievance Redressal Committee meetings, which is constituted in every state,
the PLHIV network also participates as a member of the Committee. This Committee meets from
time to time and the feedback provided by the PLHIV networks is immediately acted upon by
initiating corrective measures including the issue of stock-out of ARV drugs at the ART centres.
Recommendation/Observation
1.9 The Committee feels that the slow rate of scale up of ART treatment over the last decade
has forced patients into the private sector where inappropriate HIV drug regimens are often
prescribed, leading to a long term public health problem of drug resistance. Many economic and
bureaucratic barriers have been noted in the eligibility criteria for enrolling in the programme for
those needing alternative first line or second line HIV drugs. As a result, patient groups have had
to approach the Supreme Court. These barriers must be addressed and must not be created for
patients who will need third line HIV medicines. Currently the proportion of HIV patients who have
failed to the second-line treatment is probably very small. The programme must start planning for
ART Centres of Excellence to take in these few patients. This will control drug resistance. Cost
alone should not be the only criteria. Failure to procure the third line drugs will have future public
health complications as PLHIVs could develop a very resistance HIV which could prove costly.
Planning and treating third line in a few patients will build capacity and experience of public health
facilities classified as centres of excellence by Department of AIDS Control. (Para 8.5)
Action Taken
It is submitted that ART was started in 2004 with 8 ART centres, which have been rapidly
scaled up to existing 355 centres (March 2012) against a target of setting up of 250 such ART
centres by 2012.
As per the information available with Deptt. of AIDS Control, only 35,000 patients are on
ART in private sector against around 5,42,000 patients in the public sector in the country.
As per the need of the programme, the second line ART was rolled out in two Centres of
Excellence (COE) in 2008 and was extended to 10 COEs and 18 ART Plus centres to expand this
service across the country. In addition, 7 COEs for Paediatric HIV Care are also providing the
services of second line ART.
The criteria for enrolling patients on second line were stringent as options for drugs in
management of HIV/AIDS were limited. This has helped in continuance of first line therapy to a
large number of patients who were failing due to factors other than drug resistance and actually
did not require the second line regimen. This has also provided a broader base of ARV drugs for
such patients who might require the same in future. The same approach was explained to Hon’ble
Supreme Court and as per directions, the criteria for inclusion of patients on treatment failure was
relaxed. Even after relaxation, the number of patients on second line ART is 4208 (as on March
2012) in all the designated centres.
All the COEs and ART Plus centres are well equipped to manage all types of patients on
HIV/AIDS care. As the HIV virus is constantly mutated, the Drug Resistance is not only related
to Treatment Adherence alone. As and when required and recommended by the Technical Resource
Group on ART, the programme will look into use of newer drugs for subsequent therapy (third line
ARV regimen) in public interest and with public health approach.

7
National AIDS Control Programme lays great emphasis on issues related to proper
counselling of patients to ensure complete adherence to treatment, so that patient do not develop
resistance early and continue the first line regimen as long as possible. The second line treatment
is also provided under NACP. The overall Drug Resistance in the country is very low and as of
now, there is no major public health threat of large number of PLHIV developing resistance to the
virus.
Recommendation/Observation
1.10 The Committee is constrained to observe that the Department has not treated the matter of
phasing out Stavudine with the urgency and seriousness it deserves. The Committee feels that the
inordinate delay on the part of the Department in this regard is a sad commentary on the working
of the Department and calls for introspection. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Department should start phasing out of Stavudine in a time bound manner. The Committee desires
to be kept apprised of the action taken in this regard. (Para 8.7)
Action Taken
The World Health Organisation (WHO) has released the guidelines for Antiretroviral Therapy
(ART) for HIV infection in adults and adolescents (2010 revision). The guidelines mainly describe
the newer strategies with regard to the starting of treatment and the drugs needed to be used at
the time to starting.The WHO also recommended country adaptation of these guidelines based on
the context of each country’s HIV epidemic, the strengths and weakness of health systems, and
the availability of financial, human and other essential resources.
WHO recommends phasing out of ARV drug Stavudine from ART regimen. Two meetings
of the Technical Resource Group on ART were held in Aug’ 10 and Dec’11to discuss this issue.
Subsequently, it was decided that Stavudine would be phased out from the national ART programme
for both existing and new patients. This phase out will be done once the drugs from the
procurement cycle of 2012-13 are in place. Thus, during 2012, phase out will start by not using
any Stavudine based regimen for new patients and later on the old patients will be shifted to non-
Stavudine based regimen in a phased manner.
X. ADOLESCENCE EDUCATION PROGRAMME (AEP)
Recommendation/Observation
1.11 The committee is impressed that with consistent efforts of the Department, the programme
is running in most of the States. The Committee feels that the Department should vigorously take
up with the States where the programme is still under suspension, the reasons for the delay in
implementation of the programme and resolve their apprehensions in this regard without any further
delay, in view of the fact that HIV/AIDS is a hydra headed monster which usually attacks the
vulnerable adolescent population due to lack of awareness of the devastating effects the diseases
could have on them. The states, that have suspended, should also reconsider their decision.
(Para 10.3)
Action Taken
Adolescence Education Programme (AEP) is promoted by State AIDS Control Societies of
NACO in collaboration with the Departments of Education in secondary and senior secondary
schools to build up life skills of adolescents to cope with the physical and psychological changes
associated with growing up and to enable them to protect themselves from HIV/AIDS/STI. After

8
it was suspended in eight States (Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Kerala, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh,
Maharashtra, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh), due to a serious follow up and revision of the toolkit
(Educational Material) in 2008, by NACO, the programme was resumed as part of school health
programme under NRHM or through NGOs in the States of Kerala, Gujarat and Rajasthan. Serious
efforts are on for resumption of the programme in the other five States (Chhattisgarh, Karnataka,
Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Uttar Pradesh) where it continues to be suspended.
NACO is continuing its efforts through the State AIDS Control Societies (SACS), in States
where the Adolescence Education Programme, is still under suspension (Chhattisgarh, Karnataka,

CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES
NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES
I. INTRODUCTION
Recommendation/Observation
2.1 Prima facie , a look at the communicable and non-communicable disease burden profile of
the country suggests there could be more pressing issues which could have been the prioritized
over HIV/AIDS, and yet the Ministry in its wisdom went on to create a separate Department for
it. While the committee understands that HIV/AIDS is a genuine health problem which requires
timely addressal, it fails to understand the reason why the Ministry went on to create a dedicated
Department to take care of the issue. The Committee also appreciates the fact that while resource
constraint is a reality given our circumstances, it, at the same time mandates more prudence while
allocating national priorities. During evidence, the Committee queried the Department to justify this
act, and to the Committee’s dismay no satisfactory answer was provided. Further, a post-evidence
written query was made and the Department forwarded the same to the Ministry to be replied.
Answer to this is still awaited till the compilation of this Report. The Committee takes serious view
of this delay on part of the Ministry as time crunch at the time of DFGs is to be anticipated as
is prompt response.The Committee recommends that the response be communicated to them in
detail at the time of the presentation of the ATN within the stipulated three months from the date
of presentation of this Report in the Parliament. (Para 1.1)
Action Taken
India is a low prevalence country but has the third largest population of HIV infected people
in the world. Even a small percentage increase in prevalence will result in a large number of HIV
infection on account of population size. Though a series of measures, including the organizational
framework at the governmental level i.e. the National AIDS Control Organization (NACO) were in
place, the magnitude of the problem warranted a more focused attention.
2. AIDS related issues were handled by the Department of Health and Family Welfare.
However, the overall ambit of that Department was very large. Therefore, in the then existing set
up, a more focused attention and a multi-dimensional approach was not possible. Moreover, the
gravity of the problem also needed to be gauged by the fact that it affects the population in the
most productive age groups. Similarly, there was a need for coordinated action for a high focused
cutting edge research in this area.
3. In the above context, it was felt necessary to create a separate Department of AIDS Control
to be located within the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare by amending the Government of
India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961. This was done to create the necessary space to take
up a whole range of programmes to effectively tackle the problem and provide viable solutions. The
Department was to be oriented exclusively for building an all encompassing response to contain the
spread of this menace by reaching out to the diverse population, dissemination of accurate,
complete and timely information about HIV/AIDS, promotion of measures that are effective for
protection against its spread and provision of free treatment for all those who need it.

12
4. To sum up, Department of AIDS Control was created to provide a sharper focus to
government initiatives in effectively tackling the threat posed by HIV/AIDS in the country. Further,
it was felt that the gravity and magnitude of the problem could be better assessed by a dedicated
Department for the purpose which would spearhead as well as coordinate programmes dealing with
AIDS related issues.
PREVENTION
Recommendation/Observation
2.2 The Committee recommends that treatment should be recognized as a cornerstone of
prevention activities explicitly by Department of AIDS Control. Outcomes of recent scientific
studies show that if an HIV-positive person adheres to an effective antiretroviral therapy regimen,
the risk of transmitting the virus to their uninfected sexual partner can be reduced by 96%. Studies
suggest that antiretroviral therapy reduces the sexual transmission of HIV in generalized epidemics,
especially among sero-discordant couples. There is also growing evidence of the impact of ART
on community-level HIV transmission, both, in generalized and concentrated epidemics including
among injecting drug users. Most importantly the availability of Treatment for Prevention will not
only empower people to get tested for HIV , but also to disclose their HIV status, but significantly
contribute to reducing the stigma and discrimination surrounding HIV . Therefore, it is crucial for
Department of AIDS Control to recognize and use antiretroviral drugs as a prevention tool to
control the epidemic in India. The Committee feels that to capitalize on the scientific evidence,
continued investment in ART treatment is necessary in the coming five years to prevent new
infections. (Para 1.5)
Action Taken
Department of AIDS Control has taken note of a recent scientific study indicating that
treatment with ARV drugs reduces the risk of transmitting the virus to other un-infected sex
partners by 96%. This PHTN 054 study is a multi centric/multi country study conducted at two
sites in India located at NARI, Pune and YRG Care, Chennai. The data from these two sites has
not yet been analysed with specific reference to India. However, the overall preliminary analysis
on this variable at NARI, Pune site, will be done only after the completion of study.
The major concern on this study is that the sites in all other countries are ‘generalised
epidemic’ sites except in India where the epidemic is ‘concentrated epidemic’. The results as
outcome of this study will only be restricted to discordant couples.
The issue of making available treatment for prevention to empower people to get tested for
HIV , which is stated as contributing factor to reduce the stigma and discrimination, was discussed
in the last meeting of the Technical Resource Group (TRG) on ART held in December 2011. The
TRG was of the opinion that the issue of side-effects and emergence of resistance among these
people will be a major deterrent to providing anti-retroviral drugs as prevention tool in our country,
presently. Further, as the high risk populations in the context of HIV are largely divided into two
parts. One, most at risk populations (MARP’s) who are not infected and the other, who are HIV
infected. In the first group ART as prophylactic treatment is currently ruled out in the programme
while for others the ART will be given to those who have CD4 count as < 350.
As a part of planning of NACP – IV, it has been well recognised that providing Care,
Support and Treatment services to PLHIV will be an important component of the programme
during the next five years. Although, Lost to Follow Up (LFU) is presently within acceptable limits,
more efforts will be made to further bring it down during NACP IV.

13
CARE, SUPPORT AND TREATMENT
Recommendation/Observation
2.3 The committee recommends that all persons living with HIV should be offered and
counseled to test for Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C by Department of AIDS Control. As a next step,
clear guidelines, resources and training for the testing of Hepatitis in ICTCs and management of
the Hepatitis co-infection should be provided to ART centers. Costs of Hepatitis drugs alone should
not be a factor to refuse treatment of this co-infection that can cause liver cirrhosis. Efforts to
boost local production of Hepatitis drugs and variety of measures such as bulk Procurement and
health safeguards in the Patent law should be used to reduce prices. (Para 1.6)
Action Taken
The diagnosis and management of Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C to people attending the
hospitals is the mandate of the general health system, as these facilities are to be provided in the
existing health care delivery system.
Thus, Department of AIDS Control may not be asked to duplicate efforts to provide such
facilities in the set up of National AIDS Control Programme. Moreover, a large number of NACO
facilities are located in the same institutions belonging to larger health system like Facility Integrated
Counselling & Testing Centres and ART centres etc.. Whenever a PLHIV attending ART centre is
diagnosed to be co-infected with Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C, he/she is referred to the general health
system for confirmatory diagnosis and management of these diseases.
Recommendation/Observation
2.4 The Committee clearly recommends that Department of AIDS Control strengthen TB
infection control in ART centers to prevent transmission of TB among people living with HIV. The
Committee also clearly recommends that with new tests that can detect DR-TB in less than two
hours, it’s a perfect time for Department of AIDS Control to take immediate action to boost
diagnosis of DR TB in people living with HIV . At ART Centres implementation of intensified TB
case finding (active TB screening) has been abjectly neglected despite clear WHO
recommendations. HIV+ patients often arrive in health facilities in very bad condition and even die
before their DR TB treatment can be diagnosed and appropriate treatment can be started. The
Committee feels that Intensified case finding with access to culture/DST testing can increase
access to early treatment of DR TB for people living with HIV in the public programme with
appropriate drug regimens. Usually people living with HIV have already been treated in the private
sector with inappropriate TB drug regimens. The Committee notes that recent studies in scientific
journals like PLoS have documented that the proliferation of TB formulations in the private market
coupled with the casual over-the-counter sale of antibiotics, of which some are used for DR TB
treatment, is fuelling the development of drug resistance, which is also affecting people living with
HIV . There is an urgent need for Department of AIDS Control to work with RNTCP and the
DCGI’s office for regulatory control of sale and administration of TB Drugs in the private sector
in order to address the growing incidence of severe forms of DR-TB in India. (Para 1.7)
Action Taken
The Department of AIDS Control is providing support to all ART centres for ensuring
infection control measures to be adopted in these facilities including measures to ensure prevention
of transmission of TB among PLHIV . This is regarded as an integral part of HIV-TB activities at
the ART centres.

14
The Intensified TB Case Finding (ICF) activities are being implemented in all Integrated
Counselling and Testing Centres (ICTCs) and ART centres across the country. The diagnosis of TB
among HIV infected people, who attend the ART centres, is done by referring them to designated
TB Diagnostic facilities in the same institution, where the ART centre is located. As the testing
facilities for diagnosis of TB already exists in the same institute, the Deptt. of AIDS Control is not
duplicating the efforts in this regard.
The diagnosis of Drug Resistant TB (DR TB) by newer technologies is the mandate of
Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) being implemented by Central TB Division in
Department of Health. In this regard, there is a Joint National Technical Working Group (NTWG)
for coordination of HIV & TB activities. This group explores and directs both programmes to
initiate such activities in improving the management of HIV/TB co-infection. Similar State level
Committees exist at state level to ensure the proper coordination between the two programmes so
that the activities both at TB clinic and ART centres (HIV/AIDS clinic) are well coordinated for
the benefit of patients with HIV/TB co-infection.
As regards regulatory control of sale and administration of TB drugs in the private sector,
in order to address the growing incidence of severe forms of Drug Resistant TB cases in the
country, it is conveyed that this is the mandate of Drugs Control Authority i.e. Drugs Controller
General (India) and RNTCP. However, this will be taken up by the Department in the next meeting
of NTWG.

Recommendation/Observation

III. ROLE OF NGOs
Recommendation/Observation
2.9 The Committee is dismayed to note that the Department has not been able to recover the
unspent balances available with the discontinued NGOs. There appears to be some slackness on the
part of the Department and other implementing agencies. The Committee, therefore, recommends
imposing severe penalties on the NGOs which indulged in fraud or financial embezzlement. If need
be, the Department should sound the law enforcement agencies of the concerned States to proceed
with action against such NGOs as fraud or financial embezzlement comes within the domain of

Action Taken
State AIDS Control Societies are responsible for contracting NGOs/CBOs for
implementation of targeted intervention projects through a transparent process of expression of
interest followed by Technical Appraisal Committee doing a desk review and Joint Appraisal
Committee (JAT) doing a field verification of the capacity of NGO before the contracting is
approved by the Governing Body headed by Secretary/Principal Secretary of the State. The
performance of the NGO is monitored and the poor performing NGOs/CBOs are terminated based
