V. RCH FLEXIBLE POOL
Recommendation/Observation
1.16 The targets set under the National Rural Health Mission for Maternal Mortality Ratio
(MMR), Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) and Total Fertility Rate (TFR) were 100 per 100,000 live
births, 30 per 1000 live births and 2.1 respectively by 2012. As per the latest Sample Registration
System (SRS) report 2007-09 of the Registrar General of India (RGI-SRS), Maternal Mortality
Ratio (MMR) showed a decline from 254 per 100,000 live births in the period 2004-06 to 212
per 100,000 live births in the period 2007-09, Infant Mortality Rate declined from 58 per 1000 live
births in the year 2005 to 47 per 1000 live births in 2010 and Total Fertility Rate declined from
3.0 in 2003 to 2.6 in 2009. By these figures the Committee feels that the targets set to be achieved
by 2012 would not have been achieved till now. The Committee notes that none of the targets set
by the Eleventh Plan for reduction in MMR, IMR and TFR has been met during the Eleventh Plan
period. The Committee feels that the strategies adopted to achieve the goals of reduction in MMR,
IMR and TFR need to be evaluated afresh so that with suitable modifications, they would correct
the imbalance and help meet the targets set for MMR, IMR and TFR in the coming years.
(Para 5.2)

59
Action Taken
Under the National Rural Health Mission, the following steps are being taken to ensure the
reduction in Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR), Infant Mortality Ratio (IMR) and Total Fertility Rate
(TFR) and improve the health status of children across all the States of the country:
Strategies Adopted for achieving target set for MMR
• For accelerating the pace of reduction in MMR, GoI has identified delivery points
throughout the country based on a minimum benchmark and in the PIP for the year
2012-13 funds are being given to the States for strengthening these delivery points for
improving service delivery.
• States have also been asked to monitor the performance of identified delivery points to
improve its working.
• Name Based web enabled tracking of pregnant women and children under the Mother
& Child Tracking System (MCTS) has been started to ensure and monitor full services
to them.
• A Joint MCP Card of Ministry of Health & Family Welfare (MoHFW) and Ministry of
Women and Child Development (MoWCD) has been launched to provide a tool for
monitoring services for MCH including ANC, INC & PNC and Nutrition interventions
being implemented by both Ministries.
• The Government of India has taken a policy decision to review every maternal death
both at the health facilities and in the community. The purpose of the review is to
identify causes of maternal deaths and the gaps in service delivery for taking corrective
action and not for taking punitive action against service providers.
• Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakaram (JSSK): A new initiative namely JSSK has been
launched, which entitles all pregnant women delivering in public health institutions to
absolutely free and no expense delivery including Caesarean section. The initiative
stipulates free drugs, diagnostics, blood and diet, besides free transport from home to
institution, in-between facilities in case of a referral and drop back home.
Strategies Adopted for achieving target set for IMR
• Promotion of Institutional Delivery through Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY): Promoting
Institutional delivery by skilled birth attendant is a key to reducing both maternal and
neo-natal mortality.
• Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakaram (JSSK): A new initiative namely Janani Shishu
Suraksha Karyakaram has been launched, which entitles all sick newborns being
delivered in public health institutions to absolutely free and no expense for treatment till
30 days after birth. The initiative stipulates free drugs, diagnostics, blood and diet,
besides free transport from home to institution, in-between facilities in case of a referral
and drop back home.
• Sick Newborn such as Special New Born Care Units (SNCUs), New Born Stabilization
Units (NBSUs) and New Born Baby Corners (NBCCs) at different levels are being set
up at different levels to reduce Child Mortality.
• Home based newborn care (HBNC) through ASHAs has been initiated to improve new
born practices at the community level and early detection and referral of sick new born

60
babies through series of home visits. In case of institutional deliveries six visits on days
3, 7, 14, 21, 28 & 42nd days and one additional visit within 24 hours of delivery in
case of home deliveries. Additional visits will be made for babies who are pre-term, low
birth weight or ill. ASHA is being paid Rs. 250 for conducting home visits for the care
of the newborn.
• Mother and Child Tracking System: A name based Mother and Child Tracking System
has been put in place which is web based to ensure registration and tracking of all
pregnant women and new born babies so that provision of regular and complete services
to them can be ensured.
• Capacity building of health care providers: Various trainings are being conducted under
NRHM to train doctors, nurses and ANM for early diagnosis and case management of
common ailments of children and care of mother during pregnancy and delivery. These
trainings are on IMNCI, NSSK, SBA, LSAS, EMOC, BMOC etc.
• Management of Malnutrition: 657 Nutritional Rehabilitation Centres have been established
for management of severe acute malnutrition cases.
• Appropriate infant and young child feeding practices are being promoted in convergence
with Ministry of Woman and Child Development. Village Health and Nutrition Days
(VHNDs) are organized for imparting nutritional counselling to mothers and to improve
child care practices.
• Universal Immunization Programme: Vaccination protects children against many life
threatening diseases such as Tuberculosis, Diphtheria, Pertussis, Polio, Tetanus,
Hepatitis B and Measles. Infants are thus immunized against seven vaccine preventable
diseases every year. The Government of India supports the vaccine programme by
supply of vaccines and syringes, Cold chain equipments and provision of operational
costs.
Strategies Adopted for achieving target set for TFR
• Emphasising more on spacing methods like IUCD.
• Promoting Post-partum Family Planning services especially PPIUCD.
• Increasing the basket of choices.
• Leveraging huge workforce of ASHAs for delivering contraceptives at doorstep as well
as counselling couples for ensuring delay in first child birth and having spacing between
first and second child.
• Ensuring availability of fixed Day family planning services at all facilities.
• Ensuring quality care in Family Planning services by establishing Quality Assurance
Committees at State and District levels.
• Accreditation of more private/NGO facilities for family planning services under PPP.
Increasing male participation and promoting Non-scalpel vasectomy.

PULSE POLIO PROGRAMME
Recommendation/Observation
1.19 The Committee appreciates that the Department has been able to eradicate polio in the

Ministry of Health & Family Welfare is fully geared up and alert and is not showing any
slackness due to the success achieved in polio programme. The India Expert Advisory Group
(IEAG) consists of International and National experts who review the polio programme, its
epidemiological situation etc. periodically. The last meeting of the IEAG was held on 15th and 16th

VI. NATIONAL VECTOR BORNE DISEASE CONTROL PROGRAMME (NVBDCP)
Recommendation/Observation
1.21 The Department had informed that against a Plan Allocation of Rs.430 crore for 2011-12,
the expenditure was Rs. 412.66 crore till 23.03.12. Further, the target of bringing the number of
cases to less than 1 per 10,000 populations could not be achieved by 2010 as envisaged by
National Health Policy (2002), for elimination of Kala Azar. However, the target is set to be
achieved by 2015. The Department has been allocated at outlay of Rs. 447.00 crore for the year
2012-13. The Committee is at pains to understand that a period of 10 years was not enough to
eliminate Kala Azar and the target date has been further set back by three years. The Committee
feels that the initiatives taken earlier for Kala-Azar elimination did not have the desired impact. The
Committee would, therefore, like to be enlightened about the short-comings identified in the Kala
Azar elimination programme and how the Department plans to re-orient its policies for achieving
the desired results in terms of elimination of Kala-Azar. The Committee also desires that an
evaluation of the implementation of the programme may be undertaken. (Para 6.3)
Action Taken
• Against plan allocation of Rs.430 crore (excluding NE) for 2011-12, the expenditure is
Rs.433.19 crore (excluding NE) till 31.03.12.
• During 2012-13, the plan allocation of Rs.455.73 crore (excluding NE) has been made.
• The target of Kala-Azar elimination (number of cases less than 1 per 10,000 population
at block level) could not be achieved by 2010. However, target data is revised to 2015.
The constraints and shortcomings identified in the Kala-Azar Elimination Programme for
such a delay and revising the target date are as under:
• Till 2008, diagnosis of kala-azar was being done by bone marrow aspiration or
splenic puncture which was possible at District hospital. This used to delay
institution of treatment and allowing transmission to continue.
• Injectable Sodium Stibo Gluconate (SSG) was the drug of choice for treatment of
kala-Azar cases till 2008 and needed hospitalization for institution of treatment.
Moreover, long duration of treatment (one month) lead to non-compliance and non-
responsiveness to SSG.
• Social mobilization for the control of kala-Azar including for indoor residual spray
had been limited and inadequate attention has been paid to behaviour change
communication.
• Because of administrative delays often funds were not received at the District/PHC
level due to non-release of funds. Non-submission of SOE & UCs by the States
hampered release of funds by the Government of India.
• The suggestion of the Committee to undertake an evaluation of the implementation
of the programme has been acted upon by the Department and a meeting of central
panel of experts has been held to finalize the methodology for the same.
Department proposes following initiatives to be undertaken during Twelfth Five year Plan
Period:

63
Surveillance and Case Management
• Strengthening of early case detection and complete treatment:
• Upscaling the use of rapid diagnostic test kits at the PHC level.
• Treatment with new oral drug Miltefosine which has been expanded to all the Kala-Azar
endemic Districts as first line treatment on Directly Observed Treatment (DOT) pattern
as a supervised treatment with patient coding system for tracking.
• ASHAs would be trained and fully involved to ensure complete treatment compliance
with incentive of Rs. 200/- per case.
• Incentive to the patient towards compensation for loss of wages for 28-30 days @ Rs.
50/- per day during the period of treatment.
• Active case detection by increasing the frequency of door to door visit by observing
Kala-Azar fortnight twice in a year and also through camp approach and also to
intensify the searches for PKDL cases.
• Monitoring of diagnosis and treatment will be accelerated by frequent visits by
programme personnel as well as by proposed coordinators.
• Additional human resource, their capacity building and intensive IEC/BCC.
Vector Management
• Indoor residual spraying (IRS) for interruption of transmission will be taken up in all
the 52 endemic Districts of the country to ensure good quality spray and coverage
above 80 %.
• Monitoring of the process and impact of indoor residual spraying would be stepped out
through independent studies on the effect of spraying on vector populations and
susceptibility studies.
• Environment sanitation will be given considerable importance in a BCC campaign to
eliminate the breeding sites of the vector species.
Initiatives are underway for the provision of alternative housing sites to the poor and
marginalized population in the Kala-Azar villages, who are the most common victims of disease,
under the Indira Vikas Yojana.

VIII. NA TIONAL LEPROSY ERADICATION PROGRAMME
Recommendation/Observation
1.24 As per information available to the Committee, the following States have shown the highest
number of cases where leprosy has been detected during the last three years i.e. 2008 to 2011
namely Chhattisgarh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal. The Committee
is constrained to note that India still accounts for more than 50% of the new leprosy cases
worldwide. The efforts made so far have still not yielded the desired results. The Committee
would, therefore, strongly recommend to the Department to monitor the measures taken so far to
eliminate this disease. (Para 8.4)
Action Taken
Elimination of leprosy i.e. less than one case per 10,000 population was achieved at National
level in Dec., 2005. The prevalence of leprosy has been decreasing in India over the years. From
a level of 42 cases per 100,000 population in 2001-02, it has come down to 7 cases per 100,000
population in 2010-11. However, considering very long incubation period of the disease which could
be from few weeks to 20 years, India will continue to have new leprosy cases for many more
years to come.
Government of India continues to accord high priority to elimination of leprosy within the
overall framework of National Rural Health Mission (NRHM). Leprosy diagnosis and treatment
services have been integrated into general health care system, and village level functionaries like
ASHAs and Anganwadi Workers are involved in bringing leprosy suspects to the health care system
for their detection and proper treatment. The Government of India is advocating a District specific
approach for elimination of leprosy during the Twelfth plan period (2012-17). The special measures
for achieving elimination at District level include improved and early cases detection and case
management through intensified activities like active case finding, IEC/BCC in the community,
capacity building of medical, para-medical, community workers and improved monitoring and
supervision.

Recommendation/Observation

Action Taken
1. Johnson & Johnson’s (USA) research subsidiary, TIBOTEC, is managing the clinical
development of TMC 2007.
2. The Phase I trial was completed in South Africa and results published in 2008.
3. Phase II (part A) was done in South Africa and published in 2009. The study results
showed it reduced the time to sputum conversion to negative and TMC eliminated TB
bacteria more quickly and was shown to be safe and well tolerated in the patients.
4. The second stage of the Phase II (part B) was initiated in late 2009 as a multi-national
trial involving patients in South Africa, Peru, Latvia, India, Brazil, Thailand, the
Philippines and Russia. The stage is still on-going and for which the results are likely
to become available by end 2012 or early 2013.
After successful Phase II trials, the drug will enter Phase-III clinical trials (minimum 5
years) before it is available for routine patient care.

3.13 To accelerate the pace of reduction of Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) in the country, the

Recommendations/Observations

burden is indicative of the magnitude of the problem and reminds of the challenges ahead. Though

for cost-escalation. (Para 4.2 & 4.3)
V. DR. RAM MANOHAR LOHIA HOSPITAL
The Committee observes that fixing a time-frame for completion of the projects is
extremely important from the point of view of efficient utilization of scarce resources. The
Committee would, therefore, reiterate its earlier recommendation regarding fixing a time-
frame and striving to adhere the same. (Para 5.6)
VIII. LADY HARDINGE MEDICAL COLLEGE
The Committee while noting the Department’s reply, feels that there seems to be a
sorry state of affairs in the recruitment for various posts due to non-completion of
additional facilities under Comprehensive Re-development Plan – Phase I. The current
situation is that neither the re-development plan has been completed and nor the vacancies
are filled. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should initiate steps
to fill up the 409 posts on the premise that the process may take upto six months by which
time the additional facilities under phase I (August, 2013) would be in place as committed
by the Department in its reply. (Para 8.5)
IX. ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES (AIIMS)
The Committee is extremely dismayed at the tenor of the reply of the Department.
Instead of apprising the Committee of the cogent reasons for non-setting up of a Burns
Units at AIIMS, the Department has been offering various alibis for the same. If the
ground reality indeed did not warrant setting up of a Burns Unit at AIIMS, why was the
Unit conceived in the first place. The Committee would, therefore, like the Department to
submit detailed explanation in this regard. (Para 9.9)
The Committee is pained to note that despite its repeated recommendation to
liquidate the vacancies, not much headway has been made towards wiping out the vacancies
which is evident from a substantial number of 2409 vacancies. The Committee is
constrained to observe that though it has been claimed that all efforts are being made to
fill the vacancies, the facts project an altogether different picture. The Committee is aware
that the efforts made in the past to fill the vacancies have not borne fruit due to ambiguous
recruitment policy. The Committee would, therefore, expect the Department to pay focussed

87
attention to the recruitment of qualified personnel and impresses upon the Department to
launch Special Recruitment Drives so that the perennial shortage of qualified personnel is
addressed. (Para 9.11)
XII. NORTH EASTERN INDIRA GANDHI REGIONAL INSTITUTE OF HEALTH AND
MEDICAL SCIENCES (NEIGRIHMS), SHILLONG
Only Recruitment Rules have been modified. But it appears the recruitment drive
has not been commenced. The Committee reiterates its recommendation to take up special
recruitment drive. (Para 12.6 & 12.7)
XIV. DEVELOPMENT OF NURSING SERVICES
The Committee does not agree with the reasons given by the Department for under-
utilization of funds. The Committee is of the opinion that reasons cited for under
achievement like unavailability of audited statements of expenditure, agency details for
release and undertakings etc. from the concerned State Government could have been sorted
out, had the Department pursued the matter with the State Governments vigorously. The
Committee accordingly recommends to the Department to take a more proactive approach
in this matter. (Para 14.3)
The Department has not indicated about the assessment of demand and availability
of residential accommodation for nurses that was to be done by the Department. The
Committee desires that this may be done at the earliest. (Para 14.12)
XV. NATIONAL MENTAL HEALTH PROGRAMME
The Department only indicated about the meetings planned. Apparently no meeting
was held till the receipt of ATN. The Committee observes that at this rate, the targets
cannot be achieved. There needs more pro-active approach on the part of the Department.
(Para 15.5)
The Committee observes that though the Department claims to have held meetings
to identify the loopholes in the implementation of the Scheme, it has not indicated the
outcome of such meetings. The Institutes need to take necessary steps to achieve the
targets. (Para 15.9)
XVI. CENTRAL DRUGS STANDARD CONTROL ORGANISATION (CDSCO)
The Committee observes that the Drug Inspector plays a vital role in ensuring that
pharmaceutical products are of legal standards and grading. It is in this context that the
filling up of 100 vacant posts of Drug Inspector assume added significance. Even though
written test was held in 2011, the interviews were not held till ATN was sent by the
Department. The Committee would like to urge that the Department, pursue the matter of
recruitment of Drug Inspectors with UPSC so that they are in place at the earliest.
(Para 16.3)
The Committee views with concern the status of labs for testing of drug samples and
is surprised to know the sub-optimal capability of these labs in view of the menace of
availability of spurious and substandard drugs in the market. Moreover, the Committee is
also disappointed to know about the efforts put in by the Department providing sophisticated
equipments and additional manpower in these labs for the last four years yet the capability
of the labs for testing of samples of drugs is sub-optimal. Opening of new budget line for

88
strengthening the drug regulatory systems at the State level, with Central assistance may
be effectively used to address the bottlenecks which restrain the forward movement in this
regard. (Para 16.5)
The Committee notes from the submission made in Annexure-VI that the Central
Pharma PSUs has a critical role to play in the promotion of quality generic drugs. The
Committee is also convinced that the supply of low cost quality medicines cannot be
sustained without the participation of the Central Pharma PSUs. The Committee is,
however, aware that the revival of Indian Drugs and Pharmaceuticals company which had
been declared sick in 1992 by Board of Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) and
is still hanging fire. Besides, the production and sales turnover of Karnataka Antibiotics and
Pharmaceuticals Limited and Rajasthan Drugs and Pharmaceuticals are more or less static
in value terms since 2007-08. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of
Health and Family Welfare should urgently take up the matter of revival/ modernisation of
all Central Pharma with the nodal Department ( i.e. Department of Pharmaceuticals) so that
the objective of access to quality generic medicines could be realised within the shortest
possible time. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the progress made towards
finalisation of the new initiative, namely “Free medicines for all through Public Health
Facilities”. (Para 16.7)
XVII. V ACCINE MANUFACTURING UNITS
The Committee expresses its displeasure over the slow pace of the revival of the
three vaccine units and feels that the Department is not pursuing the matter vigorously
which has very serious implications on the vaccine prices and the resultant impact on
Universal Immunisation Programme. The Committee, therefore, exhorts the Department to
shed its casual attitude and ensure that the work regarding upgradation of these vaccine
manufacturing units be completed at the earliest. (Para 17.3)
The Committee observes that the Department has not addressed its concern
regarding under-utilisation of funds allocated for CRI, Kasauli in a satisfactory manner. In
a resource constrained country like India, optimal and judicious utilisation of allocated
funds is of paramount importance. The Committee would expect the Department to apprise
it of the roadmap for better financial performance under this head. (Para 17.9)
XXII. TELEMEDICINE
The Committee notes that the Scheme was approved by SFC in December, 2010/
January, 2011. Two years have elapsed since then, but the matter is still under examination.
The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department to quickly finalise the issues
involved and implement the project at the earliest. (Para 22.3)
XXV. HUMAN RESOURCE FOR HEALTH
The Committee had presented its 60th Report on the NCHRH Bill, 2011 to both the
Houses of Parliament in the Winter Session of the Parliament (December, 2011). While
the Committee expects that the Government has taken into account the
recommendations, nevertheless for the sake of clarity it recommends that while
redrafting the said Bill special emphasis on restoring the autonomy of the existing
Councils; setting up of other Councils; inclusion of AYUSH; adequate participation of
State Governments, etc. be made. (Para 25.4)

89
PART-B
NRHM
I. BUDGETARY PROVISIONS
The Committee notes that the gap between the expected targets and the
achievements are too wide to be comfortable within the first phase of NRHM (2005-2012).
In response to the Committee recommendation to the Department to undertake a review
of NRHM and to take concrete and concerted efforts to plug the gaps and bottlenecks in
the implementation of programme that existed in the first phase, the Ministry has stated
generically that the Ministry has taken note of the above recommendations of the
Committee for compliance, without spelling out the mechanisms envisaged to be employed
to identify the inadequacies and iron them out. The Committee again impresses upon the
Ministry to undertake a thorough review before the second phase (2012-13) is implemented
on the ground and take corrective measures accordingly. (Para 2.5)
The Committee notes the observations of the Planning Commission on the
recommendations of the Committee. The Committee feels that the observation of the
Planning Commission on the absorptive capacity of the State Health Systems require
attention of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The Committee feels that
increasing the public spending on health from 1% to 2.5% of GDP by the end of 12th Plan
is a sin-qua-non  for the success of the NRHM flagship scheme. However, the same cannot
be achieved without strengthening the absorptive capacity of State Health Systems. Ministry
of Health and Family Welfare should playa vital role in augmenting the absorption capacity
of State Health Systems. The Committee, therefore, impresses upon the Department to
seriously set its sights on strengthening of the State Health Systems in order to ensure that
the funds released for health systems are capable of being absorbed properly by the State
Health Systems. (Para 2.6 & 2.7)
III. INFRASTRUCTURE STRENGTHENING
HEALTH CARE UNITS
While making the above recommendations, the Committee had expected the
Department to indicate its reaction to desirability or otherwise of contractual appointments
and their impact on offering quality healthcare services and formulate appropriate policy
response accordingly. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that the Department
has sought to wash its hands off the matter by merely stating that the vacancies are filled
up by State/UT Governments and the matter is being taken up with them. Since the
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is the principal financier of NRHM, it is its
obligation to see that the quality of healthcare services is not compromised in any way and
help the States devise appropriate strategies for the purpose.
The Committee notes from a perusal of the statement (as on 31st December, 2011)
of staff appointed under NRHM on contractual basis across the country that the number of
contractual staff are still substantial as they may not be amenable to punctuality, discipline,
and control. The Committee would also like to be enlightened on the total number of in-
position posts vis-a-vis  sanctioned strength as per RHS 2011 and the measures taken/
contemplated to be taken to overcome the deficiencies as pointed out in RHS 2011.
(Para 3.3 & 3.4)

90
V. RCH FLEXIBLE POOL
The Committee had directed the Department to put in place a rigorous monitoring
mechanism of evaluation of the effectiveness of the measures so taken. However, the reply
of the Department is silent on this aspect. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its
recommendation made in its 54th Report to provide details of monitoring mechanism of
evaluation of the effectiveness of the measures so taken in this regard. (Para 5.3)
JANANI SURAKSHA YOJANA
The Committee is aware that the Expert Group submitted its Report on the
evaluation of the Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY). A considerable period of time has elapsed
since then. By now the Ministry must have initiated follow-up action on the
recommendations contained in the said Report. The Committee is therefore unhappy to note
that the Department instead of acquainting the Committee with the follow-up action taken
on the findings of the Expert Group has sought to give an evasive reply. The Committee
recommends that a concrete and specific action plan be prepared for removing the gaps.
(Para 5.22 & 5.23)
VI. NATIONAL VECTOR BORNE DISEASES CONTROL PROGRAMME (NVBDCP)
The Committee notes that a considerable period of time has elapsed since the
recommendation of the Group of Ministers was sent for approval. The Committee,
therefore, feels that the Ministry needs to be more proactive to push its case for approval
as delays in approvals lead to delay in implementation. (Para 6.9 & 6.10)
VII. NA TIONAL T.B. CONTROL PROGRAMME
The Committee notes that the default rate under the programme has declined from
6.9% in 2006 to 5.5% in 2011. The Committee expresses displeasure with the mere decline
of only 1.4% in the 5 year period mentioned above. The Committee feels that T.B being
a highly contagious disease, reduction of just 1.4% over a period of 5 years is not sufficient.
The Committee feels that the Department ought to take more stringent steps to increase
the tempo of curative as well as preventive aspects under the programme; otherwise all
measures taken so far would fall by wayside. (Para 7.4)
IX. NATIONAL TRACHOMA AND BLINDNESS CONTROL PROGRAMME
While making the above recommendation, the Committee had expected to be
provided with the details of progress made towards setting up of the Eye banks. However,
the Committee is dismayed to note that the Department has merely stated that funds have
been released to States/Union Territories for setting up of 57 Eye Banks. The Department
should have made efforts to collect the updated status of physical performance of the
project and apprised the Committee accordingly. The Committee, therefore, deprecates the
Department for its casual approach and exhorts it to use greater care while formulating its
reply in future. (Para 9.4)

ANNEXURE-VII TO PARA 16.7
BRIEF NOTE ON JAN AUSHADHI SCHEME
(QUALITY MEDICINES AT AFFORDABLE PRICES)
The Need - Over the years, India has developed a strong capability in producing generic medicines in
almost all the therapeutic categories. These medicines are being sold mostly as branded medicines,
which pushes up the retail price of these medicines. There is still a large population of poor people
in the country which finds it difficult to afford these medicines. In fact access to quality health care
is a challenge in a developing country like India. According to NSO estimates, upto 79% cost of health
care in rural areas is due to cost of medicines. This problem gets further aggravated as upto 80% of
expenditure on health care is out-of-pocket. With 65% of India’s population not having access to
modern health care (WHO estimates 2000 the entire problem is compounded several times.
Unbranded Generic Medicines Vs. Branded Medicines - Therefore, access to quality medicines at
affordable prices is a key challenge for the Government. In this connection the prices of branded
medicines are generally higher than generic medicines due to various reasons inter-alia including
branded drugs having patent protection and a number of drugs having limited regulation through the
Drug Prices Control Order, 1995 etc. A sample comparison of some of the prices is given below:
Name of salt Dosage Pack Market Generics Difference
Price (Rs.) Price (Rs.)
Antibiotic: Ciprofloxacin 250 mg 10 55.00 1 1.10 5 times higher
Pain Killer: Diclofenac 100 mg 10 36.70 3.50 10 times higher
Common Cold: Cetrizine 10 mg 10 20.00 2.75 7 times higher
Fever: Paracetamol 500 mg 10 10.00 2.45 4 times higher
Pain and Fever: Nimesulide 100 mg 10 25.00 2.70 9 times higher
Cough Syrup 110 ml bottle 33.00 13.30 2.5 times higher
For the above reasons therefore, making available medicines at affordable prices has been taken up by
the newly created Department of Pharmaceuticals.
Jan Aushadhi Campaign -  For fulfillment of this goal, a Campaign in the name of Jan Aushadhi
Campaign has been launched in 2008. The aim of this campaign is to make available quality medicines
at afforadable prices for all, especially the poor and the disadvantaged. Under this campaign, less priced
quality unbranded generic medicines will be made available through Jan Aushadhi Stores which
inherently are less priced but are of same and equivalent quality, efficacy and safety as compared to
branded generic medicines.
The generic medicines are being supplied in the first instance by the Central Pharma PSUs which will
ensure both quality and timely supply. Medicines not available currently with the CPSUs will be sourced
from quality SME units. This will also give support to the Pharma SME sector also as well as promote
public-private partnership and avenues for achievement of corporate social responsibilities geared
towards affordable medicare for the masses. The Jan Aushadhi Campaign has now been formalized as
Generic Drug Scheme with the approval of the Planning Commission.

124
Scheme Details -  Under this Scheme, the State Government has to provide space in Government
Hospital premises for the running of the outlets (JAS) Government hospitals, NGOs, Charitable
Organisations and public societies like Red Cross Society. Rogi Kalyan Samiti typically constituted for
the purpose can be operating agencies for the JAS. The operating agency for JAS is nominated on the
basis of the recommendations of the State Government. Operational expenditure is met from trade
margins admissible for the medicines. The State Government has to ensure prescription of unbranded
generic medicines by the Government doctors. The Jan Aushadhi Programme is accordingly being a
self sustaining business model not dependeation Government subsidies or assistance. It runs on the
principle of “Not for Profits but with Minimal Profits”. In order to incentivise and provide the initial
trigger for above, it is envisaged that the Central Government would provide, if need be, a token
amount of Rs. 50,000/- as infrastructural support and one-time financial support of Rs.2.00 lakhs to
NGO etc. on reimbursement basis, setting up the Jan Aushadhi Outlet.
Jan Aushadhi Stores -  The Jan Aushadhi Campaign of the Central Governemnt is exprected to make
a contribution by way of achieving the socio-economic goal of affordable health are through ensuring
availability of quality drugs at affordable prices for all. At present, 231 medicines are being supplied
in the 121 JAS opened (till 10
th May, 2012) in the States of Punjab, Haryana, Uttarakhand, Odisha,
Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Union Territories of
Chandigarh and Delhi. A list of Jan Aushadhi Opened is given below:
The scheme is also expected to lead to reduction of state health expenditure on branded medicines,
more patient coverage, popularization of the use of unbranded generic medicines which will bring down
the actual out-of-pocket costs of medicines, for the common man due to wider availability (at present
only 2% of the total medicines supplied in the market are unbranded medicines) and finally better and
more affordable health care driven by the reduction in costs of medicines as the majority coponent of
health care expenses.
People’s Participation -  The assistance sought is for just one time facilitative incentive to the Jan
Aushadhi outlet operating agency which would be an NGO/Charitable body/Cooperative body/health care
driven societies like the Red Cross Society/Rogi Kalyan Samiti, etc. who would do the actual operation
of the outlet on the principle of minimal profits obtained from the minimal margins included in the cost
of the medicine itself. There is no subsidy or recurring assistance envisaged either by the State or the
Central Gvoernment. Additionally it may be appreciated that if there are no dedicated outlets at strategic
locations, it may not be possible to promote the usage of unbranded generic medicines as mere media
campaigns without commensurate ready availability would be a wasted effort Cooperation of the State
Governments is essential for locating the outlets in the district hospital premises. The Generic Drugs
Scheme is an attempt in this direction based on a viable business model not requiring Government
subsidy. The Programme does not envisage grant of any upfront subsidy other than the assistance
indicated above to provide some support from the Government/BPPI to NGOs etc.
Benefits of the Scheme -  The Jan Aushadhi Campaign will help:
(i) Improve access to healthcare in as much as cost of treatment would come down
substatially. This would enable the public Health System to increase the coverage.
(ii) Secure a socio-economically viable mechanism/institutional arrangement for efficacions
sales of Pharma CPSU products, thereby improving their viability.
(iii) Promote and encourage private industry to sell their quality unbranded generic products
through these retail outlets.
(iv) Ensure successful implementation of the Jan Aushadhi campaign would dispel the myth
that quality of medicines is linked to price and demonstrate that quality medicines can be
sold at substantially lower prices.

125
(v) Educate dotors that unbranded generic medicines provide a better option than branded
products since quality of generic medicines can be equally efficacious and safe at much
lower prices.
(vi) Create Consumer awareness and involve private and charitable bodies and NGOs by
making them part of the campaign.
(vii) Reduce promotional cost and profits for the benefit of patients etc.
Constraints -
(i) Availability of space for Jan Aushadhi Stores at Hospital premises.
(ii) Prescription of medicines in generic form by Government Doctors/Private Doctors
(iii) A wareness among general public. Ministry of Health and Family Welfare may take suitable
action to help overcome the above constraints.

PREFACE
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and
Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee hereby present this 65 th Report of the
Committee on the proposal to introduce the Bachelor of Science (Community Health) course in the
country.
2. The Committee, at its meeting held on 18 th January, 2011, took note of the media reports
regarding Government’s move to introduce Bachelor of Rural Health Care (BRHC) course (now
Bachelor of Science (Community Health)) to overcome the shortage of the doctors in the country.
The Committee felt that it would be in the fitness of things to take up the subject for detailed
examination for studying all the pros and cons of the proposed move of the Government, since
the Committee felt that shortage of doctors looming in the country is a cause of serious concern
and needed to be addressed immediately.
3. The Committee deliberated on the issue in its meetings held on the 27
th January,
06th May, 1 st July, 22 nd, 27 th December, 2011, 20 th March, 09 th April, 8 th November, 2012,
8th February, 2013 and 13 th March, 2013.
4. During the course of examination of the subject mentioned above, the Committee heard the
views of Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare along with the Chairman, Board of
Governors and Medical Council of India on 27
th January, 22 nd December and 27 th December, 2011
and 8 th November, 2012. The Committee also had the benefit to hear the views of certain experts
in this field during its meetings held on 06 th May and 01 st July, 2011 (List of Experts at
Annexure-I). The Committee expresses its wholehearted thanks to all the witnesses who
enlightened the Committee with their views.
5. During the course of the examination of the subject under reference and finalization of its
Report thereon, the Committee relied upon the following documents/papers:–
(i) Status Note and Concept Note received Department of Health and Family Welfare
and Medical Council of India (MCI);
(ii) Report of the Task Force on Medical Education for the National Rural Health Mission
headed by Shri Javid Chowdhury, Ex-Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare
(iii) O ral evidence tendered by the Secretary and other officers of the Department of
Health and Family Welfare and representatives of Board of Governors, Medical
Council of India;
(iv) Write-up received from Prof. K. Srinath Reddy, President, Public Health Foundation
of India and Dr. Meenakshi Gautham, Post doctorate fellow with the Institute of
Health Policy and Management, Erasmus University, Netherlands.
6. The Committee at its meeting held on the 13
th March, 2013 considered and adopted the
Draft Report.

7. For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.
 BRAJESH PATHAK
