PREFACE
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and
Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do
hereby present this Sixty-seventh Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand
No. 47) of the Department of Health and Family Welfare, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare,
for the year 2013-14.
2. The Committee held one sitting on 6
th April, 2013 for examination of Demands for Grants
(2013-14) of the Department of Health and Family Welfare and heard the Secretary (Health and
Family Welfare) and other Officers thereon.
3. The Committee while making its observations/recommendations has mainly relied upon the
following documents:–
(i) Address by the President of India to both Houses of Parliament assembled together on
21
st February, 2013;
(ii) Speech of Finance Minister on 28th February, 2013 while presenting the Union Budget
2013-2014;
(iii) Implementation of Budget Announcements 2012-2013;
(iv) Detailed Demands for Grants of the Department of Health and Family Welfare for the
year 2013-2014;
(v) Annual Report of the Department for the year 2012-2013;
(vi) Outcome Budget of the Department for the year 2013-14;
(vii) Detailed Explanatory Note on Demands for Grants of the Department of Health and
Family Welfare for the year 2013-2014;
(viii) Physical and financial targets fixed and achievements made during the Eleventh Plan
period;
(ix) Projection of outlays for the schemes to be undertaken by the Department during the
Twelfth Five Year Plan;
(x) Details of under-utilization of the allocations made under different heads during the last
three years;
(xi) Written replies furnished by the Department to the Questionnaires sent to them by the
Secretariat;
(xii) Presentation made by the Secretary (Health and Family Welfare) and other concerned
officers; and
(xiii) W ritten clarifications furnished by the Department, on the points/issues raised by the
Members during the deliberations of the Committee.
4. The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on
23rd April, 2013.

5. For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.
 BRAJESH PATHAK

PART-A
HEALTH SECTOR
I. INTRODUCTION
1.1 The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is instrumental and responsible for
implementation of various programmes on the national scale in the areas of Health and Family
Welfare, prevention and control of major communicable diseases and promotion of traditional and
indigenous systems of medicine. Apart from these, the Ministry also assists the States in preventing
and controlling the spread of seasonal diseases’ outbreaks and epidemics through technical
assistance.
1.2 The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare incurs expenditure either directly under Central
Schemes or through its four Departments:–
• Department of Health and Family Welfre
• Department of AYUSH
• Department of Health Research; and
• Department of AIDS Control
1.3 The National Health Policy framed from time to time provides the framework for the
implementation of policies and programmes for health care. The Eleventh Five Year Plan had
focused on the poor and the underprivileged. Accessible, equitable and affordable health care was
a priority concern and therefore emphasis was accorded to reducing disparities in health across
regions and communities by ensuring access to affordable health . The Twelfth Plan envisages
building on the achievements of the Eleventh Plan for extending outreach of public health services
and for moving towards the long term objective of establishing a system of Universal Health
coverage through National Health Mission.
1.4 The Department of Health and Family Welfare comprises of Health Sector and NHM Sector.
The various activities under the Health Sector to name a few include Pradhan Mantri Swasthya
Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY), Central Government managed hospitals and autonomous institutions of
Medical Education under the Department,Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS), Central
Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), various National Programmes, etc. Similarly, the
National Health Mission is comprised of two sub-copmponents viz. National Rural Health Mission
(NRHM) and National Urban Health Mission (NUHM). The Main activities being covered under both
Health and NHM Sector are described in detail below.

that in future utilization must reflect the allocation policy objectives to the extent possible.
2.3 In the Twelfth Plan the proposed and approved outlays for the Department of Health and
Family Welfare (Health Sector) are Rs. 184788.24 crore and Rs. 75145.29 crore respectively. The
Committee was informed that this reduction in outlay was likely to affect implementation of a
number of ongoing schemes. It was also informed that National Urban Health Mission which was
proposed to be rolled out in the year could be provided only a token provision of Rs. 1.00 crore
during 2013-14. The Committee was further informed that several new programmes proposed in
the Twelfth Plan could not take off due to limited availability of funds. Moreover, new initiatives
like provision of free generic medicines in all public health facilities, strengthening of district
hospitals to provide advanced secondary care, Human Resources for Health, Strengthening
regulations in drugs and food sector, would be impacted negatively, as approved outlay is barely
sufficient to meet on-going health interventions. The focus has been to sustain the current
interventions, so that progress achieved so far is not reversed.
2.4 With this trend of allocation of funds and persistent under utilization, the Committee
is concerned that the Department needs to tackle the problems of shrinking resources, rising
demand and under utilization of allocated funds in a balanced manner. Utilization status of
the Eleventh Plan and for 2012-13 reveals inability of the Department to utilize the allocated
funds efficiently. During 2012-13 only 52.26 per cent of allocated funds have been utilized till
31.12.2012, thus leaving the balance to be utilized in the last quarter of the financial year.
The Committee is disappointed by this evident lack of fiscal discipline and strongly
recommends that the Department should seek target oriented allocation in sync with the
ability to utilize the allocated funds; instead of indicative allocation of funds. The Committee,
further opines that a token provision of Rs.1 crore for National Urban Health Mission during
2013-14 on account of limited availability of funds would further impact the health indicators
of poor people residing in urban slums and recommends that the Department should approach
the Planning Commission for enhanced allocation at RE stage.

for the Department of Health and Family Welfare (Health Sector) for the Annual Plan 2013-14. As

2.6 The Committee is constrained to note 41% shortfall in allocation of funds vis-à-vis

overcome the financial constraints the Department should make efforts to achieve
efficiency gain in utilization each year and also to convince the Planning Commission and
the Department of Expenditure for enhancing the Annual Plan allocation for the remaining
years of the Twelfth Plan and also at RE 2013-14 so as to achieve the ultimate target for

3.13 On the query of the Committee on the steps being taken to ensure that the instructions
issued to the CMO in charge of all the Wellness Centre to stop the pilferage of medicines is being
scrupously followed, the Department informed that CMOs in-Charge are expected to adhere to the
detailed instructions issued to them in this regard. To ensure that the instructions are followed by
them properly, the following steps have been taken:
(a) The CMOs In-charge are sensitized about it regularly by the Additional Director of the
concerned zone/city in the monthly meetings.
(b) Surprise Inspections are carried out by the superior officers to verify the stock of
drugs/medicines in the dispensary stores/counters.
(c) Internal Audit Unit of Vigilance Division of CGHS does surprise visits to know as to
whether the guidelines to stop pilferage of medicines are being adhered to.
(d) Appropriate actions are taken in case of non-compliance of the instructions.
(e) To exercise an effective check on pilferage of medicines from the CGHS Wellness
centres, an ‘SMS Alert system’ has been introduced. A system generated message is
sent to the CGHS beneficiaries indicating that he/she has been issued medicines from
the CGHS dispensary. Registration of Mobile number has also been made compulsory.
3.14 In this regard the Committee recommends that in addition to the steps already

stage. Comparable measures of quality should also be worked out at the earliest.

actions are implemented and action taken:–

and to integrate these with general health services. At present DMHP has been extended to 123
Districts in 30 States/ UTs. It envisages a community based approach to the problem, which includes:
• Training of mental health team at identified nodal institutions.
• Increase awareness and reduce stigma related to Mental Health problems.
• Provide service for early detection and treatment of mental illness in the community
(OPD/Indoor and follow up).
• Provide valuable data and experience at the level of community at the State and Center
for future planning and improvement in service and research.

16.1 Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation headed by the Drugs Controller General (India)
regulates the quality of drugs, cosmetics and medical devices in the country and administers
various provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Acts and rules framed thereunder through various
technical and statutory bodies.

and the actual utilization was Rs. 17.13 crore. For 2013-14 the BE has been fixed at Rs.125.00
crore. However, under the new Centrally Sponsored Scheme of “Strengthening of States’ Drug
Regulatory System” a budgetary provision of Rs.100 crore has been made during the financial year
2013-2014.
16.3 The Committee is deeply concerned about the underutilization of funds and would
like the Department to provide reasons for such massive under utilization. The Committee
further recommends that the Department should take necessary steps for optimum
utilization of funds and improve the quality of delivery of services with strict emphasis on
monitoring of allocated funds.

29

expenditure on additional contractual staff, strengthening and Upgradation of physical infrastructure
of the CDSCO(HQ) and its various Zonal, Sub-Zonal and Port offices and Central Drug Testing
Laboratories, enhancement of capacity of Central Drug Testing Laboratories, starting a regular
exhaustive training programme and establishment of a formal training institute for the drugs

the process. In such a situation optimum utilization of funds in efficient way is not possible.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should make realistic

XVIII. ASSISTANCE FOR CAPACITY BUILDING
18.1 The scheme “Assistance for Capacity Building” is implemented under the project
‘Upgradation and Strengthening of Emergency Trauma Care Facility in State Government Hospitals
located on National Highways’ with a view to provide immediate treatment to victims of Road
Traffic Injury.
18.2 The Department has informed that under the Scheme ‘Assistance for Capacity Building for
Trauma Care’, Plan allocation (BE) 2012-13 was Rs.100 crores including Rs.10 crores for NER.
This was reduced to Rs.50 crores (including Rs.5 crores for NER) at RE Stage. Against this
allocation, funds of Rs.23.8966 crore have been released during 2012-13 (up to 14th March 2013)
to 11 identified government hospitals. The reason for reduction of funds at RE was non-utilization
of funds and non-submission of audited utilization certificates in time by the grantee institutions
under different State Governments.
18.3 The Committee expresses its displeasure over the casual approach in the matter
which led to such drastic under-utilization of funds for such an important Scheme. The
Committee does not understand the reasons due to which the institutions/hospitals are not
coming forward to get the grants or utilize it. The Department should go into the details
and find solutions. The Committee recommends that the Department should take stringent
measures to ensure timely submission of UCs by the Institutions being given grant under
the scheme. The Committee recommends that the Department should monitor utilization of
funds allocated from time to time so that the funds allocated could be released in time. The
Committee may be apprised of the measures adopted by the Department in this regard.

during Eleventh five year Plan and 9 new government hospitals (out of the proposed 70 new
government hospitals under Twelfth five year Plan) which are yet to be finalized. Rs.900 crores

of the scheme during Twelfth Five Year Plan. The process is likely to take some time. Hence a
lower BE has been proposed. Preference will be given to states which are not covered during
Eleventh Plan. Hilly and backward states will also be given priority.

III. CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME
The Committee is disappointed to note the continuous trend of under-utilization of
Plan Funds during the Eleventh Plan and in the year 2012-13 , more so when the
Department has sought enhanced funds at RE stage during the Eleventh Plan and 2012-13.
The actual expenditure figures also indicate that the Department could not even utilize the
funds allocated at BE stage except during 2009-10. The Committee, therefore, strongly
recommends that the Department should devise strategies to utilize the allocated funds
optimally before proposing the revised estimate so that the funds are not unnecessarily
blocked and remain unspent. The Committee could not understand why such higher
allocation was sought during successive years inspite of under-utilisation in the earlier
years. The Department should look into the matter. (Para 3.3)
Despite continuous under utilization of funds during the Eleventh Five Year Plan, there is
enhanced allocation in Plan funds to Rs. 89.92 crore in 2013-14 from Rs. 85.26 crore in RE 2012-13.
The Committee has been informed that the enhanced funds allocation under Plan Head will be
utilized for meeting the expenditure on account of salary and wages, purchase of medicines and
all other administrative expenses to be incurred by some CGHS cities for which budgets are
allocated under PLAN head only. Cities where CGHS Wellness Centres are being run under Plan
Head are: Chandigarh, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Guwahati, Shillong, Dehradun, Jabalpur, Ranchi and
Thiruvananthapuram.  The Committee is of the view that for ensuring optimum utilization of
funds in CGHS the Department needs to undertake a lot of ground work. (Para 3.5)
The Committee notes that the earmarked funds for 2013-14 under the scheme are not in
tune with the projected demand of the Department. From the figures made available to the
Committee it is evident that Rs. 694.00 crore have been allocated against projected demand of
Rs. 918.48 crore under non plan Head and Rs. 62.47 crore against the projection of Rs. 80.54
crore under Plan head. The Committee is given to understand that this deficit in allocation
may adversely affect procurement of medicines and any new initiatives/projects proposed
under CGHS during 2013-14, i.e., construction of own CGHS buildings, where plots are
already allotted, opening of already sanctioned dispensaries in Delhi and NCR. The

42
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should try its best to convince the
Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance, for enhancement of allocation at RE stage
so as to ensure required procurement of medicines and also appropriate funding for
proposed initiatives/projects. (Para 3.6)
On a query regarding the current pendency of settlement of Medical Reimbursement Claims
(MRC) of CGHS beneficiaries, the Committee has been apprised that a total of 4061 claims
involving about Rs. 16.36 crore were under process in CGHS all over the country, at the end of
December, 2012. It has also been informed that a maximum time limit of 45 days has been fixed
for settlement of Medical Reimbursement Claims (MRC) and that a report of the MRCs pending
beyond 45 days will be sent by the respective Additional Directors to the Directorate on a monthly
basis. The Committee welcomes the efforts made by the Department to bring about a
significant reduction in pendency of reimbursement claims and hopes that the Department
would be able to bring this pendency further down with its sincere efforts. The Committee
likes the Department to diligently monitor the effective implementation of the said
procedure to protect the interests of the beneficiaries. (Para 3.7)
The Department has stated that for inclusion of the proposed Health Insurance Scheme for
the Central Government employees and pensioners in the Twelfth Plan an amount of Rs. 2061
crores has been provisionally indicated as outlay. The proposal needs to be placed before the
Expenditure Finance Committee and the Cabinet for approval.  The Committee desires to be
informed of the final decision taken in the matter. (Para 3.8)
The Committee notes that the initiatives taken by the Department so far to combat
the serious problem of shortage of doctors and staff in CGHS Wellness Centres have not
been enough. The Committee strongly feels that to deal with the issue of perennial shortage
of doctors, CMOs and other supporting staff in CGHS Wellness centres, initiatives should
be taken to design a framework for optimum utilization of the available resources to fill
up the vacancies and then sustain that level so as to deal with the problem in an efficient
manner. (Para 3.10)
The Committee is dismayed by the contradictory information received from many
beneficiaries that their grievances were not heard in Wellness Centres other than the
parent CGHS dispensaries. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the
Department should ensure that effective implementation of the new initiative is taken
otherwise it would be a futile exercise on papers. The Committee also feels that double
shifts in CGHS Wellness Center would be more beneficial for a large number of
beneficiaries as well as the staff. The beneficiaries need not take leave from their offices
to visit the dispensary and larger number of patients can be covered in a day and
the burden will get distributed between the shifts so as to make it easier on the staff.
(Para 3.12)
In this regard the Committee recommends that in addition to the steps already taken
by the Department, it should also be ensured that there is no leakage at the transit stage.
Comparable measures of quality should also be worked out at the earliest. (Para 3.14)
The Committee would like to be apprised of the details on how the Department would
utilize the non-plan allocation for improving the quality of medicines being provided to the
beneficiaries. (Para 3.16)
The Committee feels that still much is required to be done in this direction as the
feedback generally received by the Committee as regards the satisfaction level of
beneficiaries is not positive. A serious introspection as regards the sufficiency of efforts
made, is required. Besides, the Committee is of the opinion that effective communication

43
strategies should be designed to encourage positive partnership among the different levels
of officials so as to generate organizational support for reforms. The Committee desires
that patient satisfaction level should regularly be reviewed. (Para 3.18)

INTRODUCTION
The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) was launched in 2005, to provide accessible
affordable and quality healthcare to the population, with focus on people living in rural areas. The
various initiatives under NRHM aim to close the Inter regional and interstate disparities to promote
delivery of health services with focus on equity. The NRHM has been able to show a direction to
provide health services to the poorest household in the remotest areas with focus on strengthening
public health systems, reducing overall morbidity, mortality and establishing a fully functional
community owned decentralized health delivery system with flexibility for need based planning.
1.1 The Department has informed that the Twelfth plan would build on the achievements of the
Eleventh Plan for extending outreach of public health services and for moving towards the long
term objective of establishing a system of Universal Health coverage through National Health
Mission. As per the information put out on the website of NRHM, at the national level, the targets
in the Twelfth
 Five Year Plan would be as under:-
• Reduction of MMR to <100 per 100000 live births
• Reducing IMR to <27 per 1000 live births
• Reduction in NMR to <18 per 1000 live births
• Reducing TFR to 2.1
• Elimination of Filaria – in all 250 districts; Kala-azar in all 514 Blocks and Leprosy in
all districts
• Reduction in TB prevalence and mortality by 50%
• Reduction in Annual Malaria incidence to <1/1000 pop.
• Reduction in JE mortality by 50%
• Sustaining case fatality rate of less than 1% for Dengue
1.2 The Government plans to fill critical gaps in infrastructure and manpower planning in
recognition of fresh challenges being posed due to increasing migration from rural to urban areas.
During the Twelfth
 Plan, the interventions under National Rural Health Mission would be extended
to the urban areas under the National Urban Health Mission which will be launched as a
sub-mission under an overarching National Health Mission, with NRHM being the other
sub-mission. It would meet the long standing need to strengthen the healthcare in urban areas with
special focus on the urban poor. Accordingly, Public health care services are sought to be further
expanded during the 12th Plan. Efforts would be directed towards financial and managerial health
systems redesigning to ensure better outcomes. To encourage the participation of States in
addressing their State specific problems, the flexible pool would be enlarged. This would enable
States to prioritize the interventions there in keeping with their needs.
1.3 Accordingly, flexi pools would comprise of the NRHM-RCH flexi pool, the National Urban
Health Mission Flexi Pool, flexi pool for communicable diseases and flexi pool for non

55
communicable diseases, injury and trauma. All interventions by the Central Government under these
flexi pools would be for interventions at the district and below levels. The NRHM-RCH flexi pool
would include interventions under Reproductive Child Health and Mission flexi pools, routine
immunization, pulse polio immunization and iodine deficiency disorder control programme,
strengthening of district hospitals for providing advanced secondary care and providing free generic
medicines in all public health institutions in the country. The flexi pools for communicable diseases
would inter-alia encompass interventions under National Vector Borne Control Programme, National
T.B. Control Programme, National Leprosy Eradication Programme and Integrated Disease
Surveillance Programme. Interventions under National Programme for control of Blindness, National
Mental Health Programme, Health care for Elderly, National Programme for Prevention and Control
of Deafness, National Tobacco Control Programme, National Oral Health Programme, National
Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke
and Assistance to States for capacity building for Burns, would be included in the flexi pool for
non-communicable Diseases, Injury and Trauma. Assistance would also be given under the National
Health Mission for Infrastructure Maintenance to States.
1.4 The National Health Mission (NHM) will build on the experience gained in implementation
of the National Rural Health Mission and focus inter-alia  on augmentation of Human Resources
by encouraging States to engage health personnel including doctors, nurses and paramedics
strengthening health infrastructure by providing support to the States for new construction/
upgradation/ renovation of healthcare facilities; strengthening First Referral Units and
Operationalisation of more 24x7 facilities, decentralized planning through Village Health Sanitation
and Nutrition Committees and Rogi Kalyan Samitis, preparation of District Health Action Plan
with convergence from all health related sectors, provisioning for health service delivery
especially in un-served and underserved areas through Medical Mobile Units; providing financial
assistance to States for selection and training of Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) who
act as a link between community and healthcare facilities; establishing Emergency Transport and
Patient Transport System, taking forward the Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK) which
entitles all pregnant women delivering in public health institutions to absolutely free and no
expense delivery, including caesarian section. The initiative stipulates free diagnostics, blood,
drugs and diet, besides free transport from home to institution, between facilities in case of a
referral and drop back home. Similar entitlements have been put in place for all sick newborns
accessing public health institutions for treatment till 30 days after birth; initiatives for tracking
every pregnant women and child to ensure registration of all pregnant mothers and neonates to
monitor the ante-natal and post-natal care of mothers and immunization of children would receive
attention. Apart of this, other areas of importance would be distribution of contraceptives
(condoms and oral pills) through ASHAs to the user homes, supply of sanitary napkins through
ASHAs at subsidized rates to rural adolescent girls; weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation
Programme; the National School Health Programme and appointments of post partum counselors
for RMNCH Services at high case load facilities. Reduction in mortality, morbidity and disability
due to burn injuries during the T welfth Five Year Plan would be focus area. The initiatives taken
by the Government for prevention and control of communicable diseases and non-communicable
diseases would be strengthened.

2.2 Approved outlay for National Health Mission (NHM) for the Twelfth Plan is Rs. 193405.71
crores as against the projected outlay of Rs. 219702.45 crores. Further against a projected demand
for Rs.32,520.13 crore for NHM, the Planning Commission has approved an outlay of Rs.20999.00
crore for 2013-14. The Committee is aware that public spending on health was targeted to
be increased to 2.5% of GDP at the launch of NRHM in 2005. However, as per figures
quoted by the Economic Survey 2012-13, public expenditure on health is just 1.29% of GDP.
Private expenditure on health is 2.9% of GDP. The Committee observes that even if the
level of government expenditure on health is increased to 2.5% of GDP, there would still
be a very substantial health care expenditure which is out-of-pocket payments made by the
households in time of health distress. The cost of health care services in the private sector
is so exorbitant that it is just unaffordable for the poor and the under-privileged. It is in
this context that the reduction in approved outlay of Rs. 193405.71 crore for NHM for the
12
th Plan against the projected demand of Rs. 219702.45 crore is cause for extreme concern
to the Committee. Keeping in view the fact that illness of a family member is the most
common reason leading to a financial crisis among poor households, the Committee lends
its full support for greater health outlays. The Committee, simultaneously, recommends
that the Department should strengthen its monitoring mechanism so as to ensure that the
available resources are utilized more efficiently and responsibility be fixed to ensure timely
disbursement and utilization of funds at all levels.

57
2.3 The Committee notes that an overarching National Health Mission (NHM) which
would include National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) and National Urban Health Mission
(NUHM) as its sub-components is proposed to be launched during the Twelfth
 Plan to
strengthen healthcare in rural and urban areas as well. The Committee cannot allow NHM
to suffer due to less approved outlay of Rs. 193405.71 crores in the Twelfth Plan as
compared to the projected outlay of Rs. 219702.45 crores. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department should explore all mechanisms for augmenting resources
for health so that the objective of NHM of providing universal health coverage does not
remain a distant dream. The Committee desires to be apprised of the measures taken/
contemplated to be taken for augmenting resources for health.

2.6 The Committee is not able to comprehend as to how Department with the approved

and Family Welfare has not been able to plausibly convince the Ministry of Finance/
Planning Commission to release the funds sought by it. The Committee is not aware of the
reasons adduced by the Planning Commission for marginal increase in allocation of funds
in BE 2013-14 over BE 2012-13 and would, therefore, like to be apprised of the same.

bearing on the progress towards Universal Health Coverage that the Department is aiming
to achieve in the near future.

effect of shortfall of funds, they have informed that due to the reduction of annual outlay of
2013-14, it would not be possible to undertake NUHM and undertake pilots for implementation of

facilities, strengthening of (Sub-Health Centres) SHCs to develop them as first post of call for

2.8 The Committee feels that funds should not be a constraint with respect to vital
Schemes like NRHM-RCH Flexible Pool, NUHM-Flexible pool National Programme for
control of Blindness, Health Care for Elderly, National Programme for Control of Deafness,

assistance to States for Capacity Building(Burns) under the NHM. Similarly the funds
allocated to the Family Welfare-Central sector is quite less than the funds sought. The

61
of Finance/Planning Commission, it needs to put in place a strong and effective physically
and financially prudent system which is able to absorb the funds allocated to it, which does

2.9 On the issue of the salient findings of the review of NRHM and action taken thereon the
Department has informed that the latest Common Review Mission (sixth CRM-Nov 2012) and
Evaluation study of NRHM in 7 States (2011) has been done by Planning Commission and the
findings are detailed below:
POSITIVES
Salient findings of 6
th (Common Review Mission) CRM
• There has been accelerated progress in achievement of key health outcomes, notably
in child survival and population stabilization.
• There is considerable increase in outpatient attendance and in-patient admissions.
• The package of health care services offered in non-high focus states has expanded and
includes a wider range of communicable and non-communicable diseases.
• There is a significant improvement in immunization services including cold chain and
vaccine logistics.
• Implementation of Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK) has resulted not only in
withdrawal of user fees, but also in great reduction in out of pocket expenditure.
• There is significant progress in the creation of new facilities and infrastructure,
especially at sub-centres, CHC and DH levels.
• Service provider vacancies have decreased due to innovations in recruitment,
task-shifting and packages for attracting and retaining skilled providers.
• Availability of drugs has increased at all levels.
• All states are now progressing towards building dedicated organizational structures for
procurement and logistics.
• The ASHA programme is functioning well in almost all the States.
• There is commendable improvement in indoor residual spraying and distribution of bed
nets in the malaria programme.
• Horizontal integration of disease control programmes continues to improve, especially
at district and state levels, and amongst peripheral workers and community levels.
Salient findings of Planning Commission’s Evaluation Study of NRHM
• An increasing high number of pregnant women are availing Ante-Natal Care (ANC)
services.

62
• Impact of many program initiatives and enhanced outreach of health services is now
evident in all the States which were reviewed.
• There is a significant improvement in the institutional deliveries.
• An increasing high number of pregnant women have reported utilization of any of the
antenatal care services.
• Institutional deliveries reported comprised of 96% as normal deliveries and 4.2% as
complicated/Caesarean as per the Planning commission’s evaluation of NRHM.
• The utilization of services in respect of communicable diseases such as leprosy and TB
increased considerably.
• Planning Commissions’ Study highlights that utilization of public health facilities for the
delivery care is also primarily increasing because of motivational efforts and support
of key health workers like ASHAs/ANMs/VHNs.
GAPS
• The distribution of case load is skewed towards the DH and CHCs rendering low
utilization of services at PHCs and SCs.
• Specialist and nurse vacancies are significant in many states particularly in remote,
difficult and tribal areas.
• Lack of long term HR policy for contractual staff is leading to constant, high attrition
and inadequate replacement which affects quality and performance.
• The deployment of HR across the health facilities is more in the facilities located in
and around urban areas. Complementary specialists are also needed at many locations
to provide services such as C-Section.
• Grievance redressal mechanisms in the States are still in rudimentary stages.
• Partnerships with medical colleges and schools of public health and other academic and
research bodies or with health NGOs are weak.
• There exists a gap in supply of drugs and RDK kits to peripheral workers and the lack
of local specific action for very high endemic pockets.
• There are shortfalls in case detection for TB and slow and incomplete roll out of
MDR-TB control measures.
• There remains a minimal gap in drugs availability at sub centres.
Action Taken
• In order to increase utilization of the peripheral health facilities, the quality and extent
of outreach services is being expanded through provision of additional beds, labour
rooms, equipment and staff quarters.
• In SHCs, a 2
nd ANM is being supported in centres with high case/delivery loads.
• In terms of PHCs, an increasingly large number are being converted to 24x7 facilities,
especially for deliveries.
• Co-location of AYUSH system is also being supported for promoting choice.

63
• To promote HR retention at remote, underserviced areas, monetary and non-monetary
incentives are being supported.
• The infrastructure development has been supported under NRHM in a big way. A
special focus on the Empowered Action Group (EAG) States has been given. These
States can propose upto 33% of their resource envelope for infrastructure development
whereas non-EAG States can propose up to 25 % of the resource envelop for the
same.
• Conditionalities, that fetch incentives/disincentives, have been introduced from 2012-13
to encourage States to undertake health sector reforms.
• The concept of high focus districts has been evolved to pay greater attention to low
health indices of remote and inaccessible areas coupled with higher incentives for
service providers in a bid to reduce inequities.
2.10 The Committee feels that the Department should set a time frame within which the
Action Taken on the findings of the review of NRHM is completed, so as to ensure that the
newly introduced NHM schemes, which includes NRHM as its sub-component, should not
suffer due to the vital gaps in physical infrastructure and Human Resources which has been
the bane of proper implementation of NRHM in the first phase. Government should
concentrate on filling up the gaps particularly the gaps in terms of ‘Specialist’ and ‘Nurse’
vacancies in many States particularly in remote, difficult and tribal areas as noticed in the
review of NRHM phase-I. Unless these gaps are filled up, implementation of the ambitious
scheme under NRHM will not yield desired results.

IV. NATIONAL URBAN HEALTH MISSION-FLEXIBLE POOL
4.1 The Ministry informed that it proposes to launch National Urban Health Mission (NUHM)
as a sub-mission of National Health Mission to cater to healthcare needs of the urban population
with focus on urban poor, by making available to them essential primary healthcare services. The
Ministry will implement NUHM as soon as necessary approvals including approval by Cabinet are
obtained.
4.2 NUHM would cover all cities/towns with a population of more than 50,000. Towns below

Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP)
5.6 As per the information furnished by the Department; Tuberculosis is a major public health
concern in India. The country accounts for nearly one-fifth of the global TB incidence and in 2009,
out of the estimated annual incidence of 9.4 million TB cases, 2.0 million were estimated to have
occurred in India. The Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP), based on internationally
recommended strategy of Directly Observed Treatment Short Course (DOTS), has the objective of
detecting at least 70% of cases and curing at least 85% of new sputum positive patients. As a
result, TB mortality in the country has reduced from over 42/lakh population in 1990 to 23/lakh
population in 2009 as per the WHO global report 2010.The prevalence of TB in the country has
reduced by 67%, from 568/lakh population in 1990 to 185/lakh population.
5.7 The Department has informed that the major policy reform undertaken during 2012-13
includes:
1 Mandatory notification of all TB cases by all Health Establishments in the country, both
public and private sectors.
2 Introduction of case based web based system of electronic recording and reporting of
TB cases (NIkshay)
3 Early diagnosis of drug resistant TB cases by expansion of MDR-TB suspect criteria
to include all retreatment smear positive TB cases and positives on any follow up.
4 Introduction of CD-NAAT for early and additional case detection on pilot basis.
5 Policy to offer voluntary counselling and testing to all TB suspects for early diagnosis
of HIV in TB patients (in high prevalence areas)
6 Pilot for cross-referral of TB and diabetes patients for early diagnosis of both the
diseases.
7 Revision of dosing for paediatric TB cases with increasing the number of weight bands
for optimal dosage.

VIII. Pulse Polio Immunization
8.1 The Department has informed that in pursuance of the World Health Assembly resolution
of 1988, the Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) Programme was started nation-wide from 1995 to
eradicate polio in India covering children in the age group 0-3 years. In order to accelerate the pace
of polio eradication, all children under the age of 5 years were targeted since 1996-97. Till
1998-99, two rounds were organized in the month of December and January each year. From
1999-2000, house to house vaccination of missed children was also introduced to vaccinate
children missed during the fixed booth based vaccination of children. This resulted in increasing
coverage of 2-3 crore additional children. The annual strategy on polio eradication is decided on
the basis of recommendation of India Experts Advisory Group (IEAG). Since the PPI initiative in
1995, significant success has been achieved in reducing the number of polio cases in the country
and total cases declined gradually. Of the 3 types of polio causing viruses, type 2 (WPV-2) has
already been eradicated in 1999. In November, 2009 meeting of the India Expert Advisory Group
(IEAG) had recommended bivalent OPV vaccine effective against both type 1 and type 3 viruses
use in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. The bivalent vaccine (bOPV) was introduced in the country for
the first time in 2010. The last polio case in the country was reported from Howrah district of
West Bengal with date of onset 13
th January, 2011. Thereafter no polio case has been reported in
the country. WHO on 24 th February, 2012 removed India from the list of countries with active
endemic wild polio virus transmission. The National Immunisation Days (NID) rounds covers
approximately 172 million children and Sub-National Immunization Days (SNID) rounds cover
about 86 Million children.

ASHA
9.7 ASHA – acronym for accredited social health activist – is one of the most important strategic
interventions under the National Rural Health Mission, who is required to inform, interact, mobilize

82
and facilitate improved access to preventive and promotive healthcare and also provide basic
curative care through her drug kits. The requirement for ASHA is one per thousand population with
relaxation to this norm depending upon the workload and terrain. ASHA is necessarily a woman of
the village between the age group of 25 to 45 years, who would be selected by the Gram Sabha
following an intense community mobilization process.
Training of ASHAs
9.8 More than 80% of ASHAs in most high focus, and nearly all in the North East States have
been trained up to Module 5. In the second phase of the NRHM, all 8.63 lakh ASHAs will be trained
in Modules 6 and 7, which is a modular training of four rounds of five days each. Newly inducted
ASHAs will undergo an eight day introductory training before they are trained in Modules 6 and 7.
Since continuous training is key to building capacity of the ASHA, all ASHAs will undergo at least
15 days of training annually which could be either refresher training (based on assessment of skills
after every round) or training in topics which are state specific. This training is required for them
to retain their skills and also gain competency in newer areas as the local context demands.
9.9 The scope of the ASHA is a mix of three roles. The first is a facilitator, serving as a link
between the doctor, ANM, etc. and the community, the second is a community mobilizer who
provides community health education, and enables the marginalized to access services as an
entitlement, and the third is a provider of community level care, and enables appropriate referral
and escorts where necessary.
9.10 The Department has informed that in the second phase of the NRHM, the Department has
charted a plan to provide career opportunities for the ASHA. MOHFW proposes to enter into a
tripartite Memorandum of Understanding with the National Institute of Open Schooling (NIOS) and
the National Health Systems Resource Centre (NHSRC) to enable certification of ASHAs. ASHAs
will be certified at two skill levels. Level 1 certification will ensure skills for social mobilization and
interpersonal communication, and Level 2 will cover skills for community care provision of
mothers, new-borns, children, other reproductive health conditions of women (family planning, and
counselling for abortions, RTI and STI). In addition, those ASHAs, who would like to opt for
additional schooling, will be facilitated to take Class VIII, X or XII exams offered by the NIOS.
This will also enable admission into ANM training schools and onward into Nursing training. To
strengthen and improve the quality of training under the proposed ASHA Certification, four
components of the program is proposed to be certified:–
(1) Training curriculum
(2) State Training Sites/District Training Sites
(3) Trainers
(4) ASHAs.

10.6 The following special initiatives are being undertaken under National Rural Health Mission
to reduce Mortality among children under 5 year of age:
(i) Promotion of Institutional Delivery through Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) and Janani
Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK): Promoting Institutional delivery to ensure skilled
birth attendance is a key to reducing both maternal and neo-natal mortality. JSY
incentivizes pregnant women to opt for institutional delivery and provides for cash
assistance. JSSK entitles all pregnant women to absolutely free and zero expense
delivery including caesarean section operation in Government health facilities and
provides for free to and for transport, food, drugs and diagnostics. Similar
entitlements have also been put in place for sick neonates. This scheme has now been
extended to cover all infants in the country.
(ii) Strengthening Facility based newborn care: Reduction of Newborn mortality is one of
the important thrust area under NRHM. In this regard new born care corners (NBCC)
are set up at all health facilities where deliveries take place to provide essential
newborn care at birth to all new born babies; Special New Born Care Units (SNCUs)
at District Hospitals and New Born Stabilization Units (NBSUs) at FRUs are set up for
the care of sick newborn. As on date 401 SNCUs, 1542 NBSUs and 11508 NBCCs
are functional across the country.
(iii) Home Based Newborn Care (HBNC): Home based newborn care through ASHA has
recently been initiated to improve new born care practices at the community level and
for early detection and referral of sick new born babies. The schedule of home visits
by ASHA consists of at least 6 visits in case of institutional deliveries, on days 3, 7,
14, 21, 28 and 42
nd days and one additional visit within 24 hours of delivery in case
of home deliveries. Additional visits will be made for babies who are pre-term, low
birth weight or ill.
(iv) Capacity building of health care providers: Various trainings are being conducted under
National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) to build and upgrade the skills of doctors,
nurses and ANM for early diagnosis and case management of common ailments of
children and care of newborn at time of birth. These trainings include Integrated
Management of Neo-natal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) and Navjaat Shishu Suraksha
Karyakram (NSSK). NSSK has been launched to improve the skills of health care
providers in provision of new born care at birth. A total of 5.8 lakh health care
workers have been trained in IMNCI in 505 districts and 89,962 health workers
trained in NSSK so far.
(v) Management of Malnutrition: Emphasis is laid on reduction of malnutrition which is an
important underlying cause of child mortality. 605 Nutritional Rehabilitation Centres

85
have been established for management of Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM). Iron and
Folic Acid is also provided to children for prevention of anaemia. Recently, weekly
Iron and Folic Acid supplementation has been initiated for adolescent population. As
breastfeeding reduces infant mortality, exclusive breastfeeding for first six months and
appropriate infant and young child feeding practices is promoted in convergence with
Ministry of Woman and Child Development and recently operational guidelines have
been issued for improving infant and young child feeding practices (IYCF).
(vi) Universal Immunization Program (UIP): Vaccination against seven diseases is provided
to all children under UIP. Government of India supports the vaccine program by
supply of vaccines and syringes, cold chain equipments and provision of operational
costs. UIP targets to immunize 2.7 crore infants against seven vaccine preventable
diseases every year. Since year 2010, Measles catch up campaign has been introduced
in 14 states where Measles Immunization coverage is less than 80%. 21 states with
more than 80% coverage have incorporated second dose of Measles in their
immunization program. Pentavalent vaccine has been introduced in a phased manner
in eight State/UTs. Since December 2011. The year 2012-13 has been declared as
‘Year of intensification of Routine Immunization’. India has achieved a historic
milestone by remaining polio free for two full years now. WHO has taken India off
the list of polio endemic countries.
(vii) Mother and Child Tracking System: A name based Mother and Child Tracking System
has been put in place which is web based to enable tracking of all pregnant women
and newborns so as to monitor and ensure that complete services are provided to
them. States are encouraged to send SMS alerts to beneficiaries reminding them of the
dates on which services are due and generate beneficiary-wise due list of services
with due dates for ANMs on a weekly basis .
(viii) Recently, a new initiative “Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram” has been launched
under National Rural Health Mission with the objective to improve survival,
development and quality of life of children in the age group of 0 to 18 years through
screening of all children for early detection of Defects at birth, Diseases, Deficiencies,
Development Delays including Disability and follow-up for appropriate management
and treatment.
10.7 The Committee, while appreciating the special initiatives being taken to reduce
under-five mortality, feels that these initiatives would be more effective if these are clubbed
together under one umbrella to dispense with multiplicity of authorities and to mitigate the
ultimate beneficiary from the maze of initiatives presently being undertaken. The
Committee, therefore, recommends to bring all these initiatives under one umbrella to
ensure optimum benefits to the ultimate beneficiary. The Committee would also like to
impress upon the Department to specifically map the girl child who expires before attaining
the age of five, as the real reason for less than five mortality rate is due to the rampant
female infanticide prevalent in the country.

FAMILY WELFARE)
11.1 Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) are Eight International Development Goals that all 192
United Nations member states and at least 23 International Organisations have agreed to achieve by
the year 2015. These include, among others, reducing extreme poverty, reducing Child Mortality Rate,
improving Maternal Health, fighting disease epidemics such as AIDS and developing a global
partnership for development. From amongst them, the goal number 4, 5 and 6 relate to Health.

86
11.2 The Department in a written submission has informed that three goals of MDG, i.e.,
MDG-4, MDG-5 and MDG-6 relate to health sector.
MDG-4: Reduce Child mortality
(1) As per MDG-4, the target is to reduce the Under Five Mortality Rate (U5MR) among
children by two-third between 1990 and 2015. In case of India, it translates into a goal
of reducing U5MR from 115 per 1000 live births in 1990 to 38 in 2015.
(2) In 1990, India’s U5MR stood at 115 when Global average was 88. In 2011 (SRS
2011), U5MR in India stood at 55 against a Global average of 57. India has thus
achieved U5MR decline at an accelerated pace to bridge the yawning gap between
Global U5MR and U5MR in India.
(3) Annual rate of decline in U5MR was 2.2% during the period 1990 to 2008. In 2009,
annual rate of decline rose to 7.2% and in 2010 to 7.8%. The annual rate of decline
in 2011 is 6.8%. This points to the success of several initiatives launched under the
NRHM for health system strengthening and reproductive and child health strategies. In
points terms, India has been achieving a consistent decline of 5 points each year
during the period 2008-2010. There has been a further decline of 4 points in 2011. At
this pace, India is expected to reach the MDG target.
MDG-5: Improve Maternal Health
(1) MDG-5 target is to reduce Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) by three quarters between
1990 and 2015. Recent estimates on MMR are not available and data of MMR pertains
to 2007-09 only and puts MMR in India at 212 per 100,000 live births. Further, the
estimates of MMR in India have been reworked by UN Inter-Agency Expert Group for
the year 1990 and is estimated to be 600 instead of 437 as earlier projected. This
translates to reducing the MMR from 600 in 1990 to 150 in 2015.
(2) Decline in MMR between 2004-06 and 2007-09 has been 14 points per year, i.e. 5.5%
annual decline. Assuming that the annual rate of decline observed during 2004-06 and
2007-09 continues, India’s MMR is likely to reduce from 212 during 2007-09 to 143
in 2015. According to this, India would very well achieve the MDG target of 150 by
2015.
MDG-6: Combat HIV/AIDS, Malaria and Other Diseases
The Department has informed that the target is to halt by 2015 and begun to reverse the
spread of HIV/AIDS. In respect of other diseases, the target is to halt by 2015 and begin to reverse
the incidence of malaria and other major diseases. Regarding Malaria, its annual incidence rate
(cases of malaria/1000 population) has come down from 2.57 per thousand in 1990 to 1.10 per
thousand in 2011, achieving about 57% reduction. In the case of Tuberculosis, the prevalence rate
has come down from 586 per 100,000 population in 1990 to 249 in 2009 per 100,000 population,
achieving 57.5% reduction. In case of HIV/AIDS, new annual HIV infections have declined by 56%
during the last decade from 2.7 lakhs in 2000 to 1.2 lakhs in 2009.
11.3 Out of six diseases under NVBDCP, Kala-azar and Lymphatic Filariasis have been targeted
for elimination by the year 2015, though the global target for elimination for Lymphatic Filariasis
is by 2020. Intensive efforts are being done by Government of India for achieving the target of
elimination. Out of 584 blocks, 393 blocks have reported kala-azar cases to less than 1 per 10,000
population (as per 2011 data).

87
11.4 It is expected that all the endemic districts for Filaria will achieve microfilaria rate to less
than 1% by 2015 so that the validation and further process for elimination is initiated. The success
depends on adequate resources and commitment of the states for timely implementation of the
programme activities.Malaria is targeted for pre-elimination stage by 2017 and it is expected that
the country will achieve less than 1 API by the end of Twelfth Plan as envisaged. The viral
diseases like Japanese Encephalitis, Dengue and Chikungunya have not been targeted for elimination.
There are no specific medicines; however, the prevention and control measures will be intensified
across the country to reduce the morbidity and case fatality rate due to these diseases.The MDG
Goal for Malaria is to halt and begin to reverse the incidence of malaria by 2015. The Country
is showing good progress in achieving the Millennium Development Goal (MDG) with respect to
malaria as incidence of malaria has been contained around 1.5 cases per 1000 population annually
since 2006 and showing reverse trend in 2011 and 2012 (provisional) as API of 1.1 and 0.85
respectively have been reported.
11.5 The Committee feels that the success rate of achievements with regard to Millenium
Development Goals has been a mixed bag of success. While the department is more or less
on track with respect to MDG-4 and MDG-5, the success rate in respect of MDG-6 seems
a distant dream especially with regard to the viral diseases like Dengue,Chikungunya which
is a constant cause of worry year after year, not to mention new diseases like H1N1 which
have now started spreading across the country. The Department should, therefore, put in
place a ‘Dedicated Sentinel Force’ whose main protocol would be ensuring prevention of
entry of diseases from outside the borders(land, sea, air) of the country. Additionally, the
Committee feels that the Department should explore the possibility of tapping the additional
resources for mopping up additional funds for its various programmes particularly for the
welfare of our poverty ridden masses.
XII. IMPLEMENTATION OF NRHM (PHASE-I)
12.1 The Department has delineated the following issues during the implementation of NRHM
(Phase-I):
Problem Areas:
State Government:-
• Low capacities to manage large programmes especially in Empowered Action Group
(EAG) States. The contribution of block level and district level planning structure and
PRI in the planning process was inadequate.
• Inadequate capacities across many States to carry out infrastructure planning and
implementation e.g. lack of dedicated/exclusive civil construction wing especially under
NRHM and lack of systems with regards to external evaluation and monitoring of
construction works taken up across States.
• Non-availability and uneven distribution of skilled health care provider including critical
manpower like specialists, nurses etc. especially in EAG States is a challenge. High
attrition rates of HR, due to lack of clear cut HR Policies and inadequate career
progression opportunities. Deployment of health HR has not been fully rationalized as
there is inadequate deployment in underserved, remote and tribal areas.
• Convergence issues with various implementation agencies like ICDS, education
department, water and sanitation and rural development. Lack of coordination among
frontline providers (ANM, AWW, ASHA) for delivering services towards common goal
of health.

88
• There is no clear cut policy and systems to provide free generic medicines in public
health facilities across States. Also, States lack adequate Institutional mechanism for
procurement, and supply chain management of drugs. Many States are lacking
rationalized Essential Drugs List (EDL) and published drug formulary.
• Delay in the registration and cash disbursement to beneficiaries under JSY .
• There may be inadequate coordination between the State Health Society and the State
Health Department. Also, insufficient tenure of Mission directors causes leadership
deficit.
Private:
• NRHM continues to improve outreach mainly through strengthening of public sector
health facilities and the involvement of private sector is presently limited to a few areas
such as Blindness Control, RNTCP, family planning institutional deliveries and patient
transport. However, the presence of private sector in rural areas, particularly in remote
locations, is negligible.
Action Taken:
• States have involved PRIs in the implementation of health and family welfare
programme through progressive transfer of funds clear articulation of functions and by
training equipping and empowering them suitably to manage and supervise the
functioning of health facilities.
• Technical support agencies like NHSRC and SHSRC have been created at National and
State levels to provide handholding support to the States to aid Decentralized planning.
• States are now required to report the progress of construction works as part of
mandatory disclosures on their respective NRHM websites.
• As per conditionalities laid down in ROP 2012-13 States are required to carry out
rational deployment of HR with the highest priority accorded to high focus districts
and delivery points/priority facilities and on compliance would lead to reduction of up
to 7½% of total funds.
• There are policies in many States for monetary compensation (direct and indirect
financial incentives) to Doctors/Paramedics for serving in hand to reach and difficult
areas.
• As per conditionalities laid down in ROP 2012-13 States are incentivized for policy and
systems for providing free generic medicines to all in public health facilities (incentive
upto 5% of MFP). States have been provided support for procurement and logistics
management of drugs.
• To address the issue of interdepartmental coordination common review meeting are
being held between representatives from various social sector departments. Also
VHNDS and fixed immunization days are being conducted in Anganwadi centres.
• States are being supported to set up a integrated call centre which would create a
network of ambulances running under State budget, PPP and others to provide
comprehensive referral and emergency transport services.
• States are being supported to create dedicated infrastructure development teams and set
up robust procurement and logistics systems.

89
• Best practices are being shared across States.
• To provide more human resources for health, medical seats for undergraduate and post
graduate doctors are being increased through creating more medical colleges and
increasing seats in existing medical colleges specifically focusing in underserved areas.
Similarly, more GNM/ANM schools are proposed to be opened during Twelfth
 five year
plan.
12.2 From perusal of the above, the Committee finds that the major problem in
implementation of the NRHM (Phase-I) stems from lack of adequate infrastructure/
manpower in the States/UTs, which has a direct impact on the implementation of the
Mission on the whole. The Committee, while welcoming the initiatives being taken by the
Department to increase involvement of the States, feel that the Department should first and
foremost focus on ensuring opening of more medical colleges, district hospitals, GNM/ANM
schools without further delay along with ensuring that such colleges/schools are opened on
equitable distribution throughout the country so as to ensure that the Department’s Goal
to ensure Universal Health Coverage is implemented in both letter and spirit.
12.3 The Department has further informed that regarding the implementation of NRHM (Phase-I),
the general experience has mainly been positive. During NRHM phase-I, voluntary agencies have
not only been active in areas of community monitoring, training of VHSNC, PRI and ASHAs but
have also been active in implementation of healthcare services. In Community Monitoring, the
Advisory Group on Community Action provided support and coordination to the activities of the
voluntary agencies. The AGCA has developed guidelines and trained VHSNCs and local community
groups for monitoring the functioning of public health facilities. This has been implemented in a
few states and within them in a sample of blocks. While some states have since scaled it up, many
states have not replicated it, choosing to prioritise their limited resource envelope for other
activities. The results are encouraging and functioning of public health facilities have improved
wherever it has been tried. As regards training activities, Government of India provides grant-in-aid
to ten Regional Resource Centres and their responsibility is to provide technical support for
capacity building of NGOs, documentation of best practices, training etc. In the States the ASHA
mentoring group which is made up of key resource persons and experts in community health
programmes, drawn from voluntary organisations acts as a support organisation at the national
level. Organisations, which are part of this, also play a major role in training state level trainers
of ASHAs at designated state training sites-where these organisations have been running community
health worker programmes for long. The involvement of voluntary organisations in the States is
varied-with some states organizing all training through them-and some not involving them at all.
States who have limited institutional capacity for training are encouraged to choose appropriate
NGO partners. States also have ASHA mentoring groups. Some states have involved the mother
NGOs and field NGOs of the earlier mother NGO scheme for this training. In the area of training
of VHSNCs also, the experience is varied across states with some states seeking involvement of
voluntary organisations and some not involving them at all.With regard to involvement of voluntary
agencies in delivery of health care services, the activities of voluntary agencies range from
management of health facilities to running of mobile health clinics and ambulance service etc. For
instance, in Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Odisha and Chhattisgarh, voluntary agencies are involved
in management of SCs, PHCs and CHCs to provide health care services to the rural population.(For
example, Karuna Trust in Arunachal Pradesh and Manipur, R.K Mission in Chhattisgarh). In West
Bengal, voluntary agencies have been entrusted with the responsibility of day to day management
of the round the clock ambulances at selected RH, BPHC, PHC to meet the emergency transport
need of the underprivileged population. V oluntary agencies are also running different projects such
as Night clinic, Awareness on Snake bite management, Mobile eye care unit, Correction of cleft-lip
deformities, Training on first-aid, early detection of cervical cancer etc. In Karnataka, 125 MMUs

90
are outsourced to voluntary agencies in the underserved vulnerable areas for MCH, FP and DCP
services. In Nagaland, Medecins Sans Frontieres is involved in a partnership with the government
to improve the access and provision of quality health services in one district (Mon district) through
the district hospital.
12.4 The Department has stated that to further streamline the participation of voluntary
organisations, the following measures could be taken:
(a) Adopting Guidelines for NGO involvement so as to have a clear policy articulation and
policy clarity on long term NGO involvement and enable grant in aid structures to
emerge at state and district levels. This would greatly contribute to strengthening all
the initiatives involving voluntary agencies.
(b) Expanding NGO involvement for advocacy in a number of behaviour change areas– of
the community and of providers (for example on rational drug use) and of health
related policies in related sectors (for example tobacco control, prevention of alcohol
and substance abuse, road safety, decreased pollution etc.).
12.5 The Committee would like to be apprised of the Guidelines framed for NGOs
involvement in the various programmes under NRHM and whether there have been any
instances of blacklisting of NGOs during implementation of NRHM(Phase-I). The Committee
also recommends that while pursuing welfare measures through the NGOs, the Department
should also emphasize on recruiting more ANMs/GNMs, so as to ensure more focused
implementation of various Schemes in the rural areas during the second Phase of NRHM.
XIII. NEW SCHEMES DURING THE TWELFTH PLAN
13.1 The Department has informed that during the 12th plan period, public health care services
are sought to be further expanded to cover the urban areas. National Urban Health Mission (NUHM)
will be launched as a sub-mission of an overarching National Health Mission, with NRHM being
the other sub-mission. Apart from continuing activities, recent initiatives such as Janani Shishu
Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK), Name based Mother and Child Tracking System (MCTS), delivery of
contraceptives to doorsteps, Menstrual Hygiene Scheme, would be carried forward in the Twelfth
plan. The recently launched Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation (WIFS) Programme under
the National Iron Plus Initiative for school going adolescent girls and boys and for out of school
adolescent girls envisages administration of supervised weekly IFA Supplementation and biannual
deworming tablets to approximately 13 crore rural and urban adolescents through the platform of
Government/Government aided and municipal schools and Anganwadi Kendras to combat the
intergenerational cycle of anaemia. Further, a strategic approach to Reproductive Maternal Newborn
Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCH+A) will be launched. Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram
(RBSK) is a major initiative being launched under the NRHM in the Twelfth Plan for Universal
screening of all children for early identification and early intervention.
13.2 To address critical gaps in human resources availability in the public health delivery system
expansion of medical schools/nursing colleges/paramedical institution would continue to receive
priority. Further strengthening of health and medical regulation is envisaged in the Twelfth Plan.
Food and Drug regulations would also receive focused attention. Further the Central Government
seeks to strengthen district hospitals to provide advanced secondary care. Government seeks to
provide free generic medicines in all public health facilities during the Twelfth plan period with a
view to address concerns on the high Out of Pocket (OOP) expenditure) being currently incurred.
Further in keeping with the changing diseases profile within the country the preventive, promotive
and curative public health interventions in the areas of non-communicable disease would be
addressed.

91
13.3 The Committee, while being appreciative of the New Schemes being launched during
the 12 Plan, would like the Department to focus aggressively on provision of free generic
drugs as the high Out of Pocket Expenditure still remains a major cause of concern for the
vast majority of people in the country. The Committee also impress that the Department
should also encourage production of more generic drugs, as manufacture of Generic Drugs
by the Department and free provision of the same by the Government would reduce the
high Out of Pocket Expenses that a vast majority of the people still bear with.

II. BUDGETARY PROVISIONS
A plain reading of the allocation made vis-a-vis the utilization figures underlines the
fact that the Department of Health and Family Welfare was not able to utilize even the
allocated funds. The Committee feels that had the Government released the full approved
outlay made during the Eleventh Plan, the track record of the Department would have made
a poor reading on the efficiency of the delivery mechanism in physical as well as financial
terms. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the Department should ensure that
the expenditure incurred should commensurate with the amount allocated so as not to invite
reduction of allocation at RE stage. Huge and persistent mismatch between the Budget
Estimates, Revised Estimates and Actual Expenditure is indicative of unrealistic projection
of fund requirements without application of proper financial yardsticks and reflects poorly
on the process of formulation. of Budget Estimates. The Committee, therefore, implores
upon the Department to undertake a thorough analysis of the persistent underutilization of
the funds vis-a-vis the allocated funds and delineate the steps taken so far and to be taken
in future to plug the gaps, so as to minimize the variations between BE, RE and AE and
also for ensuring achieving the targets visualised. (Para 2.1)
Approved outlay for National Health Mission (NHM) for the Twelfth Plan is
Rs. 193405.71 crores as against the projected outlay of Rs. 219702.45 crores. Further against a
projected demand for Rs.32,520.13 crore for NHM, the Planning Commission has approved an
outlay of Rs.20999.00 crore for 2013-14. The Committee is aware that public spending on
health was targeted to be increased to 2.5% of GDP at the launch of NRHM in 2005.
However, as per figures quoted by the Economic Survey 2012-13, public expenditure on
health is just 1.29% of GDP. Private expenditure on health is 2.9% of GDP. The Committee
observes that even if the level of government expenditure on health is increased to 2.5%
of GDP, there would still be a very substantial health care expenditure which is out-of-
pocket payments made by the households in time of health distress. The cost of health care
services in the private sector is so exorbitant that it is just unaffordable for the poor and
the under-privileged. It is in this context that the reduction in approved outlay of
Rs. 193405.71 crore for NHM for the Twelfth Plan against the projected demand of
Rs. 219702.45 crore is cause for extreme concern to the Committee. Keeping in view the
fact that illness of a family member is the most common reason leading to a financial crisis
among poor households, the Committee lends its full support for greater health outlays. The
Committee, simultaneously, recommends that the Department should strengthen its
monitoring mechanism so as to ensure that the available resources are utilized more
efficiently and responsibility be fixed to ensure timely disbursement and utilization of funds
at all levels. (Para 2.2)
The Committee notes that an overarching National Health Mission (NHM) which
would include National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) and National Urban Health Mission
(NUHM) as its sub-components is proposed to be launched during the Twlefth Plan to
strengthen healthcare in rural and urban areas as well. The Committee cannot allow NHM
92

93
to suffer due to less approved outlay of Rs. 193405.71 crores in the Twelfth Plan as
compared to the projected outlay of Rs. 219702.45 crores. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department should explore all mechanisms for augmenting resources
for health so that the objective of NHM of providing universal health coverage does not
remain a distant dream. The Committee desires to be apprised of the measures taken
contemplated to be taken for augmenting resources for health. (Para 2.3)
The Committee is not able to comprehend as to how Department with the approved
outlay of Rs. 20999.00 crores for NHM which is just a shade above the Rs. 20542.00 crores
which the Department was allocated in 2012-13 for NRHM, would be able to meet the
objective of universal health coverage. The Committee feels that the Department of Health
and Family Welfare has not been able to plausibly convince the Ministry of Finance/
Planning Commission to release the funds sought by it. The Committee is not aware of the
reasons adduced by the Planning Commission for marginal increase in allocation of funds
in BE 2013-14 over BE 2012-13 and would, therefore, like to be apprised of the same.
Further from the table given above, the Committee gathers that no funds have been
allocated to ‘Assistance to States for Capacity Building(Burns)’ and Central Drug Research
Institute (CDRI), Lucknow’ and a mere Rs. 1.00 Crore have been allocated for
‘Strengthening of District Hospitals for providing advanced secondary care’; ‘Providing Free
Generic Medicines in all Public Health Institutions in the country’ and ‘National Urban
Health Mission-Flexible Pool’. The Committee would like to be apprised of the reasons for
such nil/low allocations in respect of such important Institutes/Schemes which have a vital
bearing on the progress towards Universal Health Coverage that the Department is aiming
to achieve in the near future. (Para 2.6)
The Committee feels that funds should not be a constraint with respect to vital
Schemes like NRHM-RCH Flexible Pool, NUHM-Flexible pool National Programme for
control of Blindness, Health Care for Elderly, National Programme for Control of Deafness,
National Tobacco Control Programme, National Programme for Prevention and control of
cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke. No allocation has been made for
assistance to States for Capacity Building(Burns) under the NHM. Similarly the funds
allocated to the Family Welfare-Central sector is quite less than the funds sought. The
Committee, therefore recommends to the Department that in order to convince the Ministry
of Finance/Planning Commission, it needs to put in place a strong and effective physically
and financially prudent system which is able to absorb the funds allocated to it, which does
not seem to be the case now in view of the persistent underutilization of the funds allocated
to it year after year under NRHM. The Committee recommends that the Department’s
vision to undertake Universal Health Coverage should not suffer due to non allocation of
funds for NUMH and dropping of implementation thereof. The Committee is very much
concerned with the sorry state of affairs of healthcare facilities presently available to urban
poor particularly those living in urban slums. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Department should make all out efforts to get more funds at RE stage for
implementation of some of the schemes under NUHM. Besides, the funds meant for NRHM
should not be directed for NUHM. (Para 2.8)
The Committee feels that the Department should set a time frame within which the
Action Taken on the findings of the review of NRHM is completed, so as to ensure that the
newly introduced NHM schemes, which includes NRHM as its sub-component, should not
suffer due to the vital gaps in physical infrastructure and Human Resources which has been
the bane of proper implementation of NRHM in the first phase. Government should
concentrate on filling up the gaps particularly the gaps in terms of ‘Specialist’ and ‘Nurse’
vacancies in many States particularly in remote, difficult and tribal areas as noticed in the

94
review of NRHM phase-I. Unless these gaps are filled up, implementation of the ambitious
scheme under NRHM will not yield desired results. (Para 2.10)
The Committee feels that the total Expenditure by Government (Central and State
Governments combined) as a percentage of GDP has merely increased from 1.27 in 2007-08
to 1.29 in 2011-12 which is a very telling comment on the state of affairs of public spending
on Health which directly translates into high Out-of-Pocket expenses for a majority of
population. The Committee observes that given the fact that a significant percent of India’s
population is impoverished every year due to illness of a family member, there is an
imperative need to increase the total expenditure at the Centre and the States level to at
least 3% of GDP. Since the States are themselves under fiscal stress, it is for the Centre
to assign a significant part of its resources towards health care. The Committee hopes that
the Department would be able to live up to the contention of the Planning Commission for
increasing the total Government expenditure, both at centre and state level as a proportion
of GDP in the Twelfth Plan from 1.94 percent in the last year of the Eleventh Plan to 3.04
percent in the corresponding year of the Twelfth Plan given the dismal utilization figures
of the Department in the Eleventh Plan. (Para 2.13)
