IV . National Institutes
National Institute of Ayurveda (NIA)
Recommendation/Observation
1.8 The Committee observes that the NIA is inter-alia mandated to develop high standards of
teaching in Ayurvedic System of Medicine and therefore the acute shortage of the faculty is certain
to adversely affect the functioning of this premier Institute. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Department should take immediate measures towards filling up vacancies in faculty posts
with priority and urgency. The Committee also observes that in pursuance of the recommendation
of the Committee, the Department in its Action Taken Note on the 55th Report of the Committee
had assured to take action to appoint professionally qualified persons on short-term contract or
deputation basis to overcome the staff crunch in senior faculty positions. The Committee is not
aware whether any forward movement has been made in this regard. The Committee, therefore,
recommends to the Department to take immediate action towards appointing professionally qualified

and desires to be kept apprised of the headway made in the matter.

received is being done and interview for these posts for selecting candidates will be
conducted soon.

III. Updation of Central Registers of Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy
Recommendation/Observation
2.13 The Committee is not happy to note that despite its recommendation made in its
55th Report on Demands for Grants (2012-13) of the Department that all such information should
be made available in the public domain in an updated form on the touch of a button, little progress
seems to have been made in this regard, which is evident from the fact that out of 23 States in
respect of which information pertaining to updation of Central Register of Indian Medicine has been
made available, eight States are lagging behind in sending updated information. As regards the
Status of updation of the Central Register of Homoeopathy, the Committee is surprised to note that
in three cases, i.e., Bihar, Tamil Nadu and Tripura, it took sixteen or more months to incorporate
the information in the Central Registers. The Committee is aware that there is a provision in the
IMCC Act 1970 mandating the State Boards to submit updated registers of practitioners on the
1st April every year. The Committee would, therefore, like to be intimated of the impediment
coming in the way of updation of Central Registers of Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy despite
there being mandatory legal provisions. The matter may be taken up at the Minister level and
frequent review meetings be held.
(Para 3.2)
Action Taken
Central Register of Indian Medicine:
2.14 Major impediments in the way of updating the Central Register of Indian Medicine (CRIM)
are as follows:
1. As per section 24 of the IMCC act 1970, the State councils shall submit the State
Registers of Indian Medicine from time to time to the CCIM. But it has been observed

13
that in spite of several reminders, the State Registration Boards/Councils are not
supplying the State Registers in time. Even some State boards like Assam had not
supplied the state registers for the last few years.
2. The State Registers received from the State boards are having several discrepancies in
nomenclature of degrees etc. Therefore the CCIM is compelled to return the State
Registers to the concerned boards to rectify the discrepancies.
3. Moreover, Government of India has also decided to include the name of the college/
Institution on year to year basis. Therefore, before granting registration, recognition
of the college should also be ensured by the Registrar of respective State Board/
Council. It has also been noticed from time to time that some Universities/Awarding
Bodies have been renamed. Therefore, it is mandatory to get the University
recognized by the State Government and the Central Government as well in the first
instance.
4. It has been noted that, duplicacy/multiple registrations have been found in the Central
Registers as well as the state registers of Indian medicine.
2.15 The updation of the Central Register of Indian Medicine with the help of information
technology is given highest priority by CCIM. To sort out the issues mentioned above and other
related issues the following steps have been taken by the CCIM:
1. A meeting was held with the registrars of all State Registration Board/Councils on
14.03.2013 to discuss the various issues regarding updation of the CRIM, Renewal of
registration, Duplicacy in CRIM etc.
2. Moreover to develop the software to maintain/update the CRIM a committee has been
constituted by the President, CCIM and the committee had meeting with the C-DAC
(Center for Development of advanced computing) in this regard on 7.4.2013 and the
matter is under continuous follow up.
3. One member of CCIM of the concerned State has been nominated to every State board/
council by the President, CCIM to take up the matter of discrepancies found in the
State Register supplied by the State Boards/Councils personally and the responsibility
of updating of state register of the concerned state is given to that member for
continuous follow up.
4. There are provisions in some State acts that are in conflict with the provisions of
IMCC Act 1970 in the matter of Renewal/Registration/Recognition of qualification.
Therefore instructions have been given to registrars of the concerned state councils/
boards to take up the matter with their State Governments to amend their State Acts
on the basis of the Central Act, i.e., IMCC Act 1970.
5. Some registrars of State boards stated that they have acute shortage of staff and
financial assistance from the State Government However, in order to provide financial
assistance several letters have been sent to all State Boards/Councils with the request
to inform about the estimated cost to be incurred by them for typing work of the State
Registers from the approved agencies per entry-wise so that financial assistance may
accordingly be provided. The State Registrars have been assured by CCIM to provide
financial assistance for updation of State Register. To look after this matter a
committee consisting of Vice-President (Siddha) and Vice-President (Unani) has been
constituted by the President, CCIM.

14
2.16 In some States like Maharashtra and Karnataka the process of computerization of State
Register from its inception is under process. The work relating to updatation of register and

II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation
3.1 The Committee notes that the extent of surrendered funds is substantially higher under
Centrally Sponsored Schemes (30.9% with reference to RE) than that under Central Sector
Schemes (7.8% with reference to RE). The Committee also takes note of the remedial steps for
better absorption of funds but is not impressed by the half measures taken by the Department
to overcome the sub-optimal utilization of Plan funds as it is obvious that these efforts have not
yielded the desired results. In view of the fact that the allocations have persistently remained
under-utilized in the past several years, the Department should have undertaken a comprehensive
analysis in this regard and taken corrective measures accordingly. Now that an evaluation of all
the Schemes is being done by an independent agency, the Committee is sanguine that the
corrective measures will be initiated for ensuring optimal and judicious utilization of the budgeted
funds. The Committee recommends that the evaluation be completed in a time-bound manner.
The Committee desires to be apprised of the outcome of the independent evaluation and action
taken thereon. The Committee would also like the Department to devise ways to evaluate the
impact of its various schemes. The Committee, simultaneously, impresses upon the Department
to be more prudent in their budget formulation and project their fund requirements in a more
realistic manner after timely collection of all the information pertaining to fund requirement from
the State Governments.
(Para 2.6)
Action Taken
3.2 The Department would strive to judiciously utilize the approved outlays and is
simultaneously working to handle the existing constraints. With regard to review of the norms
for the Centrally Sponsored Schemes, it is stated that as per recommendations of the Planning
Commission on restructuring of the Centrally Sponsored Schemes, Department of AYUSH is
proposing a National AYUSH Mission for implementing the Centrally Sponsored Schemes of the
Department of AYUSH. Simultaneously, the Department has initiated evaluation of 27 components
of Central and Centrally Sponsored Schemes by independent agencies. Out of these 27
evaluations, report for 20 evaluations have been received, accepted and the remaining are in
progress.
3.3 The Department has taken note of the evaluation findings and suitably incorporated changes
in the revised schemes, both in the Central as well as the Centrally Sponsored Schemes for the
Twelfth Plan. The Department has merged 4 Centrally Sponsored Schemes and dropped 2 Central
Sector Schemes (ACDP and LHT).
3.4 The Department undertakes budgetary planning meticulously. However the issue of
pending UCs got aggravated due to change of stand by Ministry of Finance and States not
21

22
coming forward to provide requisite UCs along with supporting documents. To ensure that the
entire requirement of funds is assessed realistically so that the quantum of un-utilized funds is
minimized in future, the Department has been reviewing comprehensively and adopting
appropriate strategy w.r.t. the expenditure profile of each major scheme/programme at regular
intervals and applying the result of such analysis at the time of preparing the budget estimates
and revised estimates.
Further Recommendation
3.5 The Committee while making the above recommendation intended that the
shortcomings in the mechanism of budgetary planning should be identified and necessary
corrective action taken so that the under-utilization of budgeted funds being witnessed does
not recur in future. The reply of the Department is not satisfactory. Instead of dwelling
upon the measures taken or proposed to be taken in this regard, the Department has
chosen to attribute the under-utilization of funds to change of stand by Ministry of Finance
and the States not coming forward to provide requisite Utilization Certificates (UCs). The
Committee, therefore, reiterates the need for formulating appropriate remedial measures
for projection of realistic fund requirements so that the scarce resources do not remain
locked up.
IV. National Institutes
National Institute of Homoeopathy (NIH)
Recommendation/Observation
3.6 The Committee observes that the expansion of the Hospital from 100 to 250 beds was
targeted to be achieved during 2010-11. Two years have elapsed since then, but the project is yet
to be completed. The time-overrun has led to cost overrun. The Committee has been advising the
Department to streamline its monitoring mechanism so that such slippages in timely implementing
the project and the resultant cost overrun could be minimized. The Committee is constrained to
observe that the delay in completion of the project is indicative of slack monitoring and bad
planning. The Committee, therefore, exhorts the Department to pay focused attention owards
expansion of the Hospital from its existing bed strength of 100 to 250 beds. The Committee desires
to be kept apprised of the progress of implementation of the project.
(Para 4.8)
Action Taken
3.7 On 15.05.2013 Joint Secretary (AYUSH) visited NIH to hold a meeting with the
representatives of CPWD in connection with stoppage of work of expansion/development of the
institute’s building by CPWD. The issue was sorted out with the decision that balance amount
of the Original Estimate would be released immediately and the work would be resumed.
Accordingly, payment has been made. Director, NIH has been advised to monitor the work
closely and intimate position to the Department regularly. Observations of the Committee have
been noted for compliance.
Further Recommendations
3.8 The Committee observes that the work of expansion/development of NIH’s building
was stopped by CPWD over some disputes regarding payment of dues. Though the

23
Department in its action taken note has claimed that the issue has been sorted out and
payments made, it is not clear whether the work has resumed since then. The Committee
would therefore like the Department to shed more light in this regard. The Committee
would also like the Department to explore the possibility of putting in place a dedicated
mechanism for vigorous monitoring of the work of expansion/development of NIH. A time
line may be fixed for completion of the works.
Recommendation/Observation
3.9 The Committee expresses its concern over such a large number of vacant posts in teaching
cadre which is certain to impair the functioning of NIH. The Committee observes that the main
objective of NIH is to develop excellence in homoeopathic education and conduct UG and PG
courses. It is, therefore, imperative for the Department to urgently take steps to fill up the
vacancies in a specific time-frame. The Committee desires to be apprised of the measures taken
by the Department and progress made towards filling up all vacant posts of NIH.
(Para 4.10)
Action Taken
3.10 Out of 32 vacancies in Group-A; 6 in Group-B and 37 in Group-C, the selection procedure
has been completed against 8-vacancies in Group-A, (which includes 7 posts of Lecturers and
1 post of Physiotherapist); 2 in Group-B and 16 in Group-C respectively. Moreover, the vacancy
notices has already been sent to DAVP for advertisement for remaining vacancies. In the meantime,
NIH has appointed 7 Readers and 3 Lecturers on contract basis.
Further Recommendations
3.11 The Committee observes that though some headway has been made towards filling up
the vacancies in Group A,B and C, a lot still needs to be done to overcome the problem of
shortage of manpower in NIH. It is, therefore, imperative on the part of the Department
to vigorously pursue the matter with the authorities concerned. The Committee desires to
be apprised of the progress made towards filling up the vacancies in all categories.
North Eastern Institute of Folk Medicine (NEIFM), Pasighat, Arunachal Pradesh
Recommendation/Observation

integrate them into mainstream health care system. However, its operationalisation in the true sense

priority and urgency. However, the Committee notes from the reply that the proposal for

VIII. Quality Control of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathic (ASU&H) Drugs
Recommendation/Observation
3.21 The Committee observes that there is a separate chapter-IV A in the Drugs and Cosmetics
Act 1940 which regulates the manufacture and sale of ASU&H drugs. Since the enforcement of
provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules made there under is under the purview of State
Drug Licensing and Drug Control Authorities, the State drugs regulatory framework has a crucial
role to play in ensuring safety and quality of ASU&H drugs. It is in this context that strengthening
of State Drug Testing Laboratories which are facing infrastructure constraints, and shortage of
manpower, assume added significance. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Department
to quickly revise the Quality Control Scheme and its funding pattern for greater efficacy of the
Scheme.
(Para 8.8)
Action Taken
3.22 As the evaluation report of the Centrally Sponsored Scheme meant for supporting state
Drug Testing Laboratories, Pharmacies and Enforcement mechanism has been received, the
Department has initiated action to revise the scheme with enhanced scope and suitable modification
of funding pattern in the Twelfth Plan. It is intended to make the scheme broad-based for covering
priority requirements of quality control of ASU&H drugs including improvement of infrastructural
and functional capacities of State Drug Testing Laboratories.
Further Recommendations
3.23 The Committee is not happy with the snail’s pace of the progress made in the
matter. It is already the 2
nd year of the Twelfth Plan and if the Department is still in the
process of revising the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for supporting State Drug Testing
Laboratories and Pharmacies, it is a sad commentary on its decision making process. The
Committee is at a loss to understand as to how the requirements of quality control will be
met if the revision of the Scheme is delayed inordinately. The Committee, therefore,
recommends to quickly finalize Scheme and implement the same.
X. International Cooperation
Recommendation/Observation

with the developed countries like U.K, Germany, U.S.A, Canada etc. The Committee observes that
signing of MoUs for promotion of research projects of AYUSH with the countries, which have
well-developed and credible regulatory mechanisms, will go a long way in establishing the
therapeutic credential of AYUSH medicine globally. This needs to be taken further ahead and India
should become frontrunner in alternative systems of medicine.
(Para 10.3)

Action Taken

matter. The Committee would like to be enlightened as to what concrete steps are being
taken in this direction. The Department should strive to make India frontrunner in
alternative systems of medicine.
XI. Information, Education and Communication (IEC)
Recommendation/Observation
3.27 The Committee welcomes the evaluation of IEC and desires to be apprised of the final
findings of AFCL and the action taken thereon.
(Para 11.4)
Action Taken
3.28 A report on evaluation of the Information, Education and Communication (IEC) Scheme
submitted by Agricultural Finance Corporation Ltd. (AFCL) has since been accepted by the
Department. On the basis of recommendations made by the agency, a draft note for consideration
of Standing Finance Committee (SFC) is under process of approval.
3.29 Few of the findings and key observations of AFCL are as follows:
● AROGYA programme provides a common platform to AYUSH manufacturers to display
a variety of products in which they specialize. Besides this, free distribution of
medicines at selected stalls, sale of drugs at discounted rates, demonstration of home
remedies for treatment of common ailments, display material on a healthy lifestyle and
availability of brochures, small books, pamphlets, etc. have helped in increasing the
awareness generation.
● General awareness about Ayurveda and Yoga among general public have far exceeded
than that of Siddha and Unani.
● Arogya Mela helps generate information and awareness among the people of the
district where the mela is organized.
● A unanimous view emerged about the usefulness of Arogya Mela as an effective
medium to reach out to people to inform, educate and motivate.
● Prejudices and stereotypes regarding the acceptability or rejection of all the traditional
systems of medicine was still an issue among people in general and even among
distributors.
● The communication campaigns have played an important role in changing the health
behaviors of public.
● The target audience of the audio-visual material seems quite clear in the analysis of
settings and characters that are featured in the video spots.
● The media materials under study are significantly providing information about
prevention techniques, behaviors and regimes; information about diseases, including

27
information about symptoms, prevalence and transmission; and information about the
streams of AYUSH, and their respective abilities to aid curative procedures and
recovery. In terms of the information available through media materials, the content
analysis provides an uniformly high score across materials.
● During survey, it has been observed that AYUSH media materials have focused largely
on the curative aspects of the individual streams. Focus has also been given on
preventive medication or processes.
● The information also offered curative aspects of health, the pamphlets and booklets
were quite informative, providing information about the plants or herbs that are used
under a particular stream to heal specific diseases.
● The AROGYA Mela was a good platform for networking and outreach because it
attracts people from various sections of the society and with different capacities, and
enables direct contact. There was an increase in the net knowledge level as to how
the AYUSH system can be used in its totality through the course of the Mela visit.
3.30 The Department is in the process of taking action on the suggestions/recommendations.
Further Recommendations
3.31 The Committee desires to be apprised of a point-wise action taken on the key
findings of Agricultural Finance Commission Ltd. (AFCL).
Recommendation/Observation
3.32 The Committee observes that no tangible progress has been made towards curtailing
misleading advertisements concerning AYUSH, over the electronic media and in the print media. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should pursue the matter with the
authorities concerned with renewed vigour as the issue is too important for maintaining credibility
of AYUSH systems to be left unattended. The Committee desires to be apprised of the final
outcome in the matter.
(Para 11.7)
Action Taken
3.33 As recommended by the Hon’ble Parliamentary Committee, the matter of checking
objectionable advertisements on AYUSH drugs has been taken up with Ministry of Information and
Broadcasting and Directorate of Audio-visual Publicity (DA VP) with a request to take action as
appropriate for stopping improper advertisements on AYUSH in electronic and print media. DAVP
has informed that it does not have regulatory power over private advertisement. Press Council of
India has also informed that as per the Press Council Act, 1978 the Council enjoys statutory
authority for the print media and it is sensitive on the issue of objectionable advertisements and
have norms of Journalistic Conduct-2010. However, these guidelines carry only ethical backing as
there are no enforcement powers with the Press Council of India. The Department of AYUSH has
also written to all State Drug Licensing Authorities/Drug Controllers of AYUSH to bring instances
of misleading advertisements concerning AYUSH drugs in TV , Radio and print media to the notice
of Ministry of Information and Broadcasting for remedial action and to take corrective measures
in preventing inappropriate advertisements in electronic and print media including newspapers. The
states like Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Goa, Kerala are taking action against the misleading
advertisements in respect of AYUSH drugs in channels/newspapers which are in violation of the
provisions of the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act 1954.

28
Further Recommendations
3.34 The Committee observes that there have been plenty of advertisements in electronic
and print media where tall claims are made about providing cure to Cancer, Liver Cirrhosis,
diabetes and other chronic ailments without any scientific evidence. The Department of
AYUSH has admitted that the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements)
Act 1954 has not made the desired impact on curbing misleading advertisements related to
AYUSH drugs and the Press Council of India also does not have sufficient powers to curb
such advertisements as the guidelines as laid down in the Press Council Act, 1978 carry only
ethical backing. DAVP also does not have regulatory powers over private advertisements.
Keeping all the above factors in view, the Committee observes that there is an imperative
need for stringent norms in the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements),
1954 and urgent measures need to be taken to amend the said Act to tackle the menace
of misleading advertisements related to AYUSH drugs.

recommendations contained in Seventieth Report on Demands for Grants (Demand No.50) of the
Department of AIDS Control for the year 2013-14.
2. Action Taken Notes (ATNs) have been received from the Government in respect of the

(i) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have
been accepted by the Committee: 2.5, 2.9, 2.12, 4.3, 4.5, 6.3, 7.6, 10.3, 10.5, 10.7,
11.3, 11.5 Total–12  (Chapter-I)
 (ii) Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES
OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
II. Budgetary Allocation
Recommendation/Observation
1.1 The Committee observes that in a resource constrained country like India, the efficient
deployment of the available resources is the key for success of any programe scheme. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should initiate concrete measures for
efficient use of the allocated funds and remove apparent inefficiencies at every level of programme
implementation.
(Para 2.5)
Action Taken
1.2 Annual Action Plan has been drawn, linking Activities to the timelines at State AIDS Control
Society (SACS). This is regularly monitored at periodic interval. Instructions are regularly being
issued to emphasize efficient utilization of funds.
Recommendation/Observation
1.3 The Committee expresses its serious concern that the actual expenditure of the Department
for the year 2010-11 was Rs. 1167.21 crore as against the BE of Rs. 1435.00 crore; for the year
2011-12, Rs. 1313.86 crore as against BE of Rs. 1700.00 crore, and for the year 2012-13,
Rs. 1345.16 crore as against BE of Rs. 1700.00 crore. The Committee expresses its disappointment
at this persistent trend of under-utilization of the budgeted funds and is of the view that this trend
is not only indicative of fiscal indiscipline but also points to slack monitoring of utilization of the
sanctioned provisions. The Committee feels that the reasons adduced by the Department cannot
justify shortfall in expenditure to the tune of Rs. 267.79 crore in 2010-11, Rs. 386.14 crore in
2011-12 and Rs. 354.84 crore in 2012-13. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Department should put in place a strict and effective monitoring mechanism to ensure that the
funds allocated to the Department are monitored quarterly, and exercise utmost fiscal prudence and
discipline so as to make realistic Budget Estimates in future. The Committee desires to be apprised
of the measures initiated in this regard.
(Para 2.9)
Action Taken
1.4 Regular monitoring is being done. Monthly Financial Management letter has been initiated to
keep a track on expenditure, advanced and utilization of funds in the programme.
Recommendation/Observation
1.5 The Committee appreciates that due to the efforts made by the Department, there has been
a considerable decline in unspent balances available with the SACS. The Committee would,
2

3
however, like to point out that availability of unspent balance with some SACS, like Andhra Pradesh
SACS (Rs.23.33 crore), Bihar SACS (Rs.18.23 crore), Gujarat SACS (Rs.14.58 crore), Karnataka
SACS (Rs.26.60 crore) is still quite high. The Committee emphasizes that the Department should
make concerted efforts to get resolved all the unspent balances with the societies so that funds
do not accumulate and remain unutilized. The Committee recommends that in order to ensure timely
and effective utilization of unspent balances, the Department should insist on quarterly feedback
from all the State AIDS Control Societies. Close monitoring of their activities and spending will
certainly deliver the desired results. (Para 2.12)
Action Taken
1.6 Close Monitoring has been initiated and further releases have been linked to cash balances
with SACS. Monthly, unspent balances are being initiated with SACS and instructed to liquidate the
same.
IV. Setting up of new Blood Component Separation Units (BCSUs)
Recommendation/Observation
1.7 The Committee is not aware as to what headway has been made towards concretizing the
above proposal. Considering the fact that blood transfusion is a life-saving treatment in many
situations but it can also be a quick route for the transmission of infectious agents such as HIV ,
HBC, HCV , etc; the Committee recommends that urgent measure be taken on war footing to
regulate Blood Banks. The Committee desires to be furnished with a Status Note, indicating the
initiatives taken by the Department towards ensuring quality management systems and monitoring
of Blood Banks and the outcome thereof.
(Para 4.3)
Action Taken
1.8 Blood banks are under the regulatory control of the State Drug control authorities under the
Drugs and Cosmetics Act. Blood banks cannot function without a licence, which is issued by the
state authorities following approval of the DCGI.
1.9 The efforts of department of AIDS control has taken up the initiative to set up a core
committee in the states with representatives from the state drug control authorities, blood bank
experts and representatives of state AIDS control societies/State blood transfusion councils to
periodically inspect the blood banks to monitor their conformance to existing policy guidelines and
regulations.
1.10  Comprehensive standards to ensure better quality control system on collection, storage,
testing and distribution of blood and its components have been formulated and disseminated.
V. Setting up of new District level Blood Banks
Recommendation/Observation
1.11 The Committee notes that during NACP-III, the Department had fulfilled the target of
setting up 80 Blood Component Separation Units (BCSUs) at tertiary level of public health care
delivery system and proposes to continue the support to these facilities and also take up
upgradation of existing licensed blood banks in the Government and charitable sector with annual
blood collection of over 5000 blood units at BCSUs, so as to saturate the same, by the end of

4
NACP IV. The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the progress made towards upgrading the
existing licensed blood banks in the Government and Charitable Sector. (Para 4.5)
Action Taken
1.12 Department had fulfilled the carry over targets of NACP III through setting up of 3 BCSU
in the first year of NACP IV , thereby completing the target of setting up of 80 BCSU during NACP
III and completing the set up of BCSU at tertiary level of public health care delivery system.
1.13 The Department also provides recurring grant to the existing licensed component separation
facilities in the government and charitable sector for manpower and consumables. A total of 268
component separation facilities (including 34 model blood banks) are presently being supported in
the Government and charitable sector under the programme as on 1st June 2013. The department
is also supporting capacity building for rational use of blood among clinicians to step up the
demand for blood components.
VI. Integrated Counseling and Testing Centres (ICTCs)
Recommendation/Observation
1.14 The Committee notes that the achievements vis-à-vis the targets fixed for 2010-11, 2011-12
and 2012-13 leaves a lot to be desired in the implementation of the targets. The Committee is of
the opinion that the Department needs to fine tune its ground level machinery. The Committee
therefore recommends that Department should focus on setting monitorable targets and their
realization to the maximum extent. The Committee desires to be apprised of the targets fixed for
2013-14 and the measures put in place to monitor progress in this regard.
(Para 6.3)
Action Taken

Target Ach. Target Ach. Target Ach.

1.15 The target for the year 2013-14 is 112 lakhs with the coverage up to CHCs level by the
programme and below CHCs i.e. PHCs and Sub Centre with the help of NRHM and General Health
system.
To monitor the progress the following measures are undertaken:
1. National level:
● Monthly reporting mechanism is in place under SIMS.
● Quarterly review meetings of the SACS programme officers at the national level.
● Periodic feedback to SACS on performance.
● Field visits are conducted by the department to poor performing States.
● Strong monitoring of supply chain management for HIV Rapid test kits to ensure
uninterrupted supplies.

5
2. State level:
● Monthly reporting by all facilities.
● Monthly/quarterly review meetings at State/district level
● Supervisory visits by SACS programme officers to poor performing districts.
VII. Anti Retroviral Therapy (ART) Centre
Recommendation/Observation
1.16 The Committee gathers from the information furnished by the Department that there is a
steady decline in overall prevalence of HIV/AIDS. However, a lot still remains to be done. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that during NACP-IV, additional ART Centres be established and
high quality treatment be made available to the eligible people. The Committee also recommends that
pre-ART follow-up be strengthened and all people eligible for treatment identified.
(Para 7.6)
Action Taken
1.17 Under NACP IV, it is proposed to have 600 ART Centres in the country by March, 2017
to make available quality treatment to eligible PLHIV .
1.18 The pre-ART follow up at ART centres is being strengthened. Emphasis is being given to
pre-ART care in all training programmes and during review meetings
X. New Strategies
(i) Setting up of District AIDS Prevention and Control Units (DAPCUs)
Recommendation/Observation
1.19 The Committee is of the opinion that setting up of the District AIDS Prevention and Control
Units function as a supportive structure below the state level would fill up the necessary gaps to
coordinate the activities at the district level as DAPCUs are expected to play a pivotal role in
monitoring and coordination of delivery from the different facilities in the district. The Committee
would, therefore, recommend that the Department should explore the possibility of expanding the
same to more districts in the near future so as to implement the programme more effectively.
(Para 10.3)
Action Taken
1.20 Department of AIDS Control (DAC) is working on district re-categorisation in the country
based on HIV Sentinel Surveillance, High Risk Group population, Migration, programme data and
vulnerability to get HIV in the district.
1.21 In NACP-IV , this re-categorisation of districts will be considered for expanding the network
of DAPCUs in other parts of the country. This will be based on the financial resources available
with department of AIDS Control.
(ii) Scheme of link workers in rural areas of category A and B districts
Recommendation/Observation
1.22 The Committee notes that the Link Worker Scheme is an intensive rural-based intervention
reaching out to the marginalized groups which remain uncovered even after the expansion of urban

6
based prevention programmes. The Scheme is being implemented only in 155 districts as of now.
The Committee recommends to the Department to assess the need to cover the remaining districts
and closely monitor the scheme as the success of this scheme is crucial for achieving the goal
of halting and reversing the epidemic of AIDS. Effective implementation of this scheme can bring
perceptible change.
(Para 10.5)
Action Taken
1.23 The Link Worker Scheme is being supported by Global Fund for AIDS, TB and Malaria
Round (GFATM)-VII to work in identified in 163 high prevalent and highly vulnerable districts till
August, 2013. These 163 districts were selected after considering HIV prevalence and the
vulnerability of the districts. In each district, 150 vulnerable villages were identified for extensive
mapping and based on the findings of the mapping, 100 most vulnerable villages were finalized for
implementation of LWS in the district. The scheme is operational in all 163 districts. The Scheme
has been proposed to be continued in NACP-IV with domestic funds.
(iii) Pr eferred private provider scheme for management of Sexually Transmitted
Infections (STYI) among high risk groups.
Recommendation/Observation
1.24 This is very good scheme which has the potential to penetrate to the lowest level provided
it is implemented with dedication. The Committee recommends close and strict monitoring of the
Preferred Private Providers Scheme to ensure that it is not misused for financial benefits by the
preferred private providers and strict norms should be put in place for identifying the preferred
private providers for management of sexually transmitted infection.
(Para 10.7)
Action Taken
1.25 Comments of Parliamentary Standing Committee have been noted for compliance. The State
AIDS Control Society monitor the Preferred Private Providers through mentoring and supportive
supervision in the field. Payment and reimbursement to Preferred Private Providers is disbursed on
the basis of records of number of patients managed by them. Further, the records are also
periodically scrutinized and verified by the TI NGO through their outreach network.
XI. National Pediatric HIV/AIDS Initiative
Recommendation/Observation
1.26 The Committee is of the view that the Department needs to delve deeper on the reasons
for rising trends of HIV prevalence among pregnant women in the State like Bihar, Gujarat, Uttar
Pradesh and Rajasthan. The Committee recommends that the Department should prepare specific
State-wise interventions in these States after analyzing the reasons for increase in HIV prevalence
in these States and if need be specific pilot projects for interventions on PPP mode may be mooted
with specific targets being fixed under these projects.
(Para 11.3)
Action Taken
1.27 The HIV Sentinel Survey has shown rising trends of HIV prevalence among pregnant

7
women in the states like Bihar, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan. To mitigate the impact the
following measures are undertaken:
● Scaling up of facilities for counseling and testing in these States.
● District specific strategies for increasing coverage of HIV testing among pregnant
women by working closely with NRHM/General Health System.
● In identified districts/blocks/villages, special prevention interventions for “source
migrants” are implemented.
● Increasing awareness among general population through mass media, mid media and
inter personal communication activities using folk troupes, street plays, hoardings, wall
paintings, etc to give thematic messages including PPTCT messages.
● Strong monitoring of linkages between ICTC and ART centres to ensure all pregnant
women detected HIV positive are linked to care, support and treatment services.
● Provision of single dose Nevirapine to mother and child for prevention of HIV
transmission to child.
● In a phased manner, introducing the multi drug PPTCT ARV regimen for further
reduction of parent to child transmission.
1.28 The department is already working out strategies for PPP Mode activities by working with
private industries and PSUs on a employer led model for implementing HIV prevention activities at
the work place
Recommendation/Observation
1.29 The Committee welcomes the initiatives taken by the Department in constituting a national
task force under which there is a joint proposal to pilot this intervention for children affected with
AIDS (CABA). The Committee recommends that the Department should expand similar initiatives
to other affected districts which would help in complementing and supplementing the Government’s
efforts in its fight against combating HIV/AIDS.
(Para 11.5)
Action Taken
1.30 Based on the experience of intervention for children affected with AIDS (CABA) the
initiative is being integrated into a cost – effective, Care and Support model which is inclusive of
needs of HIV infected Children.
1.31 Under NACP IV , it is proposed to set up Care and Support Centers (CSCs) for PLHIVs
(people living with HIV/AIDS) which will also address the various needs of Children affected by
HIV/AIDS. 350 care and support centers will be set up across the country The Care and support
centers shall act as the focal point from which the required services to Children affected by HIV/
AIDS will be ensured through advocacy and linkages.

8
8
CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES
NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT REPLIES
II . Budgetary Allocation
Recommendation/Observation
2.1  The Committee takes note of the submission that the increased grants to SACS is due,
transitioning of Targeted Intervention (TI) projects from Development Partners into the national
programme. The Committee observes that funding from Development Partners have played a vital
role in supporting the NACP programme interventions in the past. The Committee would, therefore,
like to be apprised of the reasons behind shifting the TI projects from Development Partners to
the national programme and its implication on funding of HIV programmes in the Country.
(Para 2.14)
Action Taken
2.2 The increased allocation to the SACS is mainly keeping in mind the increased activities that
are proposed in the 2013-14 which include setting up of new targeted intervention to reach out
high risk population (Female Sex Workers, Men have Sex with Men, Transgenders and Hijrasand

groups based on the high prevalence of HIV noted amongst them. Implementation of the revised
migrant strategy for HIV will focus on interventions at destination, source and transit with the main
objective reducing transmission amongst the high risk migrants and also prevent the HIV spreading
in hitherto low prevalences states. Setting up of new Opioid substitution Therapy centers for harm
reduction is being up scaled during the 2013-14.The development partners were supporting National
AIDS Control Programme to reach out and provide prevention services to high risk groups through
implementing Targeted interventions in high prevalent states. The support was for given time frame
and phasing out from direct implementation of targeted intervention was already planned. The
takeover of majority of TIs and high risk population covered by development partners was
completed in March 2012. The transition from the development partners have been done based on
the performance of each TI.

II. Budgetary Allocation
Recommendation/Observation
3.1 The Committee observe that the 1 st year of the Twelfth Plan Period has already elapsed and
the 2 nd Year is in progress. However, the Department is still in the process of reworking the project
cost of NACP–IV for the Twelfth Plan period. The committee observes that the delay of more than
a year in finalization of the project cost of such a critical programme like NACP-IV is a sad
commentary on the working of the Department and calls for urgent remedial measures. The
Committee feels that the delay will have an adverse impact on the intended outcomes of NACP-
IV unless timely action taken. In an era of e-governance and with IT resources currently available,
the Department should have finalized the project cost long back. The Committee, therefore,
deprecates the delay in this regard and desires to be apprised of the reasons for the same. The
Committee recommends that the Department should finalize the project cost at the earliest and in
such a manner so that the intended outcomes of this programme are not adversely affected. The
Committee may be apprised of the progress made in this regard.
(Para 2.3)
Action Taken
3.2 CCEA has approved the World Bank aided National AIDS Control Support Project in
May, 2013. The EFC has approved NACP-IV in July 2013 and is being submitted to CCEA
approval.
Further Recommendation
3.3 The Committee is not satisfied with the lackadaisical approach of the Department in
the matter. It has been more than one and a half years since 12
th Plan Period started,
however, the Department could submit NACP-IV project in July 2013 for CCEA approval.
The Committee observes that delay in this regard may undermine the desired outcome in
the NACP-IV project. The Committee would like the Department to take pro-active action
in this matter and take all possible measures to check any further delay.
III. Role of NGOs.
Recommendation/Observation
3.4 The Committee expresses its displeasure over the issue of non-recovery of unspent balances
from the NGOs by the Department, even after about two years. Out of 27 States, 11 States have
a balance of Rs.100.8 lakhs still to be recovered. The Committee recommends that the issues like
contract norms fixed for NGOs-State-wise, the reasons for delay in recovering the same along with
the details of action taken against the NGOs who have repeatedly defaulted in paying back the
13

14
unspent balances. In future, funds should be released only to such agencies which have the
capacity to utilize the allocated amount.
(Para 3.2)
Action Taken
3.5 It may be observed that out of Rs. 352.17 lakhs, Rs. 251.8 lakhs has been recovered by
SACS, which is amounted to 71% of the total outstanding dues against the NGOs implementing
Tis SACS has initiated steps to recover the balance amount of Rs. 100.8 lakhs from remaining
NGOs in 11 states. Steps like auditing, sending show cause notices, legal action to NGOs for not
responding to notices have been initiated at state level. Department suggested SACS to speed up
the legal action against such defaulted NGOs.
3.6 The DAC have intensified monitoring and control of programmatic and financial activities
regularly at DAC as well as SACS level. Computerised Financial Management System (CPFM) has
been put in place to monitor the expenditure and releases for each NGO. Department has given
instruction to all SACS to ensure utmost care while recruiting NGOs for implementing programme.
The fund utilization capacity of NGOs is assessed during the selection process and is one of the
criteria for selection of NGOs which is carried by the SACS.
Further Recommendation
3.7 The Committee takes note of the initiatives taken by the Department for recovering
the balance amount from the remaining States. However, the Committee observes that no
tangible steps have been taken or contemplated to be taken to accomplish the task. The
Committee would like the Department to indicate a specific action plan to sort out the
glitches with NGOs for achieving the targets and also put in place some tangible guidelines
on basis of which the NGOs would be identified in future.
IV. Setting up of new Blood Component Separation Units (BCSUs)
Recommendation/Observation
3.8 From the information furnished by the Department, the Committee gathers that the scheme
pertaining to setting up of four Metro Blood Banks is yet to be approved by EFC, and time-overrun
has led to the cost escalation of the scheme. The Committee deprecates the Department for not
visualizing the problems of its implementation at the planning stage, which has resulted in time-
overrun and cost escalation. The Committee recommends that the Department should expedite
revision of proposal of the scheme and proactively pursue its approval with the EFC so that this
scheme could be translated into action and there is no further cost-overrun. The Committee desires
to be kept apprised of the updated status of approval of this scheme. The proposal brooks no delay
and an expeditious action needs to be taken for its early approval. The Committee also impresses
upon the Department to speed up the process for acquisition of land for the proposed Metro Blood
Bank in Delhi.
(Para 4.7)
Action Taken
3.9 The four metro blood banks were proposed to be set up as four regional center of
excellence in Transfusion Medicine in Chennai, Delhi, Mumbai and Kolkata.
3.10 The original EFC and CCEA approval was obtained in March and August, 2008 for
Rs. 468 crore. The date of commencement of project was 1.1.2009.

3.11 HLL was identified as Project Management Consultant and consultants were engaged
for preparing the detailed project reports for these sites. DPR II prepared for 3 sites, except

project. Land for the Delhi site is still to be handed over.
3.13 A r evised cost estimate memo for Metro Blood Banks was sent to Finance Ministry for
consideration and approval amounting to Rs. 1024 Crore, along with report of standing committee
on cost and time overrun.
3.14 However, EFC in its meeting on 31.12.2012 did not concur to the proposal.
3.15 The Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance has asked for a revised proposal to
be framed incorporating their observations for consideration of EFC.
3.16 The following action has been taken by the department.
1. Eight meetings have been conducted with blood bank experts, team from Project
Management Consultant (HLL) and DPR consultants to rationally review the proposal
and bring down the cost without compromising on the basic intent of the project in

2. An expert group meeting has been conducted to reduce the cost of construction

3. The manpower, equipments and consumables in the proposal have been reviewed by
the group of experts to rationalize the cost.
4. The revised proposal would be submitted for review and approval by the steering
committee and standing committee for Metro Blood Banks.
5. As per the mandate of the project, the operations of these centres are to be taken over
by the states after five years. Therefore, a consultation with States is planned to be

6. Following submission of revised proposal to EFC and obtaining CCEA approvals, the
process of construction and set up of these centres would take 18 months, during
which time recruitments and procurements would also be done.

obtaining approval.

Recommendation/Observation
3.19 The Committee expresses its disappointment that the Department has not been able to meet
the target of setting up of 39 blood banks during NACP-III. In some states not even one blood
bank was setup which gives a dismal picture of the implementation. The Committee feels that the
above issues could have easily been sorted out, had there been a streamlined mechanism in place
and the Department had pursued the matter vigorously. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Department needs to play a pro-active role by taking up the matter with the concerned State
Governments as well as the agencies at an appropriate level to expedite the procedural formalities.
(Para 5.5)
Action Taken
3.20 As per the latest updating 29 DLBB become operational on 31.03.2013. For early functional

17
of the remaining 11 DLBB spread in different states, communications have been sent to State Health
Secretaries to remove the bottlenecks in the set up of these blood banks immediately.
Communication has also been sent to the CDSCO to expedite the issuance of pending licenses. The
Department of AIDS Control would pursue this matter closely.
Recommendation/Observation
3.21 The Committee recommends that for resolving the problem of unfunctional District level
Blood Banks (DLBBs), the Department should take up the matter with the Drug Controller General
of India regarding licencing and operationlisation of these blood banks on priority basis. The issues
of shortage of manpower and lack of infrastructure should also be taken up with the States. The
Committee also recommends that the Department should take special care of the underserved
districts of Uttrakhand, Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand.
(Para 5.7)
Action Taken
3.22 The matter is being perused with the states where the remaining 11 DLBB are to be
established for providing infrastructure facilities immediately for early operational of these Blood
Banks. The matter of issuance of license to these DLBB will be taken up with the DCG(I) after
the infrastructure facilities are made available by the State Government on priority basis.
Further Recommendation
3.23 The Committee is not satisfied with languid pace of the progress made for setting up
of 11 DLBB out of 39 DLBB which was a target of Phase-III of NACP. Most of the reasons
cited in this regard seem purely procedural. The Committee would like the Department to
sort out the hurdles in this regard so that appropriate result can come out. The Department
should also consider providing appropriate additional funds, if required, for infrastructure
and manpower related matters so that there is no delay due to financial constraints.
IX.  Adolescence Education Programme (AEP)
Recommendation/Observation
3.24 The Committee is concerned to note that Adolescence Education Programme (AEP) remains
suspended in five States namely, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar
Pradesh. The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation made in its 57
th Report on Demand
for Grants (2012-13) of the Department that it should vigorously take up with the States where
the Programme is still under suspension and resolve their apprehensions in view of the fact that
HIV/ AIDS usually attacks the vulnerable population due to lack of awareness of the devastating
effects the disease could have on them. The Department may take up the matter with all concerned
States and clarify their apprehensions. The States also should understand the necessity of the
programme.
(Para 9.4)
Action Taken
3.25 Department of AIDS Control has taken the matter for resuming Adolescence Education
Programme with the states where the programme is suspended. Secretary, DAC has written letter
to Chief Secretary of the states where the programme is suspended. In the current financial year,
AEP has been resumed Karnataka as a result of efforts made by DAC.

18
Further Recommendation
3.26 The Committee while appreciating the efforts made by the Department in resuming
AEP in Karnataka, would like to impress upon the Department to ensure that AEP is
resumed in the other States also in the current financial year.
XIII. HIV/AIDS Bill
Recommendation/Observation
3.27 The Committee observes that much delay has already taken place in introducing the AIDS
Bill in Parliament. The Committee recommends that the Department should proactively pursue the
matter for getting the Bill vetted from the Ministry of Law and Justice without any further any
delay so that the Bill may be introduced in the Parliament at the earliest. The Committee does not
understand the reasons why it should take more than ten years to finalise a Bill when a decision
was taken in 2002. The Bill is yet to be finalized. The delay is not justifiable when the problem
is enormous and India is third largest AIDS/HIV affected Country.
(Para 13.3)
Action Taken
3.28 The Department of AIDS Control is closely working with the Ministry of Law & Justice
to finalize the HIV/AIDS (Prevention & Control) Bill 2013. A Draft Note for Cabinet in this regard
has been prepared by the Department of AIDS Control and sent to the Ministry of Law & Justice
on 6.6.2013. On behalf of the Ministry of Law & Justice, the Dept. of Legal Affairs is to submit
its opinion and the Legislative Department is to vet the Draft Bill. This is currently under process
and once these steps have been completed the same will be sent for approval of the Cabinet.
Department of AIDS Control is ensuring that all due procedures are followed prior to tabling of
the Bill in Parliament.
Further Recommendation
3.29 The Committee feels that inspite of numerous recommendations made by it, the said
Bill seems to be stuck up for reasons best known to the Ministry. The Committee would
like the Ministry to take its recommendations with the seriousness it deserves and
recommends that the Secretary of the Department of AIDS Control should personally
monitor the progress of the Bill to ensure its introduction in the Parliament at the earliest.

REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Government on the
recommendations contained in Sixty-ninth Report on Demands for Grants (Demand No. 49) of the
Department of Health Research for the year 2013-14.
2. Action Taken Notes (ATNs) have been received from the Government in respect of the
recommendations contained in the 69
th Report. They have been categorized as follows:
(i)   Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have
been accepted by the Committee: 2.6, 3.3, 3.10, 3.17, 4.3, 6.3, 6.6, 7.4, 7.6, 9.4,
10.4 Total–11 (Chapter-I)
(ii) Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in
view of the Government’s replies: 2.7, 2.13, 6.2, 8.2, 9.2 Total–5 (Chapter-II)
(iii) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have
not been accepted by the Committee: 2.10, 3.5, 5.5, 6.9 Total–4 (Chapter-III)
(iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Government
are still awaited: 3.7, 10.3 Total–2 (Chapter-IV)
3. The details of the ATNs are discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.

2
CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES
OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
II. Budgetary Allocation
Recommendation/Observation
1.1 The Committee observes that the five new schemes/projects of the Department of Health
Research could not be made operational even during 2012-13 due to lack of approvals, though the
Department had come into existence in 2007 and become functional in 2008 with the appointment
of its first Secretary. The Committee is unable to comprehend the reasons for not getting the
required approvals even after a lapse of five years since the creation of the Department, which has
resulted in massive financial under-performance vis-à-vis the approved outlay of Rs. 4496.08 crore
for the Eleventh Plan. The Committee has been exhorting the Department to pay focused attention
for completing all pre-project formalities and obtaining necessary approvals on time so that the
budgeted funds are not locked up for want of approvals and surrendered later. The Committee is,
however, constrained to note that little attention seems to have been paid to its advice in this regard
which has resulted in persistent and substantial under-utilisation of budgeted funds. The first year
of the Twelfth Plan Period has already lapsed and the current year is the 2
nd year of the Twelfth
Plan. The Committee notes that the EFC approval for the three new Schemes were accorded, albeit
belatedly, on 22.03.2013. Two of the five new schemes have not been approved as yet. The
Committee, therefore, recommends to the Department to make more rigorous efforts and
proactively pursue approval of the remaining two schemes with the agencies concerned. The
Committee desires to be apprised of the updated status in this regard. The Committee also
recommends that a roadmap be chalked out to implement the Schemes and progress of their
implementation be monitored at highest level in the Department so that the desired outcomes are
achieved. The Committee desires that all the approved schemes should be made operational at least
during current financial year. Approvals to the remaining schemes may be accorded at the earliest
so that they may also become operational during the current year.
(Para 2.6)
Action Taken
1.2 Out of the five schemes formulated by the DHR, three schemes have already been
approved, viz. (1) Establishment of Model Rural Health Research Units (MRHRUs) in the States on
22.3.2013; (2) Establishment of Multi-disciplinary Research Units (MRUs) in Government Medical
Colleges on 27.6.2013 and (3) Establishment of a Network of Laboratories for Managing Epidemics
and Natural Calamities on 27.6.2013.
1.3 As regards the remaining two schemes, the appraisal process has been completed in
respect of the scheme regarding “Grants in Aid scheme for inter- sectoral Convergence and
Promotion and Guidance on Health Research” and the EFC meeting has been fixed on
27
th August, 2013. Regarding the scheme on “Human Resource Development for Health Research”
final appraisal note has been issued by the Planning Commission on 13.8.2013 and is being
processed for further action.
2

3
1.4 The matter is being vigorously pursued with the concerned departments and the position in
this regard is being reviewed periodically at the level of Secretary (DHR).
1.5 The Department has initiated the pre-implementation activities for all the five schemes by
inviting proposals. The Department has received requests from 64 Medical College for MRUs,
8 proposals for MRHRU and 10 proposals for virology laboratories from the various State
Governments. The DHR has received 531 concept proposals for GIA scheme and identified 30
faculty members for HRD fellowship for training within India and abroad.
1.6 Letters have been addressed to the Chief Secretaries and Principal Secretaries of Health/
Medical Education of the concerned States for completion of requisite formalities for
implementation of the shortlisted proposals in respect of the three approved schemes.
1.7 The Department plans to implement all the five schemes in the current financial year and
expect to utilize the allotted budget in full.
III. Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)
Recommendation/Observation
1.8 The Committee places on record its appreciation for the achievements of ICMR during the
Eleventh Plan. However, in view of the dynamic international health research scenario and the
current and future health challenges of the country, the ICMR has an uphill task to accomplish and
milestones to achieve. The Committee would, therefore, like the ICMR to collaborate with
internationally acclaimed institutions in the field of Health research in order to facilitate a vibrant
and relevant health research system in the country.
(Para 3.3)
Action Taken
1.9 The Department is thankful to the committee for appreciation of XI Plan achievements. As
per committee reference to international collaboration, it is to be stated that ICMR collaborates with
many international agencies like WHO, NIH, CDC, etc and has a separate International Health
Division, which looks after this work and many MOUs, bilateral, tripartite agreements with many
countries have been signed in the field of health research, that help in building and enhancing health
research environment in the country.
1.10 ICMR is involved in collaborative programmes in biomedical research between India and
other countries as well as with national & international agencies such as Ministry of Science &
Technology, Indian and foreign missions and WHO, etc. There are few specific agreements signed
by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare with other countries and rest are those signed directly
by ICMR with international organizations/ institutions such as INSERM in France, German Federal
Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) and Helmholtz Association (HGF) in Germany,
National Institutes of Health(NIH)/Centres for Disease Control (CDC) in USA, Canadian Institutes
of Health Research (CIHR) in Canada, University of Sydney and George Institute for International
Health in Australia, Medical Research Council (MRC) UK, London School of Hygiene and Tropical
Medicine (LSHTM) in UK, Karolinska Institute (KI)  in Sweden, Academy of Finland (AF).
1.11 The International Cooperation has helped the Indian scientists to establish collaborative links
with various countries for updating scientific knowledge, developing technologies and tools for
control and prevention of various diseases. It has facilitated resource generations, joint publications
and patents. It has increased research capacity building through trainings and fellowships and
helped in infrastructure development.

4
Recommendation/Observation
1.12 The Committee notes that a number of outcomes have been projected for the year 2013-14.
The Committee recommends that the desired outcomes be achieved within the targeted time-frame.
The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the achievements made vis-à-vis the targets set. The
Committee observes that it takes time to translate the research leads into tangible health products
or in application of the knowledge generated through research and a lot of work remains to be
done to bridge the gap between ‘what is known’ and ‘what is done’. Concerted efforts are required
to be made to bring research outcomes into application in the better interest of the public. The
Committee would, therefore, like to be apprised of the finding of the Committee constituted to
identify the leads from the completed extramural research projects. The Committee would also like
to be intimated of the specific health products/processes accruing from the above research projects.
(Para 3.10)
Action Taken
1.13 Leads emerging from intramural research as well as extramural projects during Eleventh
Plan are given in Annexure III. It is also to be added that a harvest group is proposed to be set-
up at the ICMR to identify the emerging leads from extramural projects and convert them into
products for public health. It is to further added that 30 new technologies (Annexure IV) ready
for transfer have been identified for the year 2013-14 and proposals have been invited from private
partners to take up these technologies to convert them into products for public use.
1.14 A fully functional Translational Research cell is already functioning in the ICMR for
translating the research leads under various subject heads into public health products. In addition,
area specific Committees have been/are being set up to be informed about the leads obtained from
completed extramural research projects.
Recommendation/Observation
1.15 The Committee observes that no single system of health care has the capacity to solve all
of the country’s health care needs. It is in this context that promotion of research in the area of
traditional medicines including Ayurveda, Naturopathy, Tibbia, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy
becomes vital for the public health care system. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
research projects on traditional medicines be pursued vigorously and the innovations accruing
therefrom be introduced into public health service within a designated time-frame. The Committee
desires to be kept apprised of the success achieved in this regard.
(Para 3.17)
Action Taken
1.16 Though research on Herbal products is the domain of AYUSH Department under MoHFW
but ICMR also pursue and support research in Traditional Medicine for different disease conditions
and has a full fledged Institute viz., Regional Medical Research Centre, Belgaum, which is specially
working in this area. Major recent achievements of the Institute are: (a) scientific validation of
Herbal Medicine, (b) role of herbal medicine in treating diseases in the region; (c) preparation of
database of ethno medicinal plants of Western Ghats; (d) strengthening human resource in the area
of herbal and traditional medicine; (e) collaboration with traditional and herbal medicine practitioners
in the region to create awareness, promote scientific temperament, collect, collate and disseminate
relevant scientific information in the area of herbal medicine.
1.17 The centre has also been successful in: (a) preparation of database, establishment of
museum and herbal garden of ethno medicinal plants of Western Ghats and creating awareness

5
among visitors regarding traditional medicine system in the region; (b) providing services to
neighboring research institutes and NGOs in respect of identification and authentication of medicinal
plants and information on collection, cultivation and utility of medicinal plants; (c) establishment of
molecular and microbiology laboratory for testing of herbals against highly resistant bacteria. The
observations of the Committee are being informed to the Department of AYUSH.
1.18 Extramural research in traditional medicine is supported through Center for Advanced
Research, ad hoc research schemes and fellowships as well as through interagency programs:
(a) Centre for Advanced Research in Yoga and Neurophysiology at Swami
Vivekananda Yoga Research Foundation, Bangalore: Studies demonstrated the
overall neurophysiological correlates of meditation offer objective support for
meditation as therapy and as an effective strategy to perform better in cognitive tasks
and to organize higher brain functions specific to education in children and adults. The
centre has produced 7 Ph. D thesis and 8 MSc dissertations and four Annual month
long training programs and 7[1 international] short term research trainings were
conducted.
(b) Advanced Centre of Reverse Pharmacology in Traditional Medicine , Kasturba
Health Society, Mumbai: Studies demonstrated  that Curcuma longa  and curcumin
have proliferative effects in the hippocampal neural progenitors in aged rats, with
cognitive improvement. Nyctanthes abor-tristis showed antimalarial efficacy and safety
in vitro  and in vivo . W. somnifera  showed good tolerability and strength-enhancement
in human volunteers.
1.19 Presently 44 ad-hoc research projects, 40 fellowship projects are ongoing in traditional
medicine.
1.20 Novel methods have been established for in vitro  propagation of Ancistrocladus heyneanus
which is reported to have  anticancer activity. Random amplified polymorphic DNA (RAPD)
fingerprinting has been done of the medicinal plant Saraca asoca (Roxb.) used for treatment of
gynaecological disorders. A study on status of Methicillin Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  (MRSA)
infections was conducted which indicated the high prevalence of Methicillin resistant
Staphylococcus  aureus  (MSSA) with Panton Valentine Leukocidin (PVL) gene and further
epidemiological studies will be done in hospitals and community levels in the region. Molecular
studies were carried out on diphtheria and diarrheal pathogens and the studies helped in control of
outbreak in the region.
1.21 The work on non-codified plants used in traditional medicine practice is ongoing and two
projects completed as a result of which established exclusive herbarium and plant repository for

Recommendation/Observation
2.1 The Committee notes that there is significant variation between the Budget Estimates and
the actual expenditure incurred in respect of the five new schemes of the Department. Persistent
mismatch between the Budget Estimates and the actual expenditure indicates that budget
formulation is being done without applying proper financial yardsticks. The Committee feels that
there is an imperative need to minimize the huge mismatch between the Budget Estimates and the
actual expenditure so as to observe the fiscal norms in letter and spirit. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that corrective measures be initiated and implemented for realistic projection of fund
requirements of the Department in future.
(Para 2.7)
Action Taken

Finance (Budget Division) for budget formulation, financial management and periodical
monitoring are duly followed by the Department of Health Research. Since all the schemes
formulated by DHR are new schemes to fulfil the objectives as per the mandate of the newly
created department, budget provisions for these schemes are being made from time to time
based on the total estimated project cost as well as the year-wise phasing of physical and
financial targets of the schemes. It is necessary to make requisite budgetary provisions for the
schemes as in the absence of this, the schemes are not taken up for consideration and
appraisal. However, despite best efforts by the Department, the schemes could not be approved
during the Eleventh Plan.

appropriateness and cost-effectiveness and essentiality of the available and new health technologies
in India. Department will like to apprise the committee that this Board will be an authority for
extracting available evidence and gather other data/information through model projects for
improving the research governance in health in India.
● The MTAB would examine the numerous and heterogeneous health technology
providers, payers and adopters in India.
● The MTAB would be empowered to make recommendations to the Government of
India after suitable health technology assessment systems through evaluation on the
appropriateness and cost effectiveness of medical technologies, interventions and
procedures for introduction/procurement in India.
● The MTAB would be set up through consultation with stake holders like technology
generators, industry, regulators, economists, user groups and experts knowledgeable
about similar medical/health technology assessment systems abroad like NICE, UK and
similar models from Canada, Australia, Thailand etc.
● The MTAB will be a part of the overall regulatory/promotional structure being
established in the DHR to accelerate indigenous production of health products/
instruments/medical devices that are vital for providing cost effective health care.
● As part of this initiative, a MOU has just been signed between the DHR and the

to identify areas for collaboration for exchange of knowledge on procedures used by

therefore, like the Department of Health Research to bring the above observation to the notice of
the authorities concerned for an appropriate decision. The Committee desires to be apprised of the
response of Department of Health and Family Welfare in this regard.
